text:
A US immigration agent has been charged with felony for allegedly hitting a man with a vehicle earlier this month in Texas, a prosecutor announced.

The prosecutor said US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer Mario Alberto Morales was indicted by a grand jury on a charge of aggravated assault with a deadly weapon.

Morales is accused of running over a Mexican national who was living in the US without legal documentation, leaving him with multiple leg fractures and a hip injury.

An ICE spokesperson dismissed the indictment as "nothing more than a political stunt" and described the allegations as "reckless and false".

The indictment comes amid the Trump administration's crackdown on illegal immigration and a series of violent incidents involving federal agents that have resulted in injuries and deaths.

If convicted, Morales faces between two to 20 years in prison for the second-degree felony, according to Harris County District Attorney Sean Teare.

Teare said Morales pursued a vehicle driven by Miguel Parra-Hernandez, a 48-year-old Mexican national who has lived in Texas for more than 30 years without legal documentation, on the morning of 10 October.

Parra-Hernandez and another occupant fled the vehicle on foot before Morales "aggressively steered his vehicle" into the Mexican national, Teare said at a news conference in Houston on Friday.

He said Parra-Hernandez had no criminal record and was not subject to a deportation order.

"Not only did he hit Mr Hernandez, he ran over both of his legs, leaving him seriously injured and hospitalised to this day," Teare said.

Morales then called 911 to report that Parra-Hernandez had hit his car.

Teare said that ICE was allegedly pursuing a man named Jose Mendoza-Cervantes, a Mexican national and undocumented immigrant, who has apparently been dead for nine years.

Immediately after the incident, an ICE spokesperson told the BBC's US media partner CBS News that Parra-Hernandez had run in front of the immigration agent's vehicle.

Following the indictment, ICE rejected the allegations brought by the grand jury - a panel of citizens empowered to determine whether there was sufficient evidence to bring criminal charges.

"This is nothing more than a political stunt by Houston sanctuary politicians," an ICE spokesperson said in a statement to the BBC.

"Allegations that ICE struck Miguel Parra-Hernandez intentionally are RECKLESS and FALSE," the spokesperson said, adding that the men and women of ICE "are entrusted with upholding the rule of law and are held to the highest standards of professionalism, integrity, and ethical conduct".

text:
An Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer has been indicted by a Texas grand jury after striking a man with his vehicle in Houston earlier this month, prosecutors said.

Officer Mario Alberto Morales was driving a 2025 Jeep Grand Cherokee on Oct. 10 at about 7:30 a.m. when he initiated a stop on a vehicle driven by Miguel Parra-Hernandez, a Mexican national who has been living in the United States for 30 years, Harris County District Attorney Sean Teare said at a news conference on Oct. 30.

Parra-Hernandez and another occupant fled on foot, and video footage showed Morales striking Parra-Hernandez with his vehicle, Teare said.

"As you can clearly see, Morales aggressively steered his vehicle into Parra-Hernandez. Not only did he hit Mr. Hernandez, he ran over both of his legs, leaving him seriously injured and hospitalized to this day," Teare said, adding that Parra-Hernandez is recovering in a rehabilitation facility.

Morales was indicted on a count of second-degree aggravated assault with a deadly weapon, Teare said. He could face between 2 and 20 years in prison if convicted. The officer is not yet in custody, Teare said.

Morales’ attorney, David Lindenmuth, said the collision was a tragic accident, not a crime.

"They indicted an accident," said Lindenmuth, who spent 23 years as a state and federal prosecutor in Texas before moving to defense work. "It was an unfortunate incident, but it was strictly an accident. It was not a criminal event, and they've turned it into a crime just to have a political whipping boy."

Morales was doing what any officer would do, Lindenmuth said, closing the distance on a man who had fled a lawful stop. Another vehicle appeared directly ahead of Morales, he said, forcing a split-second choice between turning and hitting it, and that is when the collision happened. He said he would not speculate on exactly how it unfolded until he had seen all the evidence.

But he said it was clear Morales never meant to hurt anyone. "He didn’t just all of a sudden become a maniac that was trying to hurt people," Lindenmuth said. If Parra-Hernandez had stayed in the truck as the law requires, he added, none of it would have happened.

Lindenmuth accused Teare of deciding the case within days of the crash, when the district attorney began speaking publicly about what the surveillance video showed. "It was like it was a foregone conclusion," he said. "He’s already made up his mind."

In a statement to USA TODAY, a spokesperson for ICE called the indictment a "political stunt," and said local government doesn't have the authority to investigate the case.

“Allegations that ICE struck Miguel Parra-Hernandez intentionally are RECKLESS and FALSE. The men and women of ICE are entrusted with upholding the rule of law and are held to the highest standards of professionalism, integrity, and ethical conduct," the spokesperson said.

What happened in ICE crash? Video, 911 audio released

Prosecutors on Oct. 30 released footage from Morales' body camera and a surveillance video, along with audio from Morales' call to 911.

The encounter unfolded the morning of Oct. 10 along a commercial stretch of Clay Road in northwest Harris County. ICE officers had been trailing a white pickup truck and, when they moved to pull it over, two men jumped out and ran, surveillance video shows.

"What happened next shocked our entire community," Teare said.

The video shows Morales' SUV driving over a median in pursuit of a man running on foot.

"I've got a runner," he says on the body camera footage.

The SUV drives into a parking area and closes in on the man running. The view of the impact is blocked by a truck parked there. Just afterward, Parra-Hernandez can be heard moaning and is seen lying on the ground as Morales gets out of the SUV. In the 911 audio, Morales tells a dispatcher, "I tried to get around him and he hit my car."

Two men Morales had detained earlier were sitting handcuffed in the back of the Jeep, officials said. Parra Hernandez’s leg was broken in three places, and he was taken to a hospital in ICE custody.

ICE said Parra Hernandez "ran in front of the vehicle," and called claims that he was hit on purpose reckless and false.

Teare said the officer drove the Jeep away before it could be impounded, erasing crash data stored in the vehicle. ICE has also begun deporting witnesses in the case, Teare said on Oct. 30.

Teare said Morales was hired by ICE in August 2025 as part of its surge into Democrat-run cities. The district attorney said he had serious concerns about the qualifications of ICE hires and how much training they have been given.

"I've reviewed thousands of job applications and resumes for law enforcement officers from around this state and I'm not familiar with a single agency that would've hired this person based on his past," he said of Morales.

Teare said he hopes the indictment "sends a loud and clear message to every ICE officer who feels they have a free pass to terrorize our streets. The time to stop is now. And if you don't, you will be held accountable."

The Department of Homeland Security did not respond to questions about the district attorney's accusations around the investigation.

Lindenmuth decried Teare's comments about his client's record. "I have his resume, and what it shows is a public servant, nothing but a public servant," he said. "This is not a man who deserves those kinds of comments."

Morales, 33, is a former service member and paratrooper who has spent most of his working life in or around law enforcement, Lindenmuth said. He has "never been in trouble before," and is a pastor at his church, he added.

“This is a good guy,” Lindenmuth said.

Victim struck by ICE had no criminal history, prosecutor says

Parra-Hernandez, 48, is an unauthorized immigrant in the United States from Mexico and had no criminal history, deportation order or any immigration proceedings at the time of the crash, Teare said.

Parra-Hernandez is a construction worker who was on his way to work that morning, according to FIEL Houston, an immigrant advocacy group.

After the incident, ICE said its officers had been looking for a different man, whom the agency described as a "public safety threat," and that officers had seen him get into the truck.

The man ICE said they were looking for "has apparently been dead for nine years," Teare said on Oct. 30.

Multiple ICE operations have led to injury and death

The Houston case is not the first in which what ICE describes as a targeted enforcement operation has ended in serious injury or death.

Two days earlier, on Oct. 8, an officer shot Oscar Belgal, 28, in New York City’s Marble Hill neighborhood as he sat in his car with his 5-year-old son in the back seat. At least one officer fired seven rounds after Belgal began pulling forward, hitting Belgal below his left ear. The boy was not hurt.

In July, an ICE officer in Houston’s East End shot and killed Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, 52, as he drove his construction crew to a job site. The agency said he tried to run over an officer – an account his family and the men in his van dispute. DHS later acknowledged he was not the man officers were looking for, saying only that he resembled their target.

In Chicago last year, federal prosecutors dropped charges against Marimar Martinez, a U.S. citizen shot five times by a Border Patrol agent, after video showed the agent steering into her car rather than the other way around. That agent, too, was accused of driving his vehicle away before it could be examined, taking it to Maine.

A federal judge in Chicago separately found the government’s accounts of its agents’ use of force against protesters and journalists not credible.

title: ICE agent appears to shove woman filming Morristown raid as local police look on
description: The town says officers were providing crowd control, not assisting immigration enforcement; mayor defends police response.
text:
This story has been updated with a response from the Department of Homeland Security.

A Morristown sidewalk was the scene of a heated confrontation Thursday morning when a federal immigration officer appeared to shove a woman who was shooting video of an enforcement action while a Morristown police officer stood watching.

The video , posted on social media, shows an unmasked immigration officer wearing a helmet and military-style uniform marked “POLICE ICE” but no badge, noticing the woman coming closer. He approaches her swiftly, and then the camera is jostled.

“You’re in the crime scene…get out!” the federal agent says.

“Did you just assault me? …this is a public sidewalk,” responds the woman, surrounded by activists who decried the raid as an attempt to terrorize and intimidate the community. A school bus passes in the background.

A moment earlier, a Morristown officer politely asked onlookers to keep their distance. The mayor’s office later issued a statement saying town police had responded to an ICE request for crowd control at 8 Abbett Ave., where 10 to 15 bystanders had gathered around 9 am.

Per state law and departmental policy, Morristown police “do not participate in or assist with ICE immigration enforcement operations, and officers were assigned to the scene solely to ensure the safety of residents, bystanders, and everyone in the surrounding area,” said Mayor Tim Dougherty’s statement, asserting police had no prior knowledge that ICE was coming.

On Friday a spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security called the woman’s assault accusation “categorically FALSE.”

As part of an ongoing investigation by the U.S. Attorney’s Office, the DHS statement said, ICE agents were conducting a targeted enforcement operation to arrest a “criminal illegal alien from El Salvador and MS-13 gang member. An anti-ICE agitator refused to observe officers’ lawful commands. Officers relied on their training to safely control the situation without incident.”

It was the latest in a year-long series of ICE sweeps in Morristown that started with January arrests of 11 people, including a high school student at a laundromat and a father separated from his 6-year-old daughter. Thursday’s episode appears to be the closest encounter so far between ICE and Morristown police.

‘IT’S MIND-BLOWING’

Residents had spread a morning alert to Latino parents about an ICE SUV spotted near a school bus stop at the corner of Abbett and Emmett avenues, said Karen Walsh of Morristown Together , a grassroots watchdog group.

“It’s mind blowing to me that on this side of town, my privileged friends are getting their kids off to school, letting their kids walk to their bus by themselves. But on the other side of the town, the same people in their community, the same people that they go to school with, are being terrorized. Like, how is this possible? We can’t do this,” Walsh said.

Dougherty echoed her concerns.

“These continued ICE raids here in Morristown and in communities throughout our country have led to devastating consequences including the deaths of several people during clashes between residents and ICE agents, and our priority in this matter was to stop something terrible like that from happening,” the mayor said.

He defended Morristown police for acting “appropriately and professionally” to protect the public and maintain peace, and said the community stands “against President Trump’s attacks on immigrants.”

“We will continue working with immigration advocates to ensure that residents know their rights and have access to legal counsel, and our officers remain committed to protecting and serving all members of our community,” Dougherty said.

The DHS reiterated its stance that criminal illegal aliens are not welcome in the U.S. under President Trump and DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin.

DHS said ICE officers receive training in de-escalation and use of force , and warned that anyone who assaults or obstructs them could face arrest and prosecution. The agency alleged a coordinated campaign of violence against federal law enforcement, citing increases of more than 1,600 percent in assaults, 3,300 percent in vehicular attacks and 8,000 percent in death threats.

A second video online purports to show an Hispanic man confronting the same federal agent, demanding to know why he was separating families. The Hispanic man identifies himself as a U.S. citizen, and then is warned to stay clear of a “crime scene.”

“Don’t test me…you may be an American, but you cannot violate the law,” the agent says.

The woman shooting the other video, whose identity is unclear, pressed the federal officer for his name, noting Morristown police had names on their uniforms.

“I am not a police officer,” the agent advised. “I am a federal agent. I am the most well known officer here. I don’t hide anything.”

When told to stop shaking, the woman responded she had been “bodychecked” and intended to file an assault complaint. “Where’s your injury?” the federal officer challenged.

He gave his “identifier” number. “That’s all you get.”

“So you’re Gestapo…you’re Secret Police,” the woman said. Eventually, the federal agent returned to the enforcement action.

“Have a nice day,” he told the woman.

Morristown has a long history of people stepping forward in pivotal moments.

    and carrying on the spirit that’s defined this town since its earliest days.

text:
SAN FRANCISCO—A federal court of appeals today denied the government’s request to stay a district court order, a move that could restore Temporary Protected Status (TPS) protections for hundreds of thousands of Venezuelan TPS holders.

The ruling by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit involves a district court order issued on September 5, 2025, in National TPS Alliance v. Mullin, which found that former Secretary Kristi Noem exceeded her authority when she issued orders vacating a TPS extension that had been granted to Venezuela and instead terminating the country’s designation. The district court order had been subject to an unreasoned stay issued by the U.S. Supreme Court on its shadow docket on October 3, 2025. That stay is set to expire next Friday, November 6.

The Ninth Circuit ruling means that, absent further intervention by the Supreme Court, hundreds of thousands of Venezuelans who were stripped of TPS would see their status reinstated on November 6 while litigation challenging the vacatur and termination continues.

In the period since the Supreme Court stayed the district court’s protections, thousands of Venezuelan TPS holders have been detained, deported, and even killed. Many have also faced separation from their American children, and some have been sent to third countries to which they had no prior connection.

Evidence before the Ninth Circuit included declarations from Venezuelan TPS holders about the harms that they suffered after the termination went into effect.

“I was deported to Liberia after I lost my TPS status. I had no prior connection to Liberia or anywhere else in Africa,” said Carlos Sanchez Villa, in a declaration filed with the court. “It felt like something out of a horror movie, but unfortunately, for me it was real.”

“Immigration officials deported me to Mexico, where I was put on a bus, driven across the country, and dumped on the street in a city near the border with Guatemala. I was given no shelter or assistance and left to fend for myself in a dangerous country that is not my own,” said Rita di Peri Castellano.

Jose Palma, Coordinator of the National TPS Alliance, said: “In the face of this administration’s brutal assault, today’s victory renews our strength to fight for the rights won by previous generations of immigrants: to be able to live and work without fear in the place we call home.”

The plaintiffs are represented by the National Day Laborer Organizing Network (NDLON), the ACLU Foundations of Northern California and Southern California, the UCLA Miñana Family Center for Immigration Law and Policy (Miñana Center), and Haitian Bridge Alliance (HBA).

At the Ninth Circuit, the government had argued that the Supreme Court’s June 2026 ruling in Mullin v. Dahlia Doe deprived federal courts of jurisdiction to review plaintiffs’ challenge. TPS holders countered that courts retain authority to consider whether the Secretary’s Venezuela- related orders exceeded her authority under the statute.

Jessica Bansal, TPS Counsel with the National Day Laborer Organizing Network and counsel for Plaintiffs, said: “Secretary Noem’s illegal termination of Venezuela’s TPS stripped over half a million refugees of lawful immigration status and devastated the Venezuelan migrant community. Today, federal courts refused the administration’s invitation to close their eyes to her lawlessness.”

Emi MacLean, senior staff attorney at the ACLU of Northern California, said: “The Trump administration has waged a xenophobic attack on immigrants, targeting TPS holders from day one in the largest de-documentation campaign in this country’s history. The district court recognized that this administration cannot exercise authority it does not have. This country was built on checks and balances; that court order must mean something.”

text:
The Trump administration is still detaining pregnant migrant youth in a region of Texas where a lack of specialized obstetric care can be life threatening for them, an investigation by The Texas Newsroom and The California Newsroom has found. The practice continues despite vocal concern from current and former government officials, and from members of Congress.

Government records show that in the first ten months of the policy, four of the 21 pregnant girls placed in the region had to be transferred out of state to receive specialized medical care, including at least one abortion, that is unavailable in Texas.

"The first time that happened should have been a wake-up call for the administration, and they should have stopped placing kids in any remote area where they can't get care," said Jen Smyers, who during the Biden administration helped oversee the Office of Refugee Resettlement (ORR), which is responsible for migrant youth who are apprehended by immigration authorities without a parent or guardian.

She called the policy to send all pregnant children to South Texas "enraging."

This spring, The Texas Newsroom and The California Newsroom published a joint investigation revealing the administration's policy of detaining pregnant unaccompanied minors as young as 13, at least half of whom were pregnant as a result of rape, at a single shelter in the city of San Benito near Texas' border with Mexico. The investigation detailed serious concerns that health experts inside and outside the government had raised about the policy, given that adolescent pregnancies are inherently high risk and there is a lack of specialized obstetric care in the region.

Since then, the administration has denied that there is such a policy and said it is ensuring that the girls have access to the care they need.

In an email in September the Department of Health and Human Services, which oversees ORR, wrote that "ORR's policies for placing children in its custody into care provider facilities are based on child welfare best practices in order to provide a safe environment and place the child in the least restrictive setting appropriate for the child's needs. This is especially true for expectant minors in ORR care."

Yet the administration's own records, as well as interviews with multiple government officials, suggest otherwise.

The documents, which were obtained through a public records request, show that ORR explicitly directed its staff in July 2025 to send all pregnant youth to the shelter in San Benito, just outside Brownsville at the extreme southern tip of Texas.

Several months later, internal agency data showed that pregnant girls started being sent to a different shelter nearby instead, according to three ORR officials who asked not to be named because they feared retaliation.

Forty-eight Democratic members of Congress demanded transparency about the policy in a pointed letter to the Department of Health and Human Services back in April. They received a response in September from an assistant secretary at HHS, Alex J. Adams, who wrote that ORR "does not make placement decisions for pregnant youth based on a blanket rule or one-size-fits-all approach" and that it "takes seriously its responsibility to protect the health, safety, dignity, and well-being of every unaccompanied alien child in its custody."

HHS did not respond to requests for comment about the discrepancy between the statements in Adams' letter and the government's own records.

"Obviously, they're not being honest about their policy," said U.S. Rep. Joaquin Castro, a Democrat from San Antonio, whose office authored the letter to HHS.

"It's irresponsible that they would wait several months to respond to basic questions about the care of some of the most vulnerable people within the system," Castro said, adding that the administration failed to explain "what seems to be an informal but strict policy of sending these girls to deep South Texas, which lacks the medical care that the girls need."

Unaccompanied migrant children have historically been placed in shelters across the United States, but this summer, the Trump administration began detaining far more of them in Texas. According to internal reports provided independently by two of the ORR officials who spoke on the condition of anonymity, 95% of the roughly 300 children apprehended by immigration officials in September were placed in detention in Texas, up from 45% in June.

Advocates for unaccompanied migrant children, former government officials, and some members of Congress have criticized the move, arguing that the state is not prepared to handle an influx of vulnerable children, some of whom need special care.

The fact that ORR has had to transfer several pregnant unaccompanied minors out of Texas to receive medical care, one congress member says, proves their point.

"If the government had to fly or transport these pregnant children across the country to get them the medical care they need, why on earth did it deliberately send them to Texas in the first place?" said U.S. Rep. Judy Chu, a Democrat from Southern California who signed the congressional inquiry letter to HHS.

"If there is a 13-year-old girl who has survived rape," she said, "she should be met with compassion, safety and appropriate medical care. Instead, this administration is placing children like her in a state where they will be deprived of access to basic healthcare. It's dangerous, and it's cruel, and there's no excuse for treating children this way."

Government records contradict Trump administration's claims

Unlike Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), which detains migrant adults and families in large, prison-like facilities, ORR holds unaccompanied children in group or foster homes overseen by private contractors. Laws, agency regulations and court orders require that the children receive comprehensive healthcare and appropriate education while they're detained.

In an emailed statement last month, HHS said that placing children in Texas is "operationally efficient" and that ORR's facilities in the state "provide all requirements and more." But records obtained through a public information request cast doubt on that assertion.

The records show between July of 2025, when ORR began placing pregnant girls in South Texas, and May of 2026, four of them had to be transferred to other states to receive medical treatment.

That's roughly one in five of the 21 pregnant girls the agency placed in the region in that time frame, according to one of the ORR officials who requested anonymity.

In detailed notes for one of those cases, ORR staff wrote that a pregnant 12-year-old girl was transferred from the Rio Grande Valley to a shelter in New York on the recommendation of ORR's division of health. The records note that the child needed access to specialists whose availability in South Texas is "extremely limited."

In a note for another case, staff wrote that a pregnant girl was transferred to California due to an unspecified "high risk medical need." In at least one case, a girl was transferred out of Texas because she had requested an abortion, the records show.

Marsha Griffin, a retired professor of pediatrics at the University of Texas Rio Grande Valley School of Medicine, said such outcomes were inevitable. Griffin said the shelters have very few medical staff on hand and the region does not have enough specialized obstetricians.

"Young girls who are pregnant, especially those from 10 to 14 years of age, are automatically a high-risk population," said Griffin, who oversaw medical students volunteering in ORR facilities in South Texas.

Internal communications, also obtained through a public records request, show that officials in ORR's own division of health warned the agency's leadership about the lack of pregnancy-related healthcare in the Rio Grande Valley.

"Texas has one of the worst rates of maternal mortality in the U.S.," wrote Joanna Gaines, who at the time was ORR's acting health director, in a July 18, 2025, email to Melissa Johnston, the agency's head of operations. She added that the state "lack[s] access to quality perinatal healthcare" and that the Rio Grande Valley's Cameron County "has one of the higher rates of infant mortality in Texas."

Four days later, ORR issued a directive to begin placing "any pregnant children" at the Urban Strategies San Benito shelter in Cameron County.

Tracey Wilkinson, a pediatrician in Indiana who specializes in reproductive healthcare access for minors, said that even if the government is transferring children to get medical care, waiting until they need it puts them in danger.

"When you're talking about labor or pregnancy complications, every minute counts," Wilkinson said. "If it was a medical emergency that required this young person to be transported out of the state, the risk to her survival would be lower for no reason other than she was placed in the middle of nowhere, far away from medical care."

"They are trying to deliberately mislead Congress members"

Shortly after The Texas Newsroom and The California Newsroom revealed the Trump administration's policy of detaining pregnant migrant youth in Texas, Castro launched an inquiry into the practice. He soon arranged a visit to the San Benito shelter.

But by the time of his visit on April 7, internal agency data showed that ORR had stopped placing newly detained children with known pregnancies at the facility, said the three officials who spoke to NPR on the condition of anonymity. Instead, the agency was sending them to a different shelter, in Los Fresnos, just 13 miles away.

Castro said he was not told of the change at the time of his visit, nor was it mentioned in ORR's formal response to the congressional inquiry last month.

In a recent interview, he described ORR's handling of his visit to the San Benito shelter as "very secretive" and said he was not allowed to see or speak with any of the children there.

Chu, the Congresswoman from California, said she believed the Trump administration made the location change in order to "deliberately mislead Congress members as well as the public from really knowing where these pregnant children have been."

An HHS spokesperson did not respond to that allegation, or to earlier questions about the location change, writing only that "there have been no operational changes regarding the placement of pregnant unaccompanied children."

Compass Connections, the San Antonio-based nonprofit that operates the shelter in Los Fresnos where pregnant girls are now being held, is one of the largest ORR contractors; it has been awarded over $1.9 billion in federal grants to house and care for unaccompanied minors over the past four years, according to figures the government has released on USASpending.gov. Asked whether it agreed to accept all pregnant unaccompanied children at the Los Fresnos shelter and how they're being cared for there, the company referred the newsrooms to HHS.

In his letter responding to the congressional inquiry, Assistant Secretary Adams wrote that "placement and transfer decisions are individualized and consider the child's safety, medical and behavioral health needs, pregnancy-related needs, available services, legal access, family unity, least restrictive placement requirements, and the best interest of the child."

"In California, they would have more access to all reproductive healthcare"

California Congress members and advocates said the state offers much more support for pregnant girls in federal custody than they can receive in Texas.

As the Trump administration has withdrawn federal support for legal representation of unaccompanied children — and at the same time streamlined the process of deporting them — the state of California and several of its cities and counties have ramped up funding for their own legal services programs for undocumented minors.

"Pregnant unaccompanied children have rights to medical care, safety, family unity and due process, but those rights mean little without a lawyer to defend them," said Marion "Mickey" Donovan-Kaloust, director of legal services at Immigrant Defenders in Los Angeles. "California's support systems can provide pregnant unaccompanied children with the stability, dignity and specialized care they need to be safe and thrive."

In addition to concerns about their access to healthcare and legal services, advocates allege that the Trump administration is knowingly putting pregnant children at risk to advance an ideological goal: denying them access to abortions by placing them in Texas, where abortion is virtually banned.

Current federal regulations require the government to move detained minors who request abortions to states where it's legal. In January, the Trump administration announced it plans to rescind that rule, though it hasn't yet done so.

An HHS spokesperson said in February that claims the department is attempting to restrict unaccompanied children's access to abortion are "completely inaccurate."

Congressman Gil Cisneros, a Democrat from Southern California who also signed the inquiry letter to HHS, said, "In California, they would have more access to all reproductive healthcare, and then they could make decisions based on discussions with their healthcare professional and what's best for them."

Mark Betancourt is a freelance journalist based in Washington, D.C.

text:
Lawmakers Argue DOJ Is Encouraging the Court to Ignore Federal Statutes and Grant AI Companies a Blanket Exemption to Copyright Laws

Washington, D.C. (October XX, 2026)— Today, Rep. Jamie Raskin, Ranking Member of the House Judiciary Committee, Rep. Jerrold Nadler, Ranking Member of the Subcommittee on the Administrative State, Regulatory Reform, and Antitrust, and Rep. Hank Johnson, Ranking Member of the Subcommittee on Courts, Intellectual Property, Artificial Intelligence, and the Internet, submitted an amicus brief opposing the Department of Justice’s (DOJ) bizarre argument that there is some sort of national security exception to current copyright law that allows AI companies to train their models on copyrighted work, including New York Times journalism, without compensation.

The brief, filed in the Southern District of New York in In re OpenAI, Inc. Copyright Infringement Litigation, reminds the court that the arguments in DOJ’s brief violate the plain text of the Copyright Act, which does not contain any national security exception to allow private companies free and unfettered use of copyrighted materials.

“National security is not a fair use factor under the Copyright Act. […] To treat it as a fair use consideration would be to add to the Copyright Act a national security exception that Congress did not enact,” the lawmakers wrote.

The dispute stems from allegations that OpenAI and Microsoft used New York Times journalism without permission to build AI products that compete with the newspaper. On September 1, DOJ intervened to support AI companies, arguing that restricting their use of copyrighted texts would threaten American AI development and national security. DOJ has no jurisdiction in this matter, and its filing reportedly surprised even the government’s own copyright and patent experts(link is external).

Copyright law allows some uses of copyrighted work without permission, under a set of rules known as “fair use.” But before “fair use” doctrine applies, the courts must consider the circumstances—including how the work was used, how much was copied and whether the copying harms the market for the original work. Instead, DOJ is inviting the court to jettison federal statutes and case law and rule that AI companies have special rights based on specious national security claims.

The lawmakers urge the court to reject DOJ’s arguments and uphold legal protections that ensure fair compensation to millions of American content creators including writers, journalists, and artists.

text:
Community members, healthcare workers, and elected officials are demanding answers after Oakland’s Highland Hospital discharged a man into the custody of federal immigration agents without confirming the agents had a warrant authorizing his detention.

At a tense Board of Supervisors meeting Tuesday evening, officials with Alameda Health System, which operates Highland Hospital, acknowledged that hospital staff never received a copy of a warrant from U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents who brought the man to the hospital earlier this month.

The revelation has raised questions about whether the public hospital system followed its own protocols and Alameda County’s sanctuary policies restricting local cooperation with federal civil immigration enforcement. It also prompted an angry response from Supervisor Nikki Fortunato Bas, who said Tuesday that hospital officials had previously assured her ICE had presented the necessary documentation.

“I am just very upset right now because I had conversations with representatives who should have known the answer to my question, which was whether or not ICE legally had that person in custody… and I was told affirmatively that they did see a warrant,” Fortunato Bas said.

The man, identified by ICE as Eduardo Antonio Ruiz-Garcia, was arrested Oct. 16 in Emeryville during what federal officials described as a targeted immigration enforcement operation. According to immigration advocates, ICE agents used excessive force during the arrest, fracturing six of his ribs.

Ruiz-Garcia was hospitalized at Highland for six days, during which ICE agents remained at the hospital, according to Nikolas De Bremaeker, managing attorney at Centro Legal de la Raza, an Oakland-based nonprofit that provides legal aid to immigrants. After he was discharged, he was returned to federal immigration custody.

Jason Sweeney, a spokesperson for the U.S. Department of Homeland Security, which oversees ICE, denied allegations of excessive force. In a statement to The Oaklandside, Sweeney alleged that Ruiz-Garcia “attempted to assault officers” and refused their commands.

“Officers relied on their training to control the situation,” Sweeney wrote.

ICE also claimed Ruiz-Garcia had disclosed a preexisting injury from falling off a ladder two days before his arrest. The Oaklandside could not independently verify the cause of his injuries.

As of Friday morning, Ruiz-Garcia remains at an immigration detention facility in the Central Valley, according to De Bremaeker.

Centro Legal worked with a pro bono attorney to file a habeas corpus petition in federal court challenging the legality of his detention. The petition is currently pending, De Bremaeker said.

What happened at Highland Hospital?

At Tuesday’s joint meeting of the Alameda County Board of Supervisors and the Alameda Health System Board of Trustees, hospital administrators outlined their procedures for responding to immigration enforcement activities.

Under California Senate Bill 81, enacted last year, healthcare facilities must establish procedures for handling requests from federal immigration authorities to access patients, confidential information, and nonpublic areas of hospitals. The law also prohibits medical staff from sharing a patient’s immigration status or birthplace with immigration authorities, unless the patient consents, or there is a valid court order or search warrant requiring it.

Kayla Bowen, associate general counsel for Alameda Health System, explained that the hospital’s protocols direct employees to refer requests from immigration authorities to an administrator on call, who can consult legal counsel to review documentation and determine the appropriate response. The intent, she said, is to allow medical workers to focus on patient care, rather than navigate complicated legal questions involving immigration enforcement.

But the discussion took a contentious turn when Fortunato Bas pressed hospital administrators on whether ICE agents had presented an arrest warrant when they brought Ruiz-Garcia to Highland Hospital.

Bowen said hospital personnel had requested documentation but never received it.

Bowen emphasized that hospital officials are not responsible for determining whether federal immigration agents have lawfully arrested someone.

“As a hospital, it’s not our determination of that legality of custody,” she said. “We are going to provide care. We’re not going to hold up the provision of care to assess for that.”

Alameda Health System officials said providing care to a person already in ICE custody does not constitute cooperation or collusion with civil immigration enforcement.

Still, Fortunato Bas questioned why hospital staff had not taken more steps to verify ICE’s authority or involve legal advocates before allowing ICE to take the patient when he was discharged.

James Jackson, CEO of Alameda Health System, acknowledged that he had previously given Fortunato Bas incorrect information about the documentation.

“It was my understanding that we did have the proper documentation,” Jackson told Fortunato Bas.

He apologized for the misunderstanding but denied allegations that hospital administrators intentionally assisted ICE agents.

“There was never any intent to collude,” Jackson said. “If we did not have the documentation that we should have had, that’s a part of our process, and we will learn, and we will be better.”

Advocates say ICE interfered with medical treatment

Immigration advocates and medical workers also raised concerns about how ICE agents behaved during the man’s hospitalization.

De Bremaeker, who helped coordinate Ruiz-Garcia’s emergency legal response, said several ICE agents were present throughout his hospital stay, including an agent whom he said injured Ruiz-Garcia during the arrest.

“He even sat on the foot of his bed, grinning at him,” De Bremaeker told The Oaklandside.

According to De Bremaeker, agents also attempted to influence medical decisions, asked hospital employees for private patient information, and refused to loosen Ruiz-Garcia’s handcuffs while medical workers treated him. The restraints, De Bremaeker said, caused additional pain and interfered with his treatment.

“As far as I know, he was able to receive the necessary treatment, but the treatment, as it was given, was definitely suboptimal,” he said.

At Tuesday’s meeting, De Bremaeker urged hospital administrators to establish clearer procedures for situations in which federal agents interfere with medical care or patient privacy. Alameda Health System officials said their existing protocols allow staff to ask immigration agents to leave treatment areas and require employees to escalate disputes to an on-call administrator.

But De Bremaeker said those policies had not adequately protected Ruiz-Garcia.

He called for stronger communication between the hospital and Centro Legal so immigration attorneys can intervene quickly when ICE shows up with an in-custody patient. Hospital officials acknowledged that Centro Legal had been contacted later than it should have been.

De Bremaeker told The Oaklandside that his organization has been in contact with Rep. Lateefah Simon, Rep. Aisha Wahab, and Sen. Alex Padilla about seeking a federal inquiry into ICE’s conduct inside hospitals.

DHS did not specifically address the allegations of interference with medical treatment in its statement to The Oaklandside. Sweeney said agents routinely accompany people in federal custody to hospitals for monitoring.

“If we have a detainee we need to take to the hospital for medical care, we have officers accompany them for their monitoring, safety of the staff, and the public. This is standard procedure for all law enforcement agencies,” he said.

ICE violated Alameda County’s sanctuary policies, advocates say

Another point of contention at Tuesday’s meeting was the presence of ICE vehicles and agents on hospital property during Ruiz-Garcia’s six-day hospitalization.

Earlier this year, Alameda County adopted an “ICE-free zones” policy prohibiting the use of county property as staging areas, processing locations, or operational spaces for civil immigration enforcement officials.

During Tuesday’s meeting, multiple medical workers and community observers said they witnessed ICE agents use a loading dock near Highland’s morgue to park vehicles and change shifts while guarding Ruiz-Garcia. They also criticized the Alameda County Sheriff’s Office, which provides security at Highland, for reportedly helping ICE agents move throughout the facility.

Alameda Health System administrators disputed advocates’ characterization of the loading dock as a staging area.

Bowen said ICE vehicles had initially parked in a garage accessible to patients, visitors, and employees. Hospital staff later moved them to a less visible area after demonstrators gathered outside the facility, raising concerns about access to the garage and hospital operations.

The decision, Bowen said, was intended to minimize interactions between immigration agents and other people at the hospital, not facilitate enforcement activities.

“With the presence of protesters outside and within the parking garage, there was a disruption to hospital operations, and we wanted to limit any disruption for the ability for patients to access care,” she added.

Bowen said sheriff’s deputies helped ensure agents traveled only between Ruiz-Garcia’s hospital room and their vehicles.

But some medical staff and immigration advocates argued that allowing agents to park, change shifts, and escort Ruiz-Garcia out of the hospital effectively amounted to collusion.

“We can’t be a sanctuary on paper and then hand over our community members to ICE agents to take away,” said Claire Chalmers, a registered nurse who has worked in Highland’s intensive care unit for nearly a decade.

Chalmers said she witnessed sheriff’s deputies escorting ICE agents around the facility. She also criticized what she described as inadequate training for nurses caring for people in immigration custody.

In an interview with The Oaklandside, Alameda County Sheriff’s Office spokesperson Sgt. Robero Morales defended the deputies’ actions. He said the sheriff’s office maintains a 24-hour presence at Highland under a contract with the hospital and was focused on ensuring the safety of patients, staff, and visitors.

He also said deputies would not question another law enforcement agency’s authority to hold someone already in its custody.

“We would never ask another law enforcement agency if they have the authority to do what they’re doing,” he said. “We would expect, we would hope, that a law enforcement agency has their reasonings for holding this person.”

Asked whether deputies had discussed ICE’s authority to detain Ruiz-Garcia, Morales said, “That conversation did not occur and will not occur.”

Deputies, he said, have no authority to interfere with ICE’s detention of Ruiz-Garcia.

Healthcare workers are demanding stronger protections and better training

During nearly an hour of public comment, dozens of hospital workers, immigrant rights advocates, and community members denounced Alameda Health System’s handling of the situation.

Nora Goodfriend-Koven said her daughter, a clinician at Highland, reported that roughly half of her pregnant patients missed routine prenatal appointments during the period when ICE agents were at the hospital. She attributed the absences to patients’ fear of immigration enforcement.

Other healthcare employees described similar experiences at clinics outside Highland. Carrie Schiff, a nurse practitioner at La Clínica’s San Antonio Neighborhood Health Center in Oakland, said approximately half of her patients missed appointments during the same week.

Some healthcare workers also challenged administrators’ assertions that existing training and written guidance were sufficient.

Gabby Wimer, a second-year emergency medicine resident at Highland, said staff had repeatedly requested hands-on training and simulations to prepare for encounters with ICE agents.

“It’s laughable to say that it’s not the hospital’s responsibility, or they’re not capable of determining if someone’s in lawful detention because a bunch of healthcare workers without legal training have been able to do that, as have a bunch of community activists,” she said.

“We need to have a strong response in place so that people can trust that Highland and all of AHS will be there for them,” Wimer added.

Councilmember Charlene Wang, whose district includes Highland Hospital, also called for an investigation into the incident and a review of the hospital’s immigration enforcement protocols. In a statement Wednesday, Wang urged Alameda Health System to publicly release the findings of a critical incident investigation within 30 days.

“Highland is a place of healing and recovery. ICE’s presence there is the opposite of that,” Wang said. “Patients and families should be able to walk into a public hospital without fear.”

Alameda County Supervisor Nate Miley also called for a written report establishing what happened, whether hospital personnel followed existing procedures, and what changes might prevent similar incidents.

Miley also cautioned against confrontations with federal immigration agents, warning that an escalation could provoke a federal response.

“The Trump administration is just looking for an excuse to invoke the Insurrection Act,” he said. “If our sheriff’s department gets into an altercation with ICE, trust me, Trump will come in and… have federal troops here in Oakland and Alameda County. I don’t want that.”

Fortunato Bas called on hospital administrators to work directly with medical workers, immigration attorneys, and community advocates to strengthen training and establish clearer procedures for future encounters with ICE. She also raised the possibility of seeking emergency court intervention when questions arise about the legality of a patient’s detention.

Fortunato Bas said she also plans to have Alameda Health System provide a report about its handling of the incident to the board’s Alameda County Together for All ad hoc committee at a public meeting in the coming weeks.

text:
In a win for voters, the Ninth Circuit denied the Trump administration’s request to resume a voter fraud investigation that targeted alleged noncitizens in nine states during midterm elections.

The order leaves in place a lower court’s preliminary injunction blocking the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) from conducting door-to-door investigations to interrogate individuals about alleged voter fraud before Election Day. The decision dampens the Trump administration’s wider campaign to intimidate naturalized citizens from voting and to fuel rhetoric about noncitizen voting.

However, moments after the order was published, an anonymous judge in the Ninth Circuit made a request for the circuit court to vote on whether the case should be reheard by the full panel. The Trump administration will likely appeal to the U.S. Supreme Court if the full panel doesn’t bite.

Pro-voting groups, along with the city of San Francisco and Santa Clara County, Calif., argued in their lawsuit that the investigations are a form of voter intimidation.

“The declarants’ fear is reasonably exacerbated by two years of highly visible aggressive conduct by federal agents in immigration enforcement operations under this administration,” the unanimous ruling from the three-judge panel reads.

The legal battle centers on the DHS’s “Unlawful Voter Initiative” launched to investigate alleged illegal voting by noncitizens. According to court documents, the program utilized artificial intelligence and unverified commercial data to generate target lists, leading often-militarized door-to-door interrogations by armed Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents.

President Donald Trump has baselessly claimed for years that noncitizens voting is a widespread problem. In reality. It’s something that rarely occurs and never on a scale capable of tipping election results.

The California Nurses Association and National Nurses United (CNA/NNU), plaintiffs who filed the lawsuit on behalf of their members — many of whom are naturalized citizens — have been afraid to participate in election-related activities due to the highly publicized raids.

The three-judge panel concluded that the federal government failed to demonstrate it would suffer irreparable harm if the program were paused through Election Day.

The court also criticized the timing of the government’s “surge” in enforcement, noting that the administration had over a year and a half to investigate past voter fraud but chose to escalate operations just as early voting began.

“To the extent that Federal Defendants are focused on preventing illegally registered noncitizens from voting in the upcoming election, Defendants’ delay in beginning the Surge has rendered it no longer practicable to prosecute anyone they could identify before Election Day,” the ruling reads.

The preliminary injunction is set to automatically expire when polls close on Election Day. The injunction covers California, Connecticut, Georgia, Missouri, Nevada, New York, Pennsylvania, Washington and Wisconsin.

text:
Washington, D.C. — Today, Rep. Robert Garcia, Ranking Member of the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform, alongside Congressional Asian Pacific American Caucus Chair Grace Meng, Congressional Hispanic Caucus Chair Adriano Espaillat, Congressional Black Caucus Chair Yvette Clarke, and Congressional Equality Caucus Chair Mark Takano, led(link is external) House Democrats in demanding the U.S. Census Bureau immediately withdraw its proposed rule that would unconstitutionally exclude millions of people from apportionment based on their immigration status. This alarming proposal would prevent the Bureau from collecting critical data on race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation needed to evaluate federal programs, identify disparities, and uphold civil rights protections.

“The Trump Administration is working to weaponize the Census as a backdoor attempt to erase entire communities from the representation and resources they deserve. This attempt would threaten civil rights protections, silence LGBTQ+ voices, and deny millions in diverse communities the representation they deserve. We will fight this rule in Congress and the courts,” said Ranking Member Robert Garcia.

“The Decennial Census is a fundamental pillar of our democracy that is required by the Constitution. It is not a tool that should be weaponized for political gain, yet Trump is yet again attempting to erase millions of Asian Americans and Pacific Islanders (AAPI) and other minority groups from census data,” said Rep. Grace Meng, Chair of the Congressional Asian Pacific American Caucus. “If enacted, Trump’s proposal will lead to the loss of representation and critical resources for millions of Americans. It will also eliminate the collection of racial and ethnic data that is critical to identifying disparities and understanding the needs of the distinct 72 ethnic origin groups that make up our diverse AAPI community. When Trump tried to include a citizenship question on the 2020 Decennial Census, I fought back and won. I am proud to again stand with my colleagues to fight this proposed rule and ensure Asian Americans, Native Hawaiians, and Pacific Islanders receive the representation they deserve.”

“Once again, the Congressional Hispanic Caucus is sounding the alarm over the Trump Administration's efforts to politicize the Census. The Constitution requires a complete count of every person residing in the United States, regardless of citizenship or immigration status. Adding a citizenship question and excluding certain noncitizens from apportionment threaten that mandate, deter participation among mixed-status households, and deepen the historic undercount of Latino communities. Eliminating race and ethnicity questions would also undermine our ability to identify and address disparities in health care, education, housing, and more. An inaccurate count jeopardizes fair representation and billions in federal resources for communities in red and blue states alike. I am proud to stand with the Tri-Caucus, the Equality Caucus, and Oversight Committee Ranking Member Robert Garcia in opposing these proposals. Every person counts, every community counts, and no administration should decide otherwise,” said Rep. Adriano Espaillat, Chair of the Congressional Hispanic Caucus.

“The census is a constitutional mandate, not a political tool to be manipulated for partisan gain. Every person living in this country deserves to be counted, and every community deserves fair representation,” said Rep. Yvette D. Clarke, Chair of the Congressional Black Caucus. “The Trump Administration’s attempt to exclude millions of people based on immigration status and eliminate critical demographic data threatens the integrity of the census and undermines the civil rights protections that depend on an accurate count. As Chair of the Congressional Black Caucus, I know that an accurate census is essential to ensuring our communities receive the representation, resources, and protections they are entitled to under the law. We will not stand by while this Administration attempts to erase people from the count and silence the communities whose voices must be heard. This proposed rule must be withdrawn.”

“Once again, Trump is attacking one of the most important pillars of our republic: the right to be fully represented in the census and in the Congress of the United States,” said Rep. Mark Takano (CA-39), Chair of the Congressional Equality Caucus. “This proposed rule attempts to not only unconstitutionally exclude noncitizens from apportionment, but also ban demographic questions on race, ethnicity and sexual orientation. We have already seen how data on race and ethnicity are critical for enforcing the Voting Rights Act and civil rights protections that ensure equal opportunity for all regardless of race. The Census Bureau should not end this data collection and foreclose the possibility of a future question on sexual orientation that could similarly help us recognize and address disparities impacting LGBTQI+ Americans, including helping protect their civil rights and ensure their equal treatment under the law. This proposed rule is just the latest attack by this Administration against marginalized communities. It should not be allowed to take effect.”

In the public comment letter, Ranking Member Robert Garcia wrote, “We write to express our opposition to the Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) titled Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions. The Trump Administration’s proposed rule would violate the Constitution’s 14th Amendment that congressional representation be apportioned based on the “whole number of persons” in each state, undermine enforcement of the Voting Rights Act and other crucial federal civil rights laws, and erase critical data on race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation needed to identify and combat discrimination. These changes would deny communities an accurate accounting of who they are and whether they are receiving equal representation, equal protection, and equal access to federal programs and resources. We demand that you immediately withdraw this unconstitutional and harmful rule.”

The public comment letter has been co-signed by 153 House Democrats.

What This Story Is About

Immigration activists filed a lawsuit on Friday challenging a new rule from the Tennessee Department of Safety and Homeland Security (TDOS).

Why It Matters

Immigration activist organizations said the TDOS’s new rule that the TIRRC said “blocks many non-U.S. citizens from getting temporary driver’s licenses, even when they have authorization from the federal government to be present in the U.S.”

What Happens Next

The TIRRC said their lawsuit is asking the court to block the new rule and to make the TDOS reinstate its previous process for issuing temporary driver’s licenses.

For Context

The TIRRC said Tennesseans who could prove they had permission from the federal government to be in the U.S. have been able to obtain driver’s licenses for many years, adding that they routinely accepted work permits and other federal documents as proof of legality in the U.S. for a period of time.

Catch Up

Among the new laws that went into effect in Tennessee on January 1 is one that mandates lawful permanent residents receive a different form of ID or driver’s license than those who are U.S. citizens.

NASHVILLE, Tenn. (WSMV) - Immigration activists filed a lawsuit on Friday challenging a new rule from the Tennessee Department of Safety and Homeland Security (TDOS).

The National Immigration Law Center, the Tennessee Immigrant and Refugee Rights Coalition (TIRRC) and Bass Berry and Sims, LLC, said the lawsuit is in response to the TDOS’s new rule that the TIRRC said “blocks many non-U.S. citizens from getting temporary driver’s licenses, even when they have authorization from the federal government to be present in the U.S.”

Old policy vs. new rule

The TIRRC said Tennesseans who could prove they had permission from the federal government to be in the U.S. have been able to obtain driver’s licenses for many years, adding that they routinely accepted work permits and other federal documents as proof of legality in the U.S. for a period of time.

In recent weeks, however, the TIRRC said the TDOS abruptly changed this policy, and now only issues driver’s licenses to certain non-citizens who can present a valid visa, I-94,I94W or temporary green card.

“The new rule excludes thousands of people living in Tennessee with federal authorization who have relied for decades on the agency’s prior practice,” the TIRRC said.

Following the implementation of the new rule, the TIRRC said many people, such as Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals (DACA) recipients, have been denied a Tennessee driver’s license. The organization also said many of those denied did not learn about the new policy until they were at the Driver Services Center.

What the lawsuit argues

The TIRRC said their lawsuit argues that the policy change was made without following legal steps, that the TDOS overstepped its authority and failed to give the public a chance to give their input.

“Tennessee’s denial of driver’s licenses to immigrants is unlawful and infringes on Tennesseans’ right to have a say in matters affecting their communities,” said Peter McGraw, legal deputy director of the National Immigration Law Center. “TDOS issued its new driver’s license policies without first seeking community input or approval, and a state agency must consult the public before implementing extreme policies that affect all of us. Tennesseans should be able to drive safely and freely, and we look forward to putting driver’s licenses back in the hands of people who depend on them.”

The TIRRC said their lawsuit is asking the court to block the new rule and to make the TDOS reinstate its previous process for issuing temporary driver’s licenses.

“Regardless of where they were born, Tennesseans rely on the ability to drive in order to work, care for their families, and access the basic needs of life - groceries, medical appointments, their children’s education. The plaintiffs in this action, like so many others across the state, have found their lives upended by the state’s abrupt rule change, which was implemented without warning or explanation” stated Spring Miller, senior legal strategy director at TIRRC. “This is why we are taking legal action. All Tennesseans expect to be treated fairly before the law, and expect their own government to follow it too.”

WSMV reached out to the TDOS for comment on the lawsuit. Spokesperson Jason Pack shared this statement, “Longstanding policy prohibits the department from publicly discussing pending litigation outside of court filings or hearings.”

text:
Reading Time: 3 minutes

Federal immigration authorities asked the U.S. Supreme Court on Wednesday to hear the case of a Mexican national whom agents arrested last year in Racine. The petition is the latest escalation in a legal fight over the Trump administration’s mandatory detention policy for immigrants facing deportation.

The justices’ decision will determine whether tens of thousands of immigrants currently in federal detention can seek release on bond.

“The question of mandatory detention thus boils down to one question: Can we lock up noncitizens without giving them a day in court first?” said Jenifer Bizzotto, the Wisconsin attorney representing Jaciel Cirrus Rojas, the man at the center of the case. “The stakes could hardly be higher.”

Arrested as ‘collateral’

U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents turned up at then-24-year-old Cirrus Rojas’ apartment in June 2025 in search of a prior tenant. They instead arrested Cirrus Rojas, who entered the U.S. in 2018 without a visa, as “collateral.” Wisconsin court records show no criminal convictions under his name.

He spent most of the next nine months in custody at the Dodge County Detention Center in Juneau, entangled in a new White House policy barring ICE detainees from posting bond — a departure from decades of precedent.

The 1996 Immigration Reform Act requires immigration authorities to detain — without bond — anyone found crossing the U.S. border without authorization. Prior administrations applied that rule narrowly, allowing many immigrants arrested in the country’s interior to seek a bond hearing in immigration court.

The Trump administration bucked that approach in July 2025, when ICE Director Todd Lyons issued a new legal interpretation requiring detention without bond regardless of where immigrants are arrested.

The Board of Immigration Appeals, a panel of judges who set the rules for the federal immigration court system, later signed off on the interpretation.

With bond off the table, tens of thousands of immigrants in ICE custody turned to a backup option: filing habeas corpus petitions in federal district courts to challenge their detention.

Unlike immigration courts, which are part of the U.S. Department of Justice, federal district courts belong to the judicial branch and, therefore, are technically independent of the White House. When a federal district court grants a habeas petition, it generally orders an immigration court judge to hold a bond hearing.

Wisconsin’s Western and Eastern District courts have received more than 100 habeas petitions over the past year.

A federal appeals court split

The 7th Circuit ruled 2-1 in Cirrus Rojas’ favor in July, joining appellate courts based in New York, Cincinnati, Denver, Atlanta and San Francisco in rejecting the policy.“If Congress had indeed demanded — but not funded — no-bond detention for all unlawful entrants, that may well have thrown the nation’s immigration system into chaos,” Judge Joshua Kolar, whom Joe Biden appointed to the court, wrote in the court’s majority opinion. “Immigration authorities might have found themselves quickly overwhelmed by a colossal unfunded mandate to arrest and detain millions.” Judge Diane Sykes, a George W. Bush appointee, dissented alone.

“At this point, only the Supreme Court can bring uniformity and settle this question once and for all,” she wrote. “I anticipate that it will do so soon.”

Cirrus Rojas left custody earlier this year after a federal district court judge in California vacated the mandatory detention rule. The San Francisco-based 9th Circuit Court of Appeals stayed that decision less than a month later.

The 7th Circuit allowed his case to move forward because federal authorities plan to re-detain him.

Supreme Court could have final say

“Nothing, absent our intervention, stops the government from making good on its promise,” Kolar wrote.The U.S. Department of Homeland Security, ICE’s parent agency, is now asking the Supreme Court to step in.

The court agreed to take up another mandatory detention dispute earlier this month. That case involves a Brazilian national arrested during a traffic stop in Massachusetts last September.

DHS asked the justices to hold Cirrus Rojas’ case until they decide the Massachusetts case.

In Bizzotto’s view, both cases “offer the Supreme Court the opportunity to affirm that the Constitution means what it says.”

A ruling against the mandatory detention policy would open the door for thousands of ICE detainees — at least those within circuits that side with the Trump administration — to request bond hearings in immigration court. It would not require immigration court judges to grant their bond requests.

The Supreme Court also quietly declined this week to revive a Biden-era policy that allowed immigration court judges to pause deportation proceedings for immigrants seeking humanitarian visas or other forms of legal status.

title: Judge in Pittsburgh holds top federal officials in civil contempt in immigration case
description:
On Jan. 13, 2023, Vasquez Gonzalez was arrested on a drug possession charge and detained by immigration officials.
“Pre-removal order immigration detention at some point, may become so prolonged that it offends due process,” the judge wrote in her April 28 decision.
They asked Vasquez Gonzalez if he was named “Fernando Daniel.” When he said no, they did not believe him.
I told him I had come out of detention and had a release order in my wallet,” Vasquez Gonzalez wrote in a declaration in the case.
“When I told him again that I had my release paper, he said, ‘That doesn’t matter, we’re just doing our job,’” Vasquez Gonzalez wrote.
text:
Body camera footage submitted to a federal judge in Pittsburgh by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents shows several men running away and being taken to the ground during a June 26 “nationwide surge enforcement action.”

They show the men being patted down and handcuffed. Some are driven away by agents often wearing masks.

But none of the video clips showed the man U.S. Magistrate Judge Maureen Kelly asked to see — the man she previously ordered released but who got swept up again.

Because of what she interpreted as a blatant disregard for her orders, Kelly this week held in civil contempt U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche; head of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin; and John E. Rife, the acting ICE field office director for enforcement and removal operations.

Kelly presides over cases in the Western District of Pennsylvania in Pittsburgh.

In a chastising opinion, Kelly said their effort to comply with her orders “involved inconsistent stories, dubious excuses, at least one inaccurate certification and at least three attempts to shield their clearly public acts from scrutiny.”

Their changing stories, the judge continued, lead to two possible conclusions: that they “willfully attempted to obfuscate the circumstances surrounding petitioner’s arrest and detention, as well as to hide the identities of the agent or agents involved therein; or 2) are unable to maintain proper records, utilize their own equipment and tools, or read and comply (with) the orders of this court.”

Kelly imposed sanctions requiring the government officials to pay attorney fees and costs for the man she said they wrongfully arrested.

The judge’s actions, immigration experts said, are unusual.

“In my read of this opinion, the court is treating the government and involved agencies in the same manner the court would hold any litigant not in compliance with the court’s order,” said Adrian Roe, an immigration attorney practicing in Pittsburgh. “That’s an even-handed way to handle these types of matters.

“It’s nice to see the rule of law is alive and well in Western Pennsylvania.”

A message seeking comment from the Department of Justice wasn’t returned.

The U.S. Attorney’s Office in Pittsburgh, which represented the federal government in the case, declined to comment.

‘Due process’

Nain Vasquez Gonzalez filed a petition in federal court last year through Legal Services of New Jersey challenging his detention by ICE at Moshannon Valley Processing Center, an immigration detention facility in Clearfield County.

He had been held there since 2023.

A citizen of El Salvador, Vasquez Gonzalez entered the United States in 2016 while still a minor. He applied for asylum in 2020, seeking protection under the Convention Against Torture Act.

On Jan. 13, 2023, Vasquez Gonzalez was arrested on a drug possession charge and detained by immigration officials. He remained there for 38 months.

The length of Vasquez Gonzalez’s detention, Kelly found, entitled him to release.

“Pre-removal order immigration detention at some point, may become so prolonged that it offends due process,” the judge wrote in her April 28 decision. “Without significant and individualized justification, supported by robust procedural protections, it may be remedied only by outright release.”

Kelly found no evidence that Vasquez Gonzalez presented a danger or risk justifying indefinite detention. She ordered Vasquez Gonzalez’s immediate release, which occurred later that day.

However, according to court records, on June 26, he was arrested again by ICE.

Mistake or bad faith?

That morning, according to court filings, Vasquez Gonzalez was in Fairview, N.J., waiting for a bus to go to a doctor’s appointment around 8:20 a.m. when four agents in two vehicles approached.

They asked Vasquez Gonzalez if he was named “Fernando Daniel.” When he said no, they did not believe him.

“The agent who talked to me asked if I was legal. I told him I had come out of detention and had a release order in my wallet,” Vasquez Gonzalez wrote in a declaration in the case. “He did not look at or let me take it out.”

Instead, the agent arrested him.

“When I told him again that I had my release paper, he said, ‘That doesn’t matter, we’re just doing our job,’” Vasquez Gonzalez wrote.

He was photographed, and the picture was analyzed by facial recognition software. Then he was transported by ICE and held for 11 hours.

He ultimately was released when his attorney learned he had been taken into custody and filed another motion with the court.

Afterward, Kelly set out to learn why Vasquez Gonzalez was rearrested in violation of her ruling.

In various orders, the judge told the federal government to provide the names of the officers who arrested him, and later, when they said they couldn’t, she asked for the body camera footage from that day. She also asked for a firsthand account from those on the scene of what happened.

In each instance, the judge found they failed to comply.

“ICE’s apparent practice of obfuscating the identities of the agents involved in arrests is deeply troubling,” the judge wrote.

By the time of the court’s deadline, ICE was able to identify the arresting officer but told the court he didn’t have his body camera activated that day.

In an unsworn memo, officials said the officer’s camera was not charged that day because he had left it activated the night before.

In a filing, the government called that “a preventable error for which there is no excuse. … But there is no basis to extrapolate from this mistake bad faith by ICE.”

When Kelly asked for the body camera footage from other agents that day, the government asked that it be filed under seal.

Kelly denied the request and then offered additional criticism of the use of masks to hide the identities of agents during ICE operations.

“The United States does not have a secret police force,” she wrote, calling their attempt to cloak their identities “deeply troubling, and — at its core — un-American.”

Eventually, the judge wrote, ICE submitted video from five agents, though none of it showed Vasquez Gonzalez’s arrest, despite there being at least 15 agents working in concert to arrest 20 people at the time.

‘Changing stories’

The attorney representing Vasquez Gonzalez asked the court to impose sanctions on the government and hold the individual officials in contempt, citing their “changing stories” and their failure to produce bodycam footage as “implausible and evasive.”

The government officials, wrote Robert Jackel of Legal Services of New Jersey, have a pattern of ignoring court orders.

“The District of New Jersey have issued multiple warnings to ICE, but the agency continues to violate court orders,” he wrote. “Warnings have not been enough. Sanctions are necessary to prevent such conduct in the future.

“Nothing the government has provided so far to this court contains a credible explanation for what happened when they arrested Nain.”

The government responded, according to court documents, by saying Vasquez Gonzalez’s statements were unfounded and speculative.

It said the agency’s failure to answer the court “resulted from ICE’s scramble to get the court the answers it requested in short order and in the wake of making a mistake that understandably frustrated the court and caused petitioner distress.”

As soon as ICE realized their mistake, Assistant U.S. Attorney Heidi Grogan wrote, they released him.

But Judge Kelly wasn’t convinced. She was critical of the government agents’ declarations in the case — made under oath — because they contained factual conclusions despite being made by people who were not present at Vasquez Gonzalez’s arrest.

“Such conduct is most disconcerting,” she wrote. “At best it undercuts the credibility of any future testimony from these individuals and wastes the resources of the court and the litigants.

“At worst, it is possibly perjury.”

‘Ask questions later’

Vanessa Stine, a senior staff attorney focusing on immigrants’ rights for the ACLU of Pennsylvania, said Kelly’s order is important for holding the federal government accountable.

“ICE’s actions in this case are both appalling and unfortunately all too common,” Stine said. “It is part of a larger pattern of indiscriminate stops and arrests that sweep people up and ask questions later.”

Roe, the Pittsburgh immigration attorney, said judges don’t hold parties in contempt too frequently. But, he continued, it’s also unusual for a party to disregard a court’s order.

“A very high percentage of parties comply with court orders without the need for sanctions,” Roe said. “But there are parties and agencies that don’t comply, and this is what happens.”
