text:
A Texas grand jury indicted an Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent on Friday for intentionally running a man over with his vehicle earlier this month.

Officer Mario Alberto Morales is facing a charge of assault with a deadly weapon after running over Miguel Parra Hernandez, who was on foot, with a black unmarked SUV. Hernandez broke his leg and also injured his hip and ankle, according to his family. He is currently undergoing rehab in ICE custody, and Morales was placed on administrative leave.

Hernandez, an undocumented immigrant from Mexico, was driving to his construction job when immigration agents tried to pull him over. Hernandez and another passenger fled from the vehicle. According to street camera and body cam footage, Morales then turned his vehicle and accelerated over Hernandez. Hernandez can be heard screaming “You ran over me,” while Morales replies, “You got hit with the car, bro.” ICE backed Morales’s version of events, saying in an official statement that Hernandez “ran in front of an ICE vehicle and was struck.”

ICE still maintains that story, saying that Morales’s indictment “is nothing more than a political stunt by Houston sanctuary politicians.” It also argues that the local government doesn’t have jurisdiction to try and investigate Morales in the first place, a claim Harris County District Attorney Sean Teare says is “false.”

“An ICE badge does not give you free rein to injure, kill, or violate the constitutional rights of anyone,” Teare said.

With just days until the midterm elections, moderate Democrats are still finding ways to undermine Michigan’s Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed.

House Speaker Emerita Nancy Pelosi criticized El-Sayed on a recent episode of the On Brand podcast. Host Donny Deutsch claimed El-Sayed had made “concerning” comments opposing the existence of a Jewish state. “That’s antisemitic as far as I’m concerned,” he said.

“No, it’s more than concerning. It’s wrong,” Pelosi said. “It’s wrong, and it isn’t a reflection of the Democrats in the Congress of the United States. This new person in Michigan, we’ll see if he gets elected to the Congress.”

Since launching his campaign, El-Sayed, who is Muslim, has been bombarded by baseless claims of antisemitism. The Democrat has stated that he opposes any state’s right to be organized around an ethnic or religious group, and has been clear that his issue is with the Israeli government, not Jewish people. “An ally that takes your money to push you into wars you shouldn’t be fighting is not an ally,” he said during one interview on ABC News.

But Pelosi appeared more interested in defending Israel than a Democrat on the eve of an important election. (Her spokesperson said Friday that she was urging people to support El-Sayed.)

Representative Haley Stevens, whom El-Sayed defeated in the Democratic primary, also took an eleventh-hour shot at her party’s only hope to keep control of the state’s Senate seat. Stevens issued a statement Friday suggesting that her support for El-Sayed was contingent on whether he condemned a political advertisement that was not even produced by his campaign.

The video was made by Rebellion PAC, a left-wing fundraising group led by Cenk Uygur of The Young Turks—who Stevens wants everyone to know is also “Hasan Piker’s uncle.” The video, which originally aired in February 2024, blamed the rising price of groceries on America’s continued support for Israel’s genocide in Gaza.

“Why does Mike Rogers care so much about what Israelis want, and so little about what you want?” the ad asks, claiming that pro-Israel PACs had poured $228,808 into Rogers’s campaign.

Stevens said she had agreed to appear at an event with El-Sayed and Representative Jim Clyburn, expecting that El-Sayed would formally condemn the ad. “A disclaimer is not condemnation, and everyone in my community knows the difference,” Stevens said in the statement.

But that wasn’t all she was expecting. Stevens called for El-Sayed to apologize for his own statements tying Israel to Michiganders’ affordability crisis, though it wasn’t immediately clear that he actually had made any such claims. She also asked him to take down another campaign advertisement that included a clip of Tucker Carlson, among a montage of right-wing media figures.

Again, with Stevens, we see Democrats placing continued support for Israel before the success of their own party and their own constituents. Is it any wonder that Stevens lost?

A federal judge on Friday announced the appointment of a special master to investigate whether Trump officials repeatedly lied to her about the president’s attempted takeover of the East Potomac Park golf course in Washington, D.C. The investigation will begin in a matter of days.

In court Friday, a Justice Department lawyer tried to play dumb about what’s going on in the park, what Trump has publicly said about the park, and how the administration has flouted court orders. When U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes asked the lawyer if he “made any false statements of material fact that you’d like to correct,” the attorney said “not to my knowledge,” drawing Reyes’s ire.

The lawyer claimed that he was new to the case, saying, “We have lots of binders.” Reyes tried to remedy the situation by calling an Interior Department official and asking them the same question, only to get the same answer: “Not to my knowledge.” When Reyes asked if the official’s boss, Interior Secretary Doug Burgum, was involved in the park project, the official asked, “What do you mean by ‘involved?’” This prompted Reyes to pull out a dictionary to read the definition of “involved.”

The official then said that Burgum was aware of the renovation project, but wasn’t involved, to which Reyes noted that he toured the golf course. “He doesn’t have a body double, does he?” Reyes quipped.

After Reyes asked when the Department of Interior became aware of plans to close the park on November 15, the official seemed ignorant, prompting Reyes to ask if she needed to look up “plan” in the dictionary.

Reyes noted that Trump wrote on Truth Social October 18 that the park was closing on November 15, and that the DOJ “swore up and down” the next day that park wasn’t closing then, only to later change its story and confirm the November 15 closure date. At that point, assistant Attorney General Stanley Woodward, the number three person at the DOJ, intervened and tried to halt the questioning of the Interior Department official.

“It sounds like you don’t want him to answer a very straightforward question,” Reyes said, before allowing the official to step away. Woodward then started answering Reyes’s questions, saying that the closure plan was “noticed” on October 28. He tried to claim that Trump’s post said the park “should” be closed, only for Reyes to correct him and point out that Trump wrote “will be” closed.

The hearing didn’t get any better from there, as Woodward attempted to explain away Trump’s posts by claiming there were no plans to close the golf course, questioning whether those words constitute “plans” or “orders.” Woodward went as far as to try to claim “executive privilege” over Trump’s social media posts, frustrating Reyes, who said, “That’s quite an extraordinary view of executive privilege.”

The entire hearing continued on in this absurdity, with the DOJ letting slip that a new seawall at the park would cost between $150 million and a whopping $400 million. Trump administration lawyers became noticeably cagey about questions regarding the renovation’s costs after that.

Trump is insisting on this project despite court orders and the law, and openly admits he’s ignoring Reyes’s rulings. Friday’s drama in court is an indication that Trump’s lawyers can’t come up with believable justifications for his haphazard decisions.

Trump Media & Technology Group, the company that owns Truth Social, expects to be paid $350,000 for running ads about America’s 250th birthday celebrations.

The 250th celebrations, a series of very disappointing events over the summer, were led by Freedom 250, a Trump-created group that took over a bipartisan committee commissioned by Congress to plan the anniversary. Freedom 250 was officially housed under the National Park Foundation, a nonprofit that is supposed to raise money for the National Park Service—on whose board Trump Media board member Meredith O’Rourke also happens to sit.

Trump still owns a 41 percent stake in Trump Media, raising further alarm about Trump essentially paying himself for ads on the social media company he owns.

A Thursday merger filing first reported on by Wendy Seigelman at NewsTRACS reveals that Trump Media, or TMTG, reported the expected $350,000 payment directly from Freedom 250.

“TMTG performed advertising services to Freedom 250 LLC, an entity created by, and administered by the National Park Foundation, the official charity of the National Park Service. Meredith O’Rourke, a member of TMTG’s Board of Directors, also serves on the Board of Directors of the National Parks Foundation,” the filing reads. For the three and nine months ended September 30, 2026, TMTG earned revenue of $175.0 related to the advertisement of Freedom 250 events. As of September 30, 2026, TMTG had $175.0 of outstanding receivables from Freedom 250 LLC.”

Freedom 250 relies mostly on taxpayer money, as National Park Foundation CEO Jeff Reinbold told the House Natural Resources Committee in February. “The majority of Freedom 250’s operating funds come from federal funds appropriated by Congress specifically for the 250th anniversary commemorations,” he said.

It appears that Trump went out of his way to create lackluster, cheap, and gaudy events, all to funnel more money into his own pockets. It is yet another example of just how committed to corruption this administration is, wringing out every penny they can get from their time in power.

The U.S. oil industry has made more than $130 billion in profit during the Iran war—while normal Americans continue to pay exorbitant prices at the gas pump.

The New York Times reported that the country’s 50 largest oil and gas companies raked in a massive profit from April to September. The $130 billion profit margin eclipses the $47 billion that these companies made during the same six-month period last year. The last comparable economic windfall was after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022, when the oil and gas industry made slightly higher profits.

American households have spent $1,100 on fuel alone since the war began. That’s an extra $147 billion all together, according to Brown University’s Climate Solutions Lab.

Once again, it is massive corporations that stand to gain the most from violence and conflict.

President Trump said it himself a few days ago.

“And while oil prices are temporarily high … the United States oil and gas business is making hundreds of billions of dollars.... Our country is making hundreds of billions of dollars ‘cause of what’s happened in the Middle East … trillions of dollars,” he told a rally crowd in Georgia on Saturday. “My people said, ‘Please don’t mention that sir, because people are paying a little higher’ ... I said, ‘I don’t give a damn, I’m gonna say it: We’re making a freaking fortune.’”

When the president says “we,” he means Exxon, Chevron, and Valero. Not you.

text:
The Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals has ruled that State Department is not required to open the FY 2027 Diversity Visa (DV) program registration period while litigation challenging the halt of the program continues. The appeals court has issued an emergency stay of an October 14 district court preliminary injunction that required the State Department to open this fiscal year’s DV registration and conduct the program according to a specified timeline.

In issuing the stay, the Ninth Circuit says that the court does not endorse the State Department’s failure to open the FY 2027 registration period, but that the plaintiff, a law firm that represents DV applicants, did not show that it met the legal requirements for a preliminary injunction. The court determined that the firm is not within the zone of interests to be protected or regulated and does not have a cause of action, as required under the preliminary injunction legal standard. The case is Red Eagle Law, L.C. v. Rubio, No. 26-6943 (9th Cir., case filed Oct 20, 2026; order issued Oct 29, 2026).

After making an announcement in November 2025 that changes were underway for the FY 2027 DV entry period, the State Department paused the program entirely in December 2025. The agency simultaneously paused immigrant visa processing under the FY 2026 DV program. Several groups sued to reinstate the DV programs underway or in the planning stages at the time of the pauses; the litigants challenging actions affecting the FY 2026 DV program had some limited success.

In August 2026, law firm Red Eagle Law, L.C. sued in a California district court to reinstate the FY 2027 DV program. On October 14, the Red Eagle court issued a preliminary injunction ordering the State Department to open the FY 2027 DV program by midnight ET, November 1, 2026 for a period of 30 days; to make an advance public announcement with all registration details on the State Department website by midnight ET, October 29, 2026; and then after DV registration closes, to notify selected foreign nationals of their selection by midnight ET on December 3, 2026. The preliminary injunction order also required the State Department to timely process any submitted FY 2027 DV immigrant visa applications in accordance with the agency’s usual procedures. The district court case is Red Eagle Law, L.C. v. Rubio, Docket No. 3:26-cv-04738 (S.D. Cal., case filed Aug 19, 2026).

The State Department quickly appealed the preliminary injunction to the Ninth Circuit, resulting in the above emergency stay of the district court order.

text:
Rio Grande Valley, Texas – Leaning over plates of tamales, pan dulce, and sugar skulls, community organisers and local residents in the border city of Brownsville remembered the dead.

This year’s Dia de los Muertos, or Day of the Dead, vigil honoured victims of state violence, including those killed in immigration enforcement and detention. Just days before the US midterm election on November 3, the event reverberated in a region long subject to Washington, DC’s shifting political winds.

Recommended Stories

list of 3 items

list 1 of 3Who is leading the US midterm polls as Trump and Harris campaign?

list 2 of 3Pentagon says Iran war has cost US taxpayers $47bn: What that means

list 3 of 3What does bourbon have to do with the US midterms?

end of list

“The atmosphere here in the Rio Grande Valley when it comes to ICE detentions and the ICE raids, there’s just the overall feeling amongst folks that there’s no real due process to this,” said Mark Anthony Vasquez, a 52-year-old community organiser.

“What is it that we can do to move together and build together to try to make it past this, and make that change that we seek?”

Down the block, at a bookstore panel on border and immigration policy, 24-year-old Juliana Garcia raised her hand to ask advice on how to find a lawyer able to navigate the aggressively shifting policies of the administration of US President Donald Trump, which has used both an increase in physical enforcement, as well as a reinterpretation of administrative policies, to fuel its mass deportation campaign.

Garcia’s aunt, a well-known member of the community in the nearby border town of Progreso, was deported just weeks ago, after being called to a Department of Homeland Security (DHS) hearing. There she learned she had missed a court date related to her immigration status.

In the stress of the moment, she signed a voluntary deportation form.

“Within 36 hours, she was deported,” Garcia told Al Jazeera, tucked between bookshelves. “People are waking up, and they’re remembering that politics, regardless of what branch you’re in, it’s going to impact you every day.”

Shifting dynamics

Views on immigration are complex in the Rio Grande Valley, a geographic and cultural region located in subtropical southeast Texas with about 1.5 million residents. That complexity has only increased in recent years as border policy and immigration enforcement have become increasingly partisan, leading, reformers say, to dramatic policy swings that prevent more sustainable solutions.

It is not difficult to find Latino – or Tejano, the local term for Texans of Latino descent – residents wary of the years preceding Trump’s return to office. After the restrictive policies of Trump’s first term, border crossings increased dramatically under US President Joe Biden, fuelled in part by the end of a COVID-era policy that made asylum seekers wait for their cases to be processed in Mexico.

Some felt the border region was left to deal with the fallout from the influx. That discontent has been credited, in part, with Trump’s success in the once-reliably Democratic region in the 2024 presidential election.

In Hidalgo County, home to the city of McAllen, Trump won 51 percent of the vote in 2024, a three-point margin over Kamala Harris. In 2020, Biden beat Trump in the county by 17 percentage points.

In neighbouring Cameron County, Trump won by about five percentage points in 2024, despite a 13-point loss in 2020.

Voter Jose Arizpe, a 40-year-old resident of Brownsville, assessed the two years since Trump took office as a “positive change”, with fewer asylum seekers waiting in the US for their cases to be processed.

Upon taking office, Trump declared a state of emergency at the border, staunching asylum claims in what rights groups say runs counter to US law. The US Supreme Court has since ruled that US border agents can physically block asylum seekers from reaching US soil to claim asylum.

“A lot of people claim that they support illegals and want to let them in,” said Arizpe, a regular Republican voter, “but then, I say ‘well let them in your house’. And they don’t want to do it, right?”

On border policy, “at first, I supported Trump,” said Martin Torres, a 55-year-old who cast his ballot for Democrats at a public library in Brownsville as part of the state’s early voting.

But domestic enforcement, and its impact on the local workforce, soured his views.

“Now he changes everything,” he said.

A report from the Caminos Institute has estimated the region has lost $180.6m in economic activity due to the Trump administration’s immigration policies, including in construction and restaurants.

Other voters saw Trump’s approach as fuelling bigotry. Last year, the US Supreme Court lifted a lower-court order barring immigration officials from considering “apparent race or ethnicity”, as well as language spoken, when on patrol. Rights groups say the decision effectively allows racial profiling.

In Texas, a state law also lets local officials stop individuals they suspect entered the country illegally.

“I just see a lot of discrimination going on,” said George Castorena, a 46-year-old department of education worker, who said he was voting for change.

To be sure, midterm elections can only offer incremental change on an issue as entrenched as immigration enforcement and border policy.

Democratic control of the House of Representatives would at best serve as a bulwark against the Trump administration legislating more immigration enforcement funding and policy, while opening the door to investigations into the administration’s approach.

Control of the Senate, which could be determined by the contest between Texas Republican Ken Paxton and Democratic challenger James Talarico, could further increase the party’s leverage.

A change in the governor’s office, meanwhile, could end Texas Governor Greg Abbott’s myriad uses of state agencies to support federal immigration enforcement. But Democrat Gina Hinojosa, if she were to pull off an upset, would be largely constrained by a likely Republican-dominated state legislature and a mountain of pre-existing law.

A galvanising moment?

Although a more lasting transformation remains far off, evidence suggests the local dismay runs deep.

A poll conducted by the American Civil Liberties Union of Texas found that only 34 percent of respondents from the area felt that immigration enforcement by both local and state officials had made their communities safer. Fifty-three percent said it made their lives harder without improving safety.

Meanwhile, 64 percent felt ICE tactics have gone too far. The numbers broadly align with polls showing Democratic challenger Bobby Pulido leading Republican incumbent Monica De La Cruz and Democratic incumbent Vicente Gonzalez leading Republican challenger Eric Flores in two Rio Grande Valley congressional districts.

Republicans, eyeing Trump’s success in 2024, viewed the races as strong prospects early in the election season.

“What this survey conveys is: people along the border in the Rio Grande Valley are not in alignment with what they probably voted for back in 2024,” Osvaldo Grimaldo, a policy strategist at ACLU of Texas, told Al Jazeera.

Even prominent community figures who support Trump’s policies acknowledge a broader change in sentiment.

Eli Lara, the lead pastor at the non-denominational New Life Family Church in McAllen, Texas, said locals have been dismayed by the wide scope with which the administration has targeted undocumented individuals.

“The immigration issue is bigger because [the community] is seeing people being taken,” he told Al Jazeera. “I don’t like the separation of families, but here’s the thing: there are consequences for choices.”

That view held even for a congregant who had recently been deported in connection with a past drug possession conviction.

“He’s been faithful [to the church] for two, three years, but they picked him up,” Lara said. “Why? Because he had a bad criminal record in the past. God forgives, but the government doesn’t.”

Voter Garcia, who volunteers with the Hidalgo County Young Democrats, was among those who believed the current situation could galvanise the Rio Grande Valley.

She pointed to several instances that have recently shaken the region, including the assault of a 17-year-old by immigration agents in the town of Alamo in the Rio Grande Valley, and the fatal ICE shooting of Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in July 2026 in the Texas city of Houston.

“I’ve had a lot of people tell me, ‘Why do I care about politics? Politics doesn’t affect me,'” she said. “And with all of these ICE raids, they realise politics does affect them, and it sucks that it took a lot of trauma to really bring that to people.”

text:
Here's what happened this week in immigration news.

Written by Emma Chen, Edited by Kate Morrissey

Welcome to another edition of Beyond the Border, which summarizes immigration news from across the country in a weekly roundup. Did we miss something? Message us via kate@daylightsandiego.org or on Instagram.

Want to support this work? Consider donating to Daylight San Diego or email lauren@daylightsandiego.org if you're interested in sponsoring this newsletter.

(Did someone forward you this email? Subscribe here.)

A short update from Kate: I wrote earlier this week about a Salvadoran man deported to Mexico. He has since set up a GoFundMe for those interested in supporting him.

ICE-related deaths

Daylight San Diego reported that a 43-year-old Guatemalan man died at Otay Mesa Detention Center on Oct. 24 after staff found him unresponsive in his cell.

San Diego County supervisors demanded that federal officials and private prison operator CoreCivic cooperate with an investigation into the man's death, citing ongoing concerns about medical care and detention conditions, Daylight San Diego reported.

The Guardian reported that a 48-year-old Salvadoran immigrant died at an Immigration and Customs Enforcement detention facility in Folkston, Georgia, amid a hunger strike protesting prolonged detention, poor conditions and mistreatment of detainees.

The Minnesota Star Tribune reported that the parents of Alex Pretti, whom federal immigration officials fatally shot in Minneapolis in January, accused federal officials of withholding evidence and obstructing accountability nine months after their son's death.

Deportations

A Migration Policy Institute analysis estimated that the Trump administration deported 980,000 people during its first 18 months, increasing removals but falling short of its stated goal of 1 million deportations annually, the Chicago Tribune reported.

Sahan Journal reported that a Minnesota Hmong family is struggling to adjust after ICE deported the father to Laos in May, leaving his wife to raise their five sons while he maintains their morning routines through video calls.

CBS News reported that ICE deported a Texas father to Ghana, where authorities subsequently sent him to Mali despite a U.S. immigration judge's order protecting him from deportation to his home country over fear of persecution.

ICE detained and ultimately deported a Bay Area nurse to Kenya despite her plans to relocate legally to Canada for a health care job, separating her from her husband and two children, the San Francisco Chronicle reported.

ICE routinely transfers detainees across state lines within 24 hours of their arrests, leaving families and attorneys struggling to locate them through an unreliable federal tracking system, The Marshall Project reported.

ICE arrests

Federal officers detained a restaurant owner and beloved community member in Paris, Illinois, disrupting the life he had built with his wife and four children in the small community that voted for President Donald Trump, the Chicago Tribune reported.

The Santa Barbara Independent reported that federal immigration officers detained and injured a 20-year-old U.S. citizen student with special needs who is nonverbal as he walked to Santa Maria High School, leaving him with a broken wrist that required surgery after officers racially profiled him.

ICE arrested more than twice as many immigrant children during the first seven months of 2026 as during the same period in 2025, bringing the total number of children arrested during Trump's second term to more than 8,500, The Marshall Project reported.

The Associated Press reported that ICE has detained Phillip James, a 39-year-old man with schizophrenia, since January despite birth records and previous U.S. passports supporting his claim to American citizenship.

The Washington Post reported that White House border czar Tom Homan visited Puerto Rico amid intensified ICE activity that prompted concerns from immigrant advocates over arrests, traffic stops and potential civil rights violations.

Community effects

NBC Chicago reported that Chicago voters will decide whether city officials should seek financial compensation from the federal government for economic losses and public expenses associated with the Trump administration's Operation Midway Blitz.

The Washington Post reported that more than 40 agricultural organizations warned President Donald Trump that his administration's immigration crackdown is disrupting food production, worsening labor shortages and threatening to increase grocery prices.

Residents of Chicago's South Shore neighborhood are seeking accountability after more than 300 federal officers raided an apartment complex in September 2025, entering homes at gunpoint and restraining residents, including U.S. citizens, Latino USA reported.

ICE use of force

The New York Times reported that an ICE officer shot Honduran immigrant José García-Sorto during a traffic stop in Phoenix last year, leaving a bullet lodged in his spine before authorities detained and deported him to Honduras, where he continues to suffer serious health complications despite facing no criminal charges related to the encounter. The outlet followed García-Sorto for months to show what happened to him.

KING 5 reported that witnesses photographed an ICE officer carrying a rifle during an immigration arrest in South Seattle, while another observer said that an officer pointed a handgun at him during a separate encounter, leading community members to worry that ICE officers are growing more aggressive in the region.

Local police are investigating after an immigration officer's SUV struck a man who documents ICE activity in Woodland, California, CNN reported. Federal officials initially claimed that the man jumped onto the vehicle, but video footage contradicted that.

The New York Times reported that video footage showed an ICE vehicle swerving toward a U.S. citizen as he rode his bicycle in Long Beach, California, contradicting the agency's denial that officers struck him and prompting the city's mayor to demand an independent investigation.

A U.S. citizen volunteer who monitors immigration enforcement activity said ICE officers chased her car through Santa Maria, California, and detained her at a local ICE field office despite her repeatedly stating that she was a U.S. citizen, The San Luis Obispo Tribune reported.

Video footage shows ICE agents slashing the car tires of volunteers monitoring and recording ICE activity in Hillsboro, Oregon, Common Dreams reported. The American Civil Liberties Union is demanding an investigation into retaliation against legal observers.

Detention conditions

More than half a dozen transgender immigrant women accused staff and fellow detainees at ICE facilities in Louisiana and Texas of sexual assault, harassment, humiliation and denial of medical care, Nómadas reported.

Georgia Sens. Raphael Warnock and Jon Ossoff demanded a federal investigation into medical neglect and retaliation against hunger-striking detainees at the Folkston ICE detention facility, including reports that staff placed protesters in solitary confinement, WABE reported.

ICE routinely transfers detainees across state lines within 24 hours of their arrests, leaving families and attorneys struggling to locate them through an unreliable federal tracking system, The Marshall Project reported.

Mother Jones reported that the GEO Group earned nearly $90 million from Pennsylvania’s Moshannon Valley Processing Center between January 2025 and May 2026. The ICE detention facility held more than 1,600 immigrants at a time, 85% of whom had no criminal record, and the facility faced allegations of mistreatment and prolonged detention.

The 5th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals ruled that immigrants who entered the United States without permission do not have a constitutional right to bond hearings during deportation proceedings, allowing the Trump administration to detain them regardless of their community ties or lack of criminal history, El Paso Matters reported.

Seven former immigration detainees filed a nationwide class-action lawsuit accusing ICE of withholding passports, work permits and personal belongings after their release, preventing some from working, driving or supporting their families, Newsweek reported.

Targeting voters

The Washington Post reported that U.S. citizenship approvals dropped 72% during the first eight months of 2026, leaving hundreds of thousands of applicants in limbo and preventing some prospective voters from gaining citizenship before the November midterm elections.

Federal prosecutors charged a 66-year-old Syracuse resident with illegally voting in federal elections after she recently discovered that she was born in Germany and never obtained U.S. citizenship despite living in the United States since childhood, Syracuse.com reported.

A federal judge ordered the Department of Homeland Security to halt voter fraud investigations across nine states after finding that officials relied on unreliable data and artificial intelligence tools that risked targeting eligible U.S. citizen voters, inewsource reported.

Hundreds of volunteer groups across the United States are organizing patrols, monitoring ICE activity and preparing to document potential voter intimidation near polling places during the November midterm elections, WIRED reported.

Other stories to watch

WIRED reported that federal immigration investigators deployed roughly 120 officers, including undercover operatives, to monitor anti-ICE activists in Minnesota and other states, using surveillance tools, infiltrated communications and financial records to investigate political organizing.

LAist reported that immigrant legal aid organizations filed a federal lawsuit challenging an ICE policy that conceals the locations of detainees with final deportation orders, arguing that the change prevents attorneys from locating and representing their clients.

The Philadelphia Inquirer reported that ICE arrests contributed to an estimated $811 million in lost consumer spending in Philadelphia as ICE arrests discouraged residents from visiting local businesses.

Oregon Live reported that Oregon State Police asked ICE to stop using its parking lots for immigration enforcement, while police departments in Hillsboro and Forest Grove also restricted federal officers' access to local resources amid increased immigration enforcement activity across the state.

ABC News 4 reported that Charleston animal shelter Pet Helpers urgently requested additional foster homes to help because of newly arrived dogs from an ICE deportation case.

Six Democratic senators urged Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. to reverse a policy that would allow government attorneys to represent unaccompanied immigrant children in deportation proceedings, warning that the arrangement creates conflicts of interest and threatens children's legal rights, Mother Jones reported.

Mission Local reported that San Francisco educators and volunteers have accompanied 137 students and immigrant families to immigration appointments since January, helping families navigate ICE check-ins without any of those accompanied facing arrest.

MPR News reported that Minnesota journalists Mukhtar Ibrahim and Ubah Ali launched The Somali Brief, a digital news outlet that aims to combat misinformation and expand reporting on Somali American communities.

Thanks for reading! Take care and stay well.

— Emma

text:
By Marcia Sowles

On Oct. 20, the Mennonite Church USA and the Church of the Brethren and their 25 co-plaintiffs won an important ruling in their “sensitive location” lawsuit, Mennonite Church USA v. U.S Department of Homeland Security. The lawsuit challenges the Department of Homeland Security’s rescission of its three-decade-old policy restricting immigration enforcement actions at or near houses of worship.

The lawsuit alleges that the government’s actions substantially burden the plaintiffs’ religious exercise, in violation of the Religious Freedom Restoration Act (RFRA) and the First Amendment. It also argues that the agency’s failure to provide an adequate justification for such a significant policy shift violates the Administrative Procedure Act.

The three-judge panel of the Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit ruled, 2-1, that a lower court judge erred in finding that the plaintiffs lacked standing to file their lawsuit. In her Opinion for the Court, Circuit Judge Florence Y. Pan wrote, “Plaintiffs’ members likely face imminent harm from increased enforcement at their houses of worship; that harm is traceable to the new enforcement policy; and the relief requested will likely redress their injury, at least in part.”

She also pointed out that the “plaintiffs have direct evidence that the government intends to increase immigration enforcement at sensitive locations—that is the whole point of the Recission Memo.”

The decision does not reach the merits of the plaintiffs’ claims nor does it provide immediate relief. The case will return to the lower court, where plaintiffs can again ask for a preliminary injunction, a temporary court order that would protect their congregations while the lawsuit continues.

Plaintiffs are represented in the lawsuit by Georgetown University Law Center’s Institute for Constitutional Advocacy and Protection.

If your congregation or ministry has observed ICE or CBP (border patrol) activity at or in the near vicinity of your place of worship, please immediately contact Marcia Sowles at msowles@brethren.org and copy the district executive of your Church of the Brethren district, so that we can document with the court any encroachment into our sacred spaces.

— Marcia Sowles is an attorney and serves as a Policy and Governmental Affairs associate for the Church of the Brethren Office of Peacebuilding and Policy.

In immigration news, the number of ICE jails nationwide has more than doubled since President Trump returned to office, with his administration allocating billions of dollars for the mass detention of tens of thousands of immigrants.

In Washington state, the troubled Northwest Detention Center in Tacoma will continue to operate for another 10 years, after the for-profit prison company GEO Group signed a $1.5 billion contract with the federal government. That amount was more than six times the cost of CoreCivic’s initial offer to sell the prison to the state of Minnesota for about $75 million. This follows an unprecedented $45 billion given to ICE to expand its detention capacity as part of Trump’s so-called One Big Beautiful Bill Act.

text:
A federal immigration agent who drove into and seriously injured a Texas man on 10 October after a botched traffic stop was indicted Friday on a charge of aggravated assault with a deadly weapon.

Mario Alberto Morales, 33, an agent with Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), deliberately veered his SUV into Miguel Parra Hernandez, 48, causing multiple leg fractures and a hip injury, journalists at a news conference in Houston were told.

In announcing the charge against Morales, Harris county district attorney Sean Teare questioned the training that Morales, a recent appointment by ICE, had received – and denounced the activities and conduct of the agency in support of the frequently violent immigration crackdown during Donald Trump’s second presidency.

His office is also investigating the fatal shooting by ICE in Houston in July of Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, an immigrant who, like Parra Hernandez, was not the intended target of an enforcement operation.

Friday’s indictment came little more than five months after Christian Castro, an ICE officer who shot and wounded a Venezuelan man in an operation in Minnesota in January, was charged with assault and falsely reporting a crime.

“Their behavior and the fear that’s being instilled in such a big, vibrant group of people, of Harris county residents, is objectively making us all less safe,” Teare told reporters, citing what he said was a documented drop-off in reports of domestic violence, aggravated robberies and sexual assaults by victims who feared deportation.

“One of the most insidious things about these tactics and the way that ICE is behaving in our community is the fear that a large percentage of our population has right now. An ICE badge does not give you free rein to injure, kill, or violate the constitutional rights of anyone.”

A grand jury empanelled to investigate the case involving Morales returned the indictment on Friday morning after hearing evidence that Teare said was “as clear as any that I’ve ever prosecuted or investigated”.

Morales was driving an unmarked Jeep Cherokee and attempted to stop a pickup truck containing two men who jumped out and fled. Surveillance video played at the news conference showed Parra Hernandez, a Mexican construction worker with no criminal record or active deportation order, running across a restaurant parking lot when the pursuing SUV swerved into him and ran him over.

In an audio recording of a 911 call Morales made requesting the assistance of paramedics and the Harris county sheriff’s office, he is heard telling the dispatcher that Parra Hernandez ran in front of his vehicle and was hit, an assertion repeated in an official ICE account of the case released the following day.

In a statement on Friday, an ICE spokesperson said: “Allegations that ICE struck Miguel Parra Hernandez intentionally are reckless and false. The men and women of ICE are entrusted with upholding the rule of law and are held to the highest standards of professionalism, integrity, and ethical conduct.”

The spokesperson said the indictment was “nothing more than a political stunt by Houston sanctuary politicians”, using a term meant to describe local officials who don’t cooperate with federal immigration authorities.

“Federal officers acting in the course of their duties can only be investigated by other federal agencies,” the spokesperson also said. “Local governments do not have the authority to run such an investigation.”

Harris county sheriff Ed Gonzalez told the press conference his investigators later found out that, at the time it struck Parra Hernandez, Morales’s SUV also contained two handcuffed detainees from a previous, unrelated operation.

“I know of no law enforcement agency that would deem that to be acceptable,” he said. “To the contrary, it’s very unsafe. If some other crash could have occurred with them being handcuffed and shackled inside the vehicle it would have been a maybe even worse situation because they were very limited in their movement and in the backseat of the vehicle.”

Teare said that ICE deported at least two “material witnesses” within a week of Parra being struck over the prosecutor’s objection and with no opportunity to interview them. Parra Hernandez, he said, “is not even able to leave the rehab facility, and they are having court dates to try to deport him”.

The district attorney said he had collected “a significant amount of information” on Morales’s background – and said he was hired by ICE in August 2025 as part of the agency’s aggressive immigration “surge” into a number of US cities.

He declined to give details of any previous employers and said he had not received any of Morales’s training records.

“Whether or not he has those, we don’t know, but I can unequivocally tell you that I’ve reviewed thousands of job applications and resumes for law enforcement officers from around this state, and I’m not familiar with a single agency that would have hired this person based on his past,” Teare said.

Lawyers for Parra Hernandez, who remains in ICE custody, have said he would need numerous operations to recover from his injuries.

The whereabouts of the person that ICE said it was pursuing when Parra Hernandez was hurt are unknown. The agency identified a man named Jose Mendoza-Cervantes as their target, and released an image of someone they said was him.

title: Opinion: Trump Administration Policies Put Immigrant Survivors of Domestic Violence at Risk
description:
Immigrant survivors face intertwined vulnerability—either the gender and sexual violence they escaped in their home countries or the intimate partner violence happening at home in the United States.
Under previous administrations, the United States afforded certain protections for noncitizens experiencing domestic violence within the U.S. and provided a safe haven for those fleeing domestic and gender-based violence abroad.
These incidents are horrifying, considering ICE recruited dozens of new agents with histories of domestic violence and other crimes during its recent hiring expansion.
The Alliance for Immigrant Survivors found 50 percent of immigrant survivors abandon legal action because they fear ICE detaining them in court.
ICE partnerships with local law enforcement further endanger immigrant survivors because calling 911 for domestic violence has led to more immigrant victims being detained.
text:
“Immigrant survivors face intertwined vulnerability—either the gender and sexual violence they escaped in their home countries or the intimate partner violence happening at home in the United States.”

From day one of Trump’s second term, the federal government began dismantling key protections that immigrant survivors have counted on to seek domestic violence support, immigration relief, and other services without fear the government would victimize them further with arrest or deportation.

This week with both National Immigrants Day and Domestic Violence Awareness Month, immigrant survivors and their advocates want to put into stark relief that escaping violence or coercion at the hands of intimate partners or family is far from the only hurdle to reaching security. Under Trump 2.0, the U.S. government is now the ultimate abuser.

As two directors from a leading civil legal services provider, we have collectively served thousands of clients who faced both domestic violence and the immigration system. Immigrant survivors face intertwined vulnerability—either the gender and sexual violence they escaped in their home countries or the intimate partner violence happening at home in the United States.

Under previous administrations, the United States afforded certain protections for noncitizens experiencing domestic violence within the U.S. and provided a safe haven for those fleeing domestic and gender-based violence abroad. While the system was far from perfect, the current administration’s combination of rollbacks of critical protections and ramped up immigration enforcement is a crisis for immigrant survivors.

On inauguration day, Trump’s Department of Homeland Security (DHS) rescinded guidelines preventing immigration enforcement arrests at “sensitive locations,” including domestic violence shelters, hospitals, and courthouses. Survivors questioned if it was safe to seek orders of protection, medical care, or shelter services.

In New York City where we serve clients, masked agents began physically restraining women, roughly handling pregnant women, and warehousing people in inadequate conditions in immigration courthouses. These incidents are horrifying, considering ICE recruited dozens of new agents with histories of domestic violence and other crimes during its recent hiring expansion.

Our attorneys who show up at immigration courts daily witnessed the chilling effect these arrests caused as immigrants must weigh the impossible: continuing their immigration case versus deportation back to an unsafe place. In a survey last year, 70 percent of attorneys and advocates for immigrant survivors reported that their clients were concerned about going to court for matters related to domestic violence protections. The Alliance for Immigrant Survivors found 50 percent of immigrant survivors abandon legal action because they fear ICE detaining them in court.

Within roughly the first week of Trump taking office, DHS stripped key protections granted to immigrant survivors of domestic violence, human trafficking and other crimes under the Violence Against Women Act (VAWA), which prevented immigration authorities from arresting, detaining, and deporting crime victims for decades.

Among the changes are more stringent requirements for survivors to provide documentation of abuse—evidence many survivors don’t have. Access to special visas granted to crime victims under VAWA, so that prosecutors can more easily pursue domestic violence or trafficking cases, are already restricted, putting thousands of immigrant survivors at risk. And if followed, Project 2025’s blueprint for the Trump agenda calls to eliminate these special visas completely.

ICE partnerships with local law enforcement further endanger immigrant survivors because calling 911 for domestic violence has led to more immigrant victims being detained. With law enforcement now deputized as immigration enforcement and incentivized to aid federal agents in deportations and arrests, ICE handed abusers a potent tool of coercion and control: the threat of deportation.

Many immigrant survivors face obstacles in safely separating from their abuser because they are forced to rely on their partner legally and financially, especially if their partner is their U.S. citizen sponsor supporting their application for a green card or legal permanent residence. Their ability to have work authorization and work lawfully is also tied to these proceedings. Making the problem worse, the Supreme Court effectively ended Temporary Protected Status and DHS proposed a policy change, both drastically limiting immigrants’ access to employment authorization.

Trump’s “Big Beautiful Bill” also unleashed a torrent of attacks on access to public benefits, including revoking SNAP, Medicaid, and Children’s Health Insurance Program eligibility for survivors of domestic violence and human trafficking. The Congressional Budget Office estimates that 90,000 people will lose SNAP food assistance benefits. Most advocates agree: “most domestic violence victims rely on SNAP to help address their basic needs and to establish safety and stability.” Trump’s proposed 2027 budget promises even more cuts, including $14 million for transitional housing and $15 million for legal assistance programs.

The Trump administration is further threatening immigrant survivors’ independence with an unlawful new “public charge” rule that will deny lawful permanent resident status if they or their children receive public benefits. Confusion surrounding which benefits might qualify—now or in the future—discourages immigrant survivors from seeking benefits they might otherwise use on their path to personal stability.

Even more cruelly, Trump’s Department of Justice ended exceptions for federal assistance previously designated as necessary for the “protection of life or safety,” which included federally-funded community-based organizations providing domestic violence and homeless services. Without these supports for basic necessities and financial independence, safety and security is dwindling under Trump 2.0.

Amid this backdrop of aggressive immigration enforcement and benefits restrictions, the demand for immigration and domestic violence legal and support services are higher than ever. In addition to calling on national elected leaders to rein in immigration enforcement and restore federal funding for public benefits, we must boost funds for the nonprofits stepping up to help fill the gaps.

Because every day, advocates like us will show up, fight against those who wield their power unjustly, and empower people to chart their own path toward safety, stability and independence.

text:
A grand jury in Texas has indicted a United States Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer accused of deliberately running over a Mexican construction worker during an operation in Houston this month.

ICE officer Mario Alberto Morales faces charges of aggravated assault with a deadly weapon for the October 10 incident, Harris County District Attorney Sean Teare announced on Friday.

Recommended Stories

list of 3 items

list 1 of 3Will ICE agents play a role in the 2026 US midterm elections?

list 2 of 3On the US border in Texas, Trump deportation drive galvanises midterm vote

list 3 of 3Trump administration attempts to take down leak of ICE personnel data

end of list

Criminal charges against federal immigration officers have been rare during President Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown, although several encounters involving officers have prompted investigations.

Morales is accused of striking 48-year-old Miguel Parra-Hernandez, an immigrant who has lived in Harris County for more than 30 years. Teare said that Parra-Hernandez had no criminal record.

Parra-Hernandez was running away from federal agents when an unmarked black Jeep Cherokee struck him in a car park near Clay Road and Highway 6, according to investigators. He suffered multiple fractures to his right leg and an ankle injury which required surgery.

The indictment follows a dispute between local prosecutors and federal authorities over what happened. ICE has maintained that Parra-Hernandez ran in front of the vehicle, dismissing the allegations that the officer intentionally struck him as “reckless and false.”

But Teare has said surveillance video contradicts the agency’s account.

It shows the SUV crossing a median and pursuing Parra-Hernandez as he runs away. Although another vehicle obscures the moment of impact, the video shows the man on the ground moments later.

Authorities also released body-camera footage on Friday. In the recording, Morales can be heard acknowledging that he struck Parra-Hernandez with his vehicle.

Teare also accused federal authorities of failing to cooperate with the investigation, including by removing the Jeep before local investigators could examine it for potential evidence.

A search warrant obtained by local media shows investigators had not been granted access to the vehicle as of October 23.

The case has also raised questions about the operation’s intended target. ICE said agents were searching for a man identified as Jose Mendoza-Cervantes, whom they believed to be travelling with Parra-Hernandez.

But Mendoza-Cervantes’s daughter told The New York Times that her father died in 2017. Parra-Hernandez’s family has disputed that the two men knew each other.

The Morales indictment comes as the Harris County District Attorney’s Office continues investigating the fatal shooting of another Mexican, Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, on July 7.

An ICE officer, Gregory Feathers, has been accused of firing at the vehicle Salgado Araujo was driving on his way to work in Houston.

Federal authorities said the officer acted in self-defence, a claim the surviving passengers in the vehicle dispute.

text:
SAN ANTONIO – Federal prosecutors in the Western District of Texas filed 256 new immigration and immigration-related criminal cases from Oct. 23 through Oct. 30, announced U.S. Attorney Justin R. Simmons. Charges were brought against alien smugglers and illegal aliens with past convictions for violent crimes, numerous DWIs, thefts, and multiple prior removals. The new batch of immigration cases brings the total number across the district’s seven offices to nearly 1,000 in October, averaging approximately 250 cases filed per week.

Among the new cases, prosecutors charged Miguel Malo Poggio with transportation of illegal aliens. Supporting an investigation led by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) Homeland Security Investigations (HSI), U.S. Border Patrol agents conducted a traffic stop on a tractor-trailer traveling north on Interstate 25 north of Las Cruces, New Mexico. The driver was identified as Malo Poggio. As alleged in a criminal complaint affidavit, agents located a black backpack containing numerous cellular devices in a storage compartment of the truck’s cab. When questioned about the devices, Malo Poggio allegedly handed an agent a set of keys from his pocket, indicating that the keys were for the cargo trailer, which was secured with a red tamper-evident seal.

According to the affidavit, agents discovered 42 illegal aliens inside the trailer, including three unaccompanied minors. The aliens were unrestrained and seated on the floor in rows and columns without an apparent means of exit. The affidavit alleges that at least one of the aliens stated they had illegally crossed into the United States less than a week prior, was taken to a stash house where their phone was confiscated and eventually loaded into the tractor-trailer where they were told to sit, remain quiet and stay hidden. This case remains under investigation and is being prosecuted in El Paso.

Also in El Paso, Omar Lorenzo Olivas-Chavez, an illegal alien from Mexico, was charged with illegal re-entry after he allegedly attempted to enter the U.S. with false information. A criminal complaint alleges Olivas-Chavez applied for admission via the pedestrian lane at the Bridge of the Americas Port of Entry on Oct. 23, stating to a U.S. Customs and Border Protection officer that he was a U.S. Citizen and had lost his entry documents. The complaint alleges Olivas-Chavez wrote down a name and date of birth for the officer, which, after further inspection, was determined to be fictitious. A fingerprint scan revealed Olivas-Chaves has been previously removed from the U.S. to Mexico six times and has been convicted of burglary of habitation twice. He’s also been previously convicted of criminal trespass, evading arrest, assault on a public servant, and escape while arrested.

Alvaro Lopez Ayala, an illegal alien from Mexico, was transferred to ICE custody and charged with illegal entry in San Antonio. Lopez was arrested in New Braunfels in May and transferred to the Travis County Jail in July to serve time pending a rape charge, according to a criminal complaint. On Oct. 21, Lopez was convicted of indecent assault in Travis County and sentenced to 300 days confinement. Lopez was previously removed from the U.S. in 2014. In addition to the indecent assault conviction, he has been previously convicted of cred card abuse, aggravated assault causing serious bodily injury, and evading arrest.

Roberto Espinoza-Ponce, also an illegal alien from Mexico, was arrested by a deportation officer in Del Valle on Tuesday. Espinoza-Ponce has been previously removed from the U.S. three times and convicted for two DWIs, a hit-and-run, and failure to ID. If convicted, this will be his second for illegal re-entry.

Selvin Noe Santos-Umana, an illegal alien from Honduras, was arrested by U.S. Border Patrol agents near Eagle Pass and charged with illegal re-entry. Santos-Umana was deported for the first time in April. He was convicted in 2024 for robbery using force, and has also been previously convicted of domestic battery, use and possession of drug paraphernalia, and interfering with a law enforcement officer.

Jose Elmer Argueta-Argueta, an illegal alien from El Salvador, was also arrested near Eagle Pass and charged with illegal re-entry. He was just deported in August for the eighth time. Argueta-Argueta has been previously convicted of two illegal re-entry charges, a DWI, forging public documents, and destruction of property with malicious wounding.

These cases were referred or supported by federal law enforcement partners, including ICE, U.S. Border Patrol, the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA), the FBI, the U.S. Marshals Service (USMS), and the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF), with additional assistance from state and local law enforcement partners.

The U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Western District of Texas comprises 68 counties located in the central and western areas of Texas, encompasses nearly 93,000 square miles and an estimated population of 7.6 million people. The district includes three of the five largest cities in Texas—San Antonio, Austin and El Paso—and shares 660 miles of common border with the Republic of Mexico.

Indictments and criminal complaints are merely allegations and all defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law.

These cases are part of Operation Take Back America a nationwide initiative that marshals the full resources of the Department of Justice to repel the invasion of illegal immigration, achieve the total elimination of cartels and transnational criminal organizations (TCOs), and protect our communities from the perpetrators of violent crime.

text:
HOUSTON (AP) — A U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer accused of intentionally ramming his car into a Mexican construction worker in Houston was indicted by a grand jury Friday on a charge of aggravated assault with a deadly weapon, prosecutors said.

The officer, Mario Alberto Morales, was driving an unmarked SUV on Oct. 10 when he struck and ran over Miguel Parra Hernandez, 48, who was running away during a pursuit through a parking lot, the Harris County District Attorney's Office said. Parra Hernandez broke his leg and remains in federal custody at a rehabilitation facility, District Attorney Sean Teare said.

READ MORE: ICE officer appeared to intentionally hit a man with a vehicle in Houston, Texas prosecutor says

ICE has asserted that Parra Hernandez ran in front of the vehicle, an account that Teare said is contradicted by video.

"The evidence we have in this case is as clear as any that I've ever prosecuted or investigated," Teare said.

Morales, 33, of Brownsville, Texas, is one of just a few federal officers who have faced criminal charges over their actions on the job during President Donald Trump's immigration crackdown, although other encounters have come under investigation, including a fatal shooting by an ICE officer this summer in Houston.

Morales' attorney, David Lindenmuth, said his client didn't commit a crime and he accused Teare of indicting Morales "for political gain." Morales had worked as an ICE Enforcement and Removal Operations officer for a little more than a year, Lindenmuth said.

"Mr. Morales is truly a good man, a former member of our military, that has given his entire life to public service either for his country or in or adjacent to law enforcement," Lindenmuth told The Associated Press. "To have him charged for what was so clearly just an accident — the DA's office, the DA himself, has invented a crime out of thin air."

WATCH: ICE shooting of man in New York with child in his car sparks outrage

Teare hinted at concerns over Morales' background but would not provide details.

Morales, who is charged with a second-degree felony, was not in custody Friday and a warrant will be issued for his arrest, according to Teare.

ICE asserted that local officials do not have the authority to investigate federal officers acting in the course of their duties.

"Allegations that ICE struck Miguel Parra-Hernandez intentionally are RECKLESS and FALSE," the agency said in a statement.

The district attorney played Morales' body camera footage

Teare has said video clearly contradicts the ICE account. Surveillance video shows a Jeep Cherokee speed over a median and drive toward Parra Hernandez as he runs away. During a news conference Friday, he played Morales' body camera footage, which shows him driving and talking about pursuing someone.

The video shows Morales making a few sharp moves with the steering wheel before the SUV shakes. Morales stops the vehicle, then gets out and turns toward Parra Hernandez, who is several feet away. The video then shows Parra Hernandez on the ground and grabbing his leg, yelling in pain.

Morales is heard saying, "He got hit with a car, bro." It is not clear to whom he is talking.

"I was coming in and I hit him with the car," Morales says.

Family says ICE was looking for a dead person during operation

Parra Hernandez has lived in Harris County for more than 30 years and did not have a deportation order or criminal background, according to Teare.

Other aspects of ICE's account have also been called into question.

READ MORE: New ICE guidance bans high-speed car chases and sets tighter rules for traffic stops, memo shows

After Parra Hernandez was taken into custody, ICE released a photo of another man, Jose Mendoza-Cervantes, and said he was the target of the operation that day. ICE said he was seen entering a vehicle with Parra Hernandez. Family members of Parra Hernandez said they had never heard of him. FIEL, an immigrant rights group in Houston that has been working with the family, said Mendoza-Cervantes' daughter told them her father has been dead since 2017.

Teare's office has previously said its investigation has not found that Parra Hernandez and the man ICE identified as Mendoza-Cervantes were in a vehicle together, contrary to ICE's statement.

ICE has not responded to claims that the suspect they were looking for has been dead for years.

Fatal summer Houston shooting also under investigation

Teare has said the Department of Homeland Security, which oversees ICE, has not cooperated with his investigators and accused ICE of destroying evidence "either intentionally or through gross negligence." He has said Morales left the scene before the vehicle could be impounded.

In July, Teare said DHS also ignored his requests for information after an ICE officer fatally shot 52-year-old Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in his van. DHS has said Salgado Araujo had "weaponized his vehicle" before the shooting and that an officer fired in self-defense. Other passengers in the van have disputed that account.

Wilder reported from Austin, Texas.

Wilder is a corps member for The Associated Press/Report for America Statehouse News Initiative. Report for America is a nonprofit national service program that places journalists in local newsrooms to report on undercovered issues.

The county also said ICE vehicles had recently been seen on a dirt road near the jail on Thursday.

However, Monterey County Supervisor Luis Alejo posted that vehicles returned shortly after leaving at around 11 a.m. and that two ICE vehicles were parked outside the entrance.

title: Trump's quiet border has relieved Democrats of their thorniest issue before the midterms | Fortune
description:
Amid the rising U.S. cost of living, a destabilizing war in Iran and a disrupted system of global commerce, the now-quiet border has relieved Democrats of their thorniest issue just in time for midterm elections.
According to The Economist/YouGov polling cited earlier, 1% of Democrats named immigration as their top issue in September 2026.
During this period, Democrats commonly cited immigrants’ acute vulnerability and their willingness and ability to fill critical low-skilled and high-skilled labor gaps.
After the global pandemic halted most human mobility in 2020, the Biden administration sought to avoid the immigration issue altogether.
No mandate for inaction Should Democrats win majorities in the Senate and House of Representatives in 2026, the issue of immigration is highly unlikely to be resolved.
text:
Scott Shuchart, a Biden appointee who joined the Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency in 2022, told the newspaper that the White House was “wishing the problem would go away so that they could focus on the things they cared about.”

But two years after Donald Trump leveraged voter dissatisfaction with the Biden administration’s management of the U.S. southern border to win the 2024 election and enforce his immigration crackdown, the issue has suddenly become a secondary matter.

Amid the rising U.S. cost of living, a destabilizing war in Iran and a disrupted system of global commerce, the now-quiet border has relieved Democrats of their thorniest issue just in time for midterm elections.

From liability to advantage

For the past three decades, the Democratic Party and its candidates have struggled to develop and pass new immigration policies and communicate related political messages.

Bipartisan attempts at comprehensive immigration reform died on Capitol Hill in 2006, 2007 and 2013. Since then, a majority of Americans has trusted Republicans more with governing the issue. That has given the GOP an advantage when the salience of immigration policy has risen due to border crises and related high-profile events, even if that edge has recently narrowed.

In a February 2024 poll, 28% of U.S. respondents told Gallup that immigration was the country’s most important problem – matching the largest share since tracking began in 1981. By May 2026, that figure was 8%, a staggering drop in such a short period.

In a different poll by The Economist/YouGov, the share of U.S. registered voters who identified immigration as the country’s most important issue fell from 14% in October 2024 to 5% in September 2026.

Erik Iverson, a Republican Senate campaign pollster, recently told Axios that declining border crossings have reduced the urgency of immigration, depriving Republicans of an issue that previously energized voters and offered conservatives an advantage.

“You become a victim of your own success,” he said.

But this success is dubious. President Trump’s approval ratings on immigration are underwater.

In the RealClear Polling average from September to October 2026, his net approval was at negative 10.8%. In a recent Fox News poll, most Americans believe the Trump administration has “gone too far” in enforcing immigration laws, including 60% of independents.

Despite Republicans’ insistence that the mass removal of undocumented immigrants and a halt to new migrants would raise wages and make housing more accessible, Americans are experiencing high inflation rates, slow gross domestic product growth and sour consumer sentiment.

Ominously for the White House, Trump’s negative 10.8% net approval score on immigration is actually among his best. On inflation, the economy and foreign policy, his net approval rating is at negative 42.8%, negative 31.7% and negative 27.8%, respectively.

These dynamics bode well for Democrats’ midterm election prospects.

Republicans are now less concerned about immigration – what has been their greatest source of political energy and the left’s greatest political liability – as both parties’ voters are focused on other matters.

Despite the White House’s aggressive and frequently violent pursuit of undocumented immigrants, its proposal to end birthright citizenship, and its near closure of U.S. borders, even Democrats are no more likely to identify immigration as the country’s top issue today than they were previously.

According to The Economist/YouGov polling cited earlier, 1% of Democrats named immigration as their top issue in September 2026. In October 2024, 3% said the same.

Remarkably, without Democrats’ endorsement of a single new immigration policy idea, independents now express greater trust in Democrats than Republicans on immigration, 41% to 27%, according to a September 2026 Marist survey.

Democrats’ trial and error

Democrats’ sudden edge arises after a decade of trialing different approaches to counter the nativism and popular discomfort that Trump has harnessed.

Before Trump’s 2016 election victory and immediately thereafter, Democratic leaders sought to ameliorate the image of foreigners in the U.S., by highlighting that immigrants start more businesses, file more patents and commit fewer crimes than native-born U.S. citizens on average.

During this period, Democrats commonly cited immigrants’ acute vulnerability and their willingness and ability to fill critical low-skilled and high-skilled labor gaps. But the praise and pity produced resentment among many Americans who did not want an admissions system that elevated foreigners to a higher pedestal.

Toward the end of the first Trump administration, Democrats began citing the immense macroeconomic and fiscal benefits driven by immigrants’ long-term settlement in the U.S.

Economists attribute to immigrants the bulk of U.S. population growth from 1990 to 2015. And economists have shown that continued immigration mitigates inflation and extends the solvency of Social Security and Medicare funds. Immigration also provides workers for industries like construction, agriculture, food production and healthcare.

However, the benefits of these relationships for average voters tend to be diffuse and realized in the medium-to-long run. That makes them hard to recognize.

After the global pandemic halted most human mobility in 2020, the Biden administration sought to avoid the immigration issue altogether. It’s a strategy that Democrats have now carried over while the dynamics of being out of power still permit doing so.

No mandate for inaction

Should Democrats win majorities in the Senate and House of Representatives in 2026, the issue of immigration is highly unlikely to be resolved. As a matter of constitutional oversight, Democrats plan to commence investigations into the Trump administration’s abusive immigration enforcement tactics, questionable case adjudication and alleged corruption.

It will be almost impossible to pass meaningful immigration legislation in such an environment.

The Biden-era approach was a pivotal electoral liability in 2024. And the Obama administration’s series of immigration executive actions instigated a tennis match of such orders between subsequent administrations ever since.

Democrats will soon feel some pressure to develop bipartisan approaches to immigration governance that ensure order at U.S. borders and a strategy for immigrant selection and integration that is designed with the national interest in mind.

Justin Gest, Professor of Policy and Government, George Mason University; Institute for Humane Studies

text:
A liberal-majority appeals court in California handed the Trump administration a victory by blocking a lower court's ruling that ordered the State Department to open its application pool for the 2027 Diversity Visa lottery, which admits roughly 55,000 immigrants from low-immigration countries each year.

In a 2-1 ruling, the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals blocked a preliminary injunction issued by U.S. District Judge Jinsook Ohta requiring the lottery pool to be opened after Secretary of State Marco Rubio issued a notice in November delaying the program's acceptance of new applications in order to "implement certain changes," but the application period never opened.

A month later, the State Department ordered an indefinite pause on issuing diversity visas after a Portuguese national who was issued a lottery visa in 2017 committed a mass shooting at Brown University, killing two people and injuring nine others. The shooter, Claudio Manuel Neves Valente, was also tied to the murder of a Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) professor two days after the Brown University shooting.

FBI REVEALS BROWN UNIVERSITY MASS SHOOTER BEGAN PLOTTING MASSACRE AS EARLY AS 2022, BLAMED VICTIMS

The Ninth Circuit has been a perennial thorn in the side of President Donald Trump, having ruled against key portions of Trump's 2017 executive order restricting travel from predominantly Muslim countries and blocked a policy barring immigrants from being eligible for asylum if they crossed the southern border between ports of entry.

However, the appeals court ruled that the lower court's preliminary injunction could not be enforced, finding that the immigration law firm Red Eagle, which represents individuals going through the visa lottery process, did not have standing to sue the federal government. The appeals court ruled that the program was intended to "encourage immigration, not generate revenue for law firms."

LIBERAL COURT STUNS WITH RULING THAT HANDS TRUMP MAJOR IMMIGRATION WIN

The court wrote, "If Red Eagle Law were allowed to allege standing based upon its hypothetical or conjectural collateral injury, we would be opening the floodgates, allowing all lawyers to ‘roam the country in search of governmental wrongdoing.’"

However, the court made clear that its ruling was based on procedural grounds and did not weigh whether the State Department failed to follow the law.

"We do not endorse the Department’s failure to open the lottery registration period," the court wrote.

Abhishek Kambli, a former federal prosecutor and partner at Holtzman Vogel, said the decision by the liberal court was a "very easy call" in a post on X.

"Here, the plaintiff was a law firm not bringing a claim on behalf of someone in the diversity visa lottery but on behalf of the firm itself," Kambli wrote. "The district court should have never gone beyond standing but CA9 corrected this one."

TRUMP ADMIN ANNOUNCES EXPANSION OF VISA RESTRICTION POLICY IN WESTERN HEMISPHERE

President Donald Trump has been vocal about his opposition to the Visa Lottery Program for years. During his January 2018 State of the Union address, he called for ending the program, arguing that visas should be issued based on merit.

Earlier that same month, Trump said during a bipartisan meeting with lawmakers at the White House that lottery visas allow the "worst of the worst" to come into the country.

"They call it ‘visa lottery,’ I just call it ‘lottery.’ But countries come in and they put names in a hopper," Trump said. "They’re not giving you their best names; common sense means they’re not giving you their best names."

Countries eligible for the 2026 lottery included Afghanistan, New Zealand, Ecuador, Iran, Uganda, Somalia and Russia. The program was designed to create an additional pathway for people seeking visas who may not qualify through traditional channels, such as employment- or family-based immigration.
