text:
Joins coalition of 17 in filing brief to protect state AG enforcement of fraud-fighting laws

October 30, 2026 (SAINT PAUL) — Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison today joined 17 attorneys general in defending a basic principle: fraud is against the law, no matter who commits it or how big or sophisticated the victim is.

Attorney General Ellison and the coalition joined a friend-of-the-court brief today in the civil fraud case that the State of New York brought against Donald Trump and his business associates for inflating the values of assets to obtain better terms on loans and insurance policies. On appeal, Trump and his fellow defendants are asking New York’s highest court to rule that the state had no business stepping in because the banks they defrauded were big, sophisticated institutions that never complained. That argument, if it prevails, could make it harder for attorneys general across the country, including in Minnesota, to go after fraud on behalf of the public.

“The biggest fraudster in America — and the most nakedly corrupt president of all time — wants a court to rule that fraud doesn’t really matter when people of his wealth and power commit it. He makes that point over and over when he pardons every billionaire fraudster he can,” Attorney General Ellison said. “Donald Trump wants to rip up our Constitution and rip off the legal guardrails holding him back from wreaking his grubbiest and most authoritarian impulses on the rest of us. But in America, everyone is equally protected under the law, and no one is above the law. Especially not Donald Trump.”

Minnesota law already provides Minnesota’s attorney general many tools to step in when charities or businesses are used to cheat or deceive — even if the people directly involved or harmed do not take action themselves. Many other states have similar laws. The brief that Attorney General Ellison and the coalition filed today explains why these laws matter:

Fraud hurts more than the people in the deal. It warps the marketplace and chips away at the idea that the rules apply to everyone.

Cheaters get an unfair edge. A business that lies to get cheaper loans can undercut honest competitors, and consumers end up paying for it.

When big institutions get hurt, regular people feel it. Fraud against a large bank puts its employees, depositors, and everyone who relies on it at risk.

Sometimes no one else will act. Powerful players may have their own reasons for staying quiet, including their own enrichment. An attorney general’s job is to look out for the public, not just the self-interested parties at the table.

The case, People v. Trump, is before the New York Court of Appeals, New York’s highest court. New York Attorney General Letitia James brought it under a state law that authorizes her office to go after repeated or ongoing business fraud. The defendants are Donald Trump, Eric Trump, Allen Weisselberg, and Jeffrey McConney.

Attorney General Ellison joined this brief alongside the attorneys general of Arizona, California, Connecticut, Delaware, Hawaiʻi, Illinois, Maine, Massachusetts, Michigan, Nevada, New Jersey, New Mexico, Oregon, Vermont, Virginia, and Washington.

The snapshot is based on 467 surveys with migrants and refugees who reported using smuggling services during their journey to or within Mauritania.
text:
Migrants expelled from Mauritania to Senegal describe violent raids, detention without explanation and days without adequate food or water after crossing the border, according to new field research by the Mixed Migration Centre (MMC).

Earlier this year, in August, an MMC project coordinator for West Africa traveled to Rosso, a town on the Senegal River that separates Senegal and Mauritania. Over one week, the coordinator spoke with people recently expelled from Mauritania and with organizations working in the town. The visit also supported the launch of MMC’s 4Mi data collection in the area.

Three group returns crossed the official border during the week. The largest involved about 100 people.

“They treat us as if we are not human beings,” was the phrase migrants repeated most often according to the MMC coordinator.

Read Also

Over 1,300 dead or missing on migration routes to Spain from January to May 2026

Raids and alleged discrimination

Migrants and local organizations described security operations in which officers did not check documents before detaining people. Some said that people with regular migration status were also taken.

Many of those interviewed said Black foreign nationals appeared to be disproportionately targeted, including people from Burkina Faso, Mali, Guinea and Côte d’Ivoire. “Once you are Black, there is a problem,” several people said.

A Togolese woman told MMC that she had spent about 500,000 CFA francs, approximately $850, to obtain her documents. She said she had the documents with her, but that no one checked them before she was expelled.

Others said their documents were torn up during raids. Without identity documents, people may struggle to prove their nationality, obtain consular assistance or access voluntary return programs.

MMC could not independently verify every individual account. The consistency of the descriptions, however, points to a broader pattern reported by people arriving in Rosso.

Read Also

Malians flee instability, 'horrors,' and Russian armed groups to head for Mauritania

Accounts of detention

People interviewed by MMC gave broadly similar accounts of detention.

They said they were taken without being able to explain their situation, placed in vehicles and driven to detention without explanation. Several said they were not allowed to contact relatives.

According to multiple accounts, people were held in cells and given one meal a day until there were enough people, around 40 or more, to be transported to Senegal.

Some said the raids were taking place in different parts of Mauritania. Many of the people who arrived in Rosso on one day said they had been detained in Nouadhibou, on the Atlantic coast, after their boat toward the Canary Islands broke down.

UNHCR told InfoMigrants that refugees and asylum seekers in Mauritanian cities, particularly Nouakchott and Nouadhibou, have reported increased immigration enforcement since late 2024, including arrests, detention and deportations.

The agency said the measures raise protection concerns, including access to asylum procedures and the risk of refoulement. It said it engages Mauritanian authorities to advocate for compliance with international refugee and human rights law and intervenes in individual cases where protection concerns are identified.

UNHCR said its monitoring, hotline and legal partner follow up on reports of arrests and detentions involving refugees and asylum seekers. It said these interventions have contributed to the release of refugees and asylum seekers in a number of cases.

Read Also

Mauritania intercepts 161 migrants as Atlantic route departures continue

Family separation also documented

Children are also affected by raids and detention. One case involved a woman who said she left her three-month-old baby upstairs while she went downstairs to buy food. She said she was detained during a raid and expelled to Rosso.

Staff from the International Organization for Migration (IOM) on both sides of the border were contacted. They located the baby and reunited the child with her mother in Rosso.

Another woman, a Guinean national living in Mauritania with her Mauritanian husband, said she was turned away when she tried to return from a family visit to Guinea. At the time of the interview, she was waiting in Rosso for her husband to find a way to bring her home.

Read Also

'Those who remain': Families of migrants mourn their disappearance in Senegal

Smuggling dynamics in Mauritania

MMC’s June 2026 4Mi snapshot on smuggling dynamics in Mauritania provides wider context for the enforcement operations described in Rosso. It says data collection took place during a period of heightened enforcement, during which more than 30,000 people were apprehended in raids and interceptions and at least 18,300 were expelled to Mali and Senegal.

The snapshot is based on 467 surveys with migrants and refugees who reported using smuggling services during their journey to or within Mauritania. Rosso was one of five survey locations, alongside Nouakchott, Nouadhibou, Chami and Sélibaby.

However, the report does not document the experiences of people who had already been expelled or abused. MMC notes that such individuals were outside Mauritania at the time of data collection and were therefore not included in the sample.

Read Also

EU reported to be considering 12 possible countries to site migrant 'return hubs'

A changing border practice

People in Rosso said the practice changed around the end of 2025, after Senegalese authorities told their Mauritanian counterparts that non-Senegalese nationals should be returned to their countries of origin rather than remain in Senegal.

According to their accounts, Mauritanian forces then began taking non-Senegalese nationals at night by pirogue to unofficial points along the river. Others said they were left on the Mauritanian riverbank and told to find their own way across to Senegal or face arrest.

MMC could not independently verify these accounts. They nonetheless reflect concerns that tighter border controls may be pushing migration into more dangerous and less visible routes.

The accounts collected by MMC echo reporting by InfoMigrants in 2025, when Mauritania began a sustained campaign of arrests and expulsions of migrants in an irregular situation. InfoMigrants reported that hundreds of people, including Senegalese, Malians, Ivorians, Guineans and Gambians, became stranded in and around Rosso, where aid workers described regular arrivals of buses carrying 60 to 70 people and severe shortages of water, food, medicine and shelter.

Mauritanian authorities described the operations as routine enforcement against irregular migration and said expulsions complied with international conventions. Then Interior Minister Mohamed Ahmed Ould Mohamed Lemine said the expulsions were carried out "in accordance with international conventions." Authorities did not publish figures on the scale of the removals.

infomigrants

Read Also

More than 250 migrants rescued off Mauritania

Limited assistance in Rosso

People expelled through the official crossing said Senegalese police questioned them and then released them without food, water, shelter or onward assistance.

A humanitarian organization that began working in Rosso about three months before the MMC visit provides water and food on weekdays. There is no regular provision on weekends. On one Saturday, about 100 people spent the entire day without food or water.

One man told MMC that, in Mauritania, he had been held in a cell but had received a piece of bread each day.

Many said they had no work and had left their belongings behind. A young Malian man, who was unable to take his luggage with him, said he slept outside a shop, paying its owner 1,000 CFA francs (about €1.50) per night.

Men can sleep in an open-sided shelter near the river run by a local organization. Women said they often had no comparable place to stay. Food, shelter and health care remain major concerns.

Read Also

Guinea-Bissau drawn into shifting migration routes and human trafficking

Documents and return

People who want to return home can register for IOM’s voluntary return program, but they need proof of nationality. Some people obtain a scan of an identity card or birth certificate from relatives at home.

People whose documents were torn up, and who cannot obtain replacements, may be unable to access the program. They are among the most vulnerable people in Rosso -- unable to remain safely, unable to return through formal channels and dependent on informal support.

On the edge of town, young Nigerian women were living in a villa with poor sanitation and said they were doing sex work.

“They clearly said this was not what they wanted,” the MMC coordinator said, adding, “They were trying to reach Morocco or Europe, but they were rounded up and ended up in Rosso, Senegal. They have no work.”

Read Also

Over 1,300 dead or missing on migration routes to Spain from January to May 2026

Enforcement and protection

Mauritania’s migration enforcement is taking place amid expanded international cooperation. In 2024, the European Union and Mauritania announced a 210 million euro partnership covering migration management, anti-smuggling efforts, refugee assistance and employment initiatives.

Mauritanian authorities have also reported repeated interceptions of boats traveling toward the Canary Islands. On October 27, 2026, the coast guard said it had located a vessel carrying 204 people, including 28 minors, who had reportedly departed from Barra in The Gambia.

Mauritania describes such operations as rescue and border management missions. But accounts from Rosso raise a separate question: what happens to people after they are intercepted, detained or expelled?

The situation in Rosso is no secret. Expelled people gather near the river, local organizations are aware of their presence and international agencies know they are there.

Yet assistance remains limited. People interviewed by field researchers said conditions were worsening rather than improving.

Read Also

Senegal: How women bear the burden of migration

text:
The 2027 business immigration outlook for employers combines new restrictions with legal uncertainty. Automatic Employment Authorization Document (EAD) extensions are ending and visa processing is slower. At the same time, several proposals face legal and procedural challenges, and courts have blocked major initiatives such as the $100,000 H-1B fee. With the midterm elections approaching, the administration has proposed further changes to the US immigration system.

In this webinar, Mintz attorneys John Quill, William Coffman, and Arash Bahar explain which changes are in effect, which proposals are pending and how likely they are to advance, and which policies are stopped in litigation. They also outline practical steps for the March 2027 H-1B lottery, PERM compliance, and international travel.

Key Takeaways for the 2027 Business Immigration Outlook

The end of automatic EAD extensions creates new work authorization risk.

A final rule issued October 14, 2026 ends automatic EAD extensions for renewals filed on or after October 30, 2026. Previously, many workers could continue working for up to 540 days while a timely filed renewal was pending. The rule affects adjustment of status applicants, H-4 spouses, asylum and refugee applicants, and Temporary Protected Status holders. STEM OPT applicants keep their 180-day automatic extension, and E and L spouses can still work incident to status.

Visa processing delays require more lead time.

Consulates now require in-person interviews for most visas. Mandatory social media vetting for H, F, J, and M applicants is adding time. Section 221(g) administrative processing holds can delay issuance for weeks or months, although in many cases these visas are eventually issued.

Several proposals with significant costs face challenges and may not take effect as written.

Pending rules would eliminate the 60-day grace period, impose a $103,265 fee on all H-1B petitions, charge universities $70,000 for an initial OPT authorization, and raise prevailing wage levels. The OPT proposal would let universities recover part of that fee from the student or the employer, though it's unclear how that would work because OPT isn't tied to a specific employer. The H-1B fee schedule is currently blocked, and the OPT fees are expected to face litigation. The prevailing wage proposal has seen no movement since March 2026.

Program Electronic Review Management (PERM) compliance is under closer scrutiny.

The Department of Labor recently barred companies from filing PERM applications on the basis that they had both sponsored PERM applications and laid off workers. That action is now in litigation. Employers should follow their normal recruitment practices as closely as possible, including acknowledging applicants and sending rejection letters if they usually do so.

Court injunctions for some of the more extreme immigration restrictions are in place, but may be temporary.

Courts have blocked the $100,000 H-1B fee, the end of duration-of-status admission for F, J, and I visa holders, the USCIS processing pause for 39 countries plus Palestine, and the immigrant visa pause for 75 countries. An appeals court could reinstate the $100,000 fee, so employers with affected petitions should consider filing as soon as possible.

Related Questions on the 2027 Business Immigration Outlook

What should employers expect from the March 2027 H-1B lottery?

The March 2027 lottery is expected to keep the weighted wage-level selection system. Selection rates in the 2026 lottery were:

Level 4: 61%

Level 3: 46%

Level 2: 30%

Level 1: about 15%

The registration pool may also be larger this year. The $100,000 fee discouraged registrations for candidates outside the US last year, and that fee is now blocked. Employers can coordinate year-end compensation decisions with lottery planning, particularly for salaries near a wage-level threshold.

How does the new EAD rule affect employers?

Employees with pending EAD renewals risk a gap in work authorization. Keeping an employee in H or L status during a pending adjustment application generally preserves their work authorization.

Are USCIS processing times changing?

USCIS is pushing premium processing as regular processing slows, and requests for evidence (RFEs) are on the rise. Some reflect closer scrutiny of filings. Others appear to be templated or boilerplate RFEs. Approval rates haven't changed meaningfully, but the process is taking longer and costing more.

How long is PERM processing?

PERM processing has improved from about 17 – 18 months to 10 – 11 months. Prevailing wage determinations now take about four months, down from 6 – 7 months.

What should visa holders know about international travel?

Travelers with valid visas have generally been readmitted without issues when they carry an employer verification letter, pay statements, and their approval notice. Travelers who need a new visa face uncertain wait times. Employers may want to consider travel policies that address device inspections, remote work, and delays in returning to the US.

description:
A 9-year-old boy with autism stepped up to a table in Kansas City Immigration Court and sat with his lawyer’s help.
Their lawyers got less than a week's notice to bring their young clients — ages 9 to 17 — to court, according to the Kansas City Asylum Clinic.
All the children have pending or approved applications for Special Immigrant Juvenile status, a classification for immigrant children who were abused, neglected or abandoned by a parent.
METHODOLOGY Immigration reporter Steph Conquest-Ware attended the Kansas City Immigration Court master calendar hearing on Oct. 30, 2026, to observe the proceedings.
In addition, they consulted Department of Homeland Security and legal service providers' documents and materials about Special Immigrant Juvenile status.
text:
A 9-year-old boy with autism stepped up to a table in Kansas City Immigration Court and sat with his lawyer’s help. He wore a long-sleeved Spider-Man shirt with jeans and sneakers. He fiddled with the knob attached to the table’s drawer.

The boy was among about a dozen children from the Kansas City metro in the courtroom on Thursday — all waiting to learn if they will be deported in the coming weeks.

Their lawyers got less than a week's notice to bring their young clients — ages 9 to 17 — to court, according to the Kansas City Asylum Clinic. The attorneys said hearings are usually conducted virtually.

The kids filled the benches in the classroom-sized courtroom for the master calendar hearing, the first step in the deportation process. Some played with fidget toys as they sat through the proceedings.

All the children have pending or approved applications for Special Immigrant Juvenile status, a classification for immigrant children who were abused, neglected or abandoned by a parent. The Trump administration ended deferred deportation for children with SIJ status in April.

At this week’s hearing, none of the children — some missing school to appear in person — were ordered deported. Their next hearings are scheduled for the coming weeks. Englander said changing court dates take a toll on children like her client.

“It has been nonstop chaos,” attorney Aly Englander said outside the courtroom on Thursday. “Kids’ hearings have been advanced and then canceled and then advanced again. It makes it near impossible for us to prepare and represent them in the way that they deserve.”

'Rampant fraud'

In April, United States Citizenship and Immigration Services rescinded its deferred action policy for Special Immigrant Juvenile applications completed after May 10, effectively stopping delayed deportation for these children.

Nationwide, at least 150,000 youth with Special Immigrant Juvenile status now face potential deportation, according to the Young Center for Immigrant Children’s Rights. Once deported, these children lose their chances to apply for green cards.

In June, Department of Homeland Security general counsel James Percival asked state court judges to take greater steps “to combat rampant fraud” in the Special Immigrant Juvenile process. In a press release, DHS said “the SIJ system is at great risk of fraud that, if not properly policed by state court judges, can allow dangerous criminals into our country.”

A group of legal services organizations from around the country sued the government in mid-October. A press release from one of the parties, the National Immigration Law Center, said the suit “challenges the government’s broad attempts to rush the deportation of unaccompanied children in violation of their rights and child protection laws passed by Congress.” The press release calls ending the deferred action policy for Special Immigrant Juvenile status “a cruel and unlawful scheme.”

Englander, the Kansas City Asylum Clinic lawyer, said SIJ status children like her client are on an emotional roller coaster.

“She came in today ready to hear the judge order her deported, and many kids are in this position,” Englander said. “The court does not care about the chaos and the impact that has on the kids."

After the hearing, Englander talked to her young client, who wore her hair in a braided bun. The lawyer told the child a deportation order is likely after her next hearing.

There are many ways you can contact us with story ideas and leads, and you can find that information here. The Midwest Newsroom is a partner of The Trust Project. We invite you to review our ethics and practices here.

METHODOLOGY

Immigration reporter Steph Conquest-Ware attended the Kansas City Immigration Court master calendar hearing on Oct. 30, 2026, to observe the proceedings. They interviewed attorneys before and after the hearings for context and insights. In addition, they consulted Department of Homeland Security and legal service providers' documents and materials about Special Immigrant Juvenile status.

text:
A U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer accused of intentionally ramming his car into a Mexican construction worker in Houston was charged Friday with aggravated assault with a deadly weapon, prosecutors said.

The Harris County District Attorney's office says Mario Alberto Morales was behind the wheel of an unmarked black vehicle on Oct. 10 when it struck Miguel Parra Hernandez, 48, who was running away. Parra Hernandez was later placed in custody with a broken leg.

Few federal officers during President Donald Trump's immigration crackdown have faced criminal charges for their actions in the field, although some encounters have come under investigation.

The case in Houston was brought by District Attorney Sean Teare, a Democrat, who is also investigating the fatal shooting of a Mexican homebuilder in July that set off protests in the nation’s fourth-largest city.

ICE did not immediately respond to a request seeking comment about the indictment charging Morales.

ICE has said Parra Hernandez stepped in front of the car and called accusations that the officer intentionally struck him false and “reckless.” Teare has said the surveillance footage clearly contradicts the ICE account.

In the video, a Jeep Cherokee speeds over a median and drives toward Parra Hernandez as he runs away. The video does not show the car hitting him — that view is blocked by another vehicle — but it shows the SUV inches away from him. The footage then shows Parra Hernandez on the ground.

Family says ICE was looking for a dead person during operation

Other aspects of ICE's account have also been called into question.

ICE released a photo of another man, Jose Mendoza-Cervantes, and said he was the target of the operation that day and was seen entering a vehicle with Parra Hernandez. Family members of Parra Hernandez said they had never heard of him. FIEL, an immigrant rights group in Houston, said Mendoza-Cervantes' daughter told them her father has been dead since 2017. She also said his real name is Jose Hector Jimenez.

Teare's office has also said its investigation has not found that Parra Hernandez and the man ICE identified as Mendoza-Cervantes were in a vehicle together, contrary to ICE's statement.

ICE has not responded to claims that the suspect they were looking for has been dead for nearly a decade.

Parra Hernandez has been in the country for more than 30 years. He was living in the U.S. without authorization, according to FIEL, which has been working with his family.

Fatal summer Houston shooting also under investigation

Teare said the Department of Homeland Security, which oversees ICE, has not cooperated with his investigators and accused ICE of destroying evidence “either intentionally or through gross negligence.” He said the ICE officer who drove the SUV that struck Parra Hernandez fled the scene before the vehicle could be impounded.

In July, Teare said DHS also ignored his requests for information after an ICE officer fatally shot 52-year-old Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in his van. DHS has said Salgado Araujo had “weaponized his vehicle” before the shooting and that an officer fired in self-defense. Other passengers in the van have disputed that account.

Teare has not given a timetable for when his office's investigation into the shooting will be complete. In September, a witness to the shooting was seen entering a courthouse area reserved for grand jury proceedings.

___

Wilder reported from Austin.

text:
A Harris County grand jury indicted a federal immigration agent Friday after he was filmed on video running over a fleeing pedestrian during an Oct. 10 vehicle pursuit in Houston.

District Attorney Sean Teare said his office launched a criminal investigation of the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent after his office reviewed footage showing an unmarked patrol vehicle striking Miguel Parra-Hernandez, 48.

Teare said ICE agent Mario Alberto Morales faces a felony charge of aggravated assault with a deadly weapon — the agent’s vehicle.

“The evidence that we have in this case is as clear as any that I’ve ever prosecuted or investigated,” Teare said at a news conference at the Harris County criminal courthouse.

Surveillance footage captured from a nearby business depicts two men getting out of a white pickup truck and running in different directions through a parking lot. The footage also shows that a black SUV pursued one of the men from behind as he ran from it.

“What happened next shocked our entire community,” Teare said. His office shared ICE body camera footage that showed Morales get out of his vehicle after running over the pedestrian’s legs. Parra-Hernandez was on the ground, crying out in agony.

ICE said that agents were searching for a man named Jose Mendoza-Cervantes, who had a deportation order, and believed that man was in the same truck as Parra-Hernandez.

But Mendoza-Cervantes’s daughter later told the New York Times that her father died nearly a decade ago.

This is a developing story that will be updated.

She also said his real name is Jose Hector Jimenez.

Teare’s office has also said its investigation has not found that Parra Hernandez and the man ICE identified as Mendoza-Cervantes were in a vehicle together, contrary to ICE’s statement.

ICE has not responded to claims that the suspect they were looking for has been dead for nearly a decade.

Parra Hernandez has been in the country for more than 30 years. He was living in the U.S. without authorization, according to FIEL, which has been working with his family.

Fatal summer Houston shooting also under investigation

Teare said the Department of Homeland Security, which oversees ICE, has not cooperated with his investigators and accused ICE of destroying evidence “either intentionally or through gross negligence.” He said the ICE officer who drove the SUV that struck Parra Hernandez fled the scene before the vehicle could be impounded.

In July, Teare said DHS also ignored his requests for information after an ICE officer fatally shot 52-year-old Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in his van. DHS has said Salgado Araujo had “weaponized his vehicle” before the shooting and that an officer fired in self-defense. Other passengers in the van have disputed that account.

Teare has not given a timetable for when his office’s investigation into the shooting will be complete. In September, a witness to the shooting was seen entering a courthouse area reserved for grand jury proceedings.

This story has been updated with additional information.

text:
A Texas grand jury indicted ICE officer Mario Alberto Morales Friday on a charge of aggravated assault with a deadly weapon, alleging he drove his vehicle into Miguel Parra Hernandez, who was on foot, earlier this month, the Harris County District Attorney’s Office said Friday.

The indictment of Morales, 33, was handed up by a Harris County grand jury Friday morning.

The indictment is the first of an immigration agent in Texas. ICE enforcement officer Christian Castro was charged in the January shooting of Julio Sosa-Celis in Minnesota.

“The evidence that we have in this case is as clear as any that I’ve ever prosecuted or investigated,” Harris County District Attorney Sean Teare said in a news conference Friday.

“An ICE badge does not give you free rein to injure, kill, or violate the constitutional rights of anyone,” Teare said.

The Oct. 10 collision left Parra with hip, leg and ankle injuries, including a broken leg, according to his family and representatives.

In a statement issued after the collision, ICE said Parra “ran in front of an ICE vehicle and was struck.” The agent was driving an SUV.

But after reviewing video collected by investigators in his office from local businesses and bystanders, Teare accused the agent of deliberately running over Parra. ICE has previously said accusations that its agent intentionally struck Parra were “reckless” and “false.”

In an emailed statement shortly after the indictment was announced, an ICE spokesperson said the indictment “is nothing more than a political stunt by Houston sanctuary politicians.”

The spokesperson stated that only federal agencies can investigate “federal officers acting in the course of their duties,” and that local governments don’t have the authority to run such an investigation.

Teare, a Democrat, said at the press conference that it’s “false” that they can’t investigate.

ICE added that allegations that the ICE officer struck Miguel Parra-Hernandez intentionally are “reckless” and “false.”

DHS placed an officer on administrative leave after the collision, a senior DHS official told NBC News earlier this month.

Security video of the incident obtained by NBC affiliate KPRC of Houston shows a white truck facing the opposite direction of traffic on a busy roadway. Parra and another man exit the white truck and run, the video shows.

At about the same time, the video shows, another vehicle jumps a yellow median and heads in Parra’s direction. The video then shows the vehicle, which is not marked, swerving left toward Parra’s path, in front of a truck stopped in a shopping center.

When the parked truck leaves, a man can be seen lying on the pavement behind the ICE vehicle, the video shows.

Teare, who worked several years as a Harris County vehicle crimes division chief, had previously told NBC News that he had sought critical data from the vehicle involved in the collision but ICE moved the car from the scene.

Parra has lived in the U.S. for 34 years, having arrived at age 14, and he has no criminal record, his attorney told NBC News. He had been doing stucco work when he was struck, according to an advocate. DHS said he was in the country without legal permission.

ICE had said it was conducting a targeted enforcement operation to arrest Jose Mendoza-Cervantes and was not targeting Parra or another man who was also in a truck with Mendoza-Cervantes before they fled on foot.

title: Appeals court suspends the order requiring the reopening of the 2027 Visa Lottery
description:
The Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals suspended on Thursday a court order requiring the Donald Trump administration to reopen the Diversity Visa Lottery for 2027 (DV-2027), leaving the start date for registrations unconfirmed.
Now, the Ninth Circuit considered that Red Eagle Law has little chance of succeeding in its lawsuit because its economic interests are not protected by the legislation governing the Visa Lottery.
"We do not endorse that the Department [of State] has not opened the lottery registration period," the judges stated.
The Visa Lottery allows for the annual issuance of up to 55,000 immigrant visas to individuals from countries with low rates of immigration to the United States.
The official Visa Lottery portal remains the only authorized site for submitting applications when registration opens.
text:
The Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals suspended on Thursday a court order requiring the Donald Trump administration to reopen the Diversity Visa Lottery for 2027 (DV-2027), leaving the start date for registrations unconfirmed.

The resolution, issued on October 29, grants the State Department, led by Marco Rubio, an emergency stay while the appeal filed by the federal government is processed.

The decision halts the deadlines set by a California judge, who had ordered the announcement of the registration period this Thursday, to open registration on Sunday, November 1, and to notify the selected individuals by December 3 at the latest

With those deadlines suspended, the program continues to not accept new applications and there is no official date for its reopening.

The litigation originated from the failure to open the registration for the DV-2027 Visa Lottery, the dates for which had been pending since November 2025, when the Department of State announced changes to the application process. In December of that year, Kristi Noem, then Secretary of Homeland Security, announced that she had ordered the United States Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) to suspend the processing of cases related to the DV1 program.

On August 31, 2026, the Department of State announced a new suspension of diversity visa issuance, following a court order that lifted the pause implemented since December 2025. This measure regarding visa issuance is different from the postponement of applications for DV-2027, the opening date of which has yet to be announced and which led to the legal dispute.

Why did the court suspend the reopening order?

The litigation began in August 2026, when the immigration firm Red Eagle Law sued the Department of State for keeping the program's registry closed.

On October 14, Federal Judge Jinsook Ohta ordered to reactivate the lottery, but the government appealed.

Now, the Ninth Circuit considered that Red Eagle Law has little chance of succeeding in its lawsuit because its economic interests are not protected by the legislation governing the Visa Lottery. The judges noted that the program aims to facilitate immigration from certain countries, not to generate income for law firms.

However, the court clarified that its ruling does not support the government's decision to keep the registry closed.

"We do not endorse that the Department [of State] has not opened the lottery registration period," the judges stated.

The resolution also does not definitively determine whether the Trump administration acted legally when it halted the program.

What does this decision mean for Cubans?

The Visa Lottery allows for the annual issuance of up to 55,000 immigrant visas to individuals from countries with low rates of immigration to the United States.

However, those born in Cuba have been excluded from the DV-2026 program because the country exceeded the limit of 50,000 immigrants during the five-year period used to determine eligibility.

For the DV-2027, the Department of State has not yet published definitive instructions confirming which countries will be eligible to participate, so the exclusion of Cuba for this new draw should not be taken for granted.

The official Visa Lottery portal remains the only authorized site for submitting applications when registration opens.

For the moment, the Ninth Circuit's decision keeps the reopening order suspended while the legal appeal continues. The future of the DV-2027 program remains unresolved.

text:
Hennepin County prosecutors had to dismiss multiple criminal cases because crime victims were afraid to travel to court during Operation Metro Surge, the Hennepin County Attorney's Office says in a report to the Minnesota Truth Council.

Operation Metro Surge began in December 2025 in Minnesota and was described by the Department of Homeland Security as the largest federal immigration law enforcement deployment in the nation's history.

The report, finalized earlier this month, lays out how the county attorney's office says the operation disrupted the county's public safety system and what prosecutors did in response.

Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty said the cases "had to be dismissed because of the federal government's behavior." That "made us all less safe," she said, and "helped defendants avoid accountability and even facilitated threats against victims." In one case described in the report, a defendant threatened a victim from abroad after U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement deported the defendant.

More than 35 crime victims in cases the county attorney's office is prosecuting reported feeling unsafe traveling to county courthouses, the report says. It says some of them left Minnesota and, in some cases, the country entirely. Prosecutors say victims must appear in person to testify at trial, even though the office expanded its remote services.

Since May 2025, ICE has detained more than 30 defendants in active Hennepin County prosecutions, according to the report. Two were taken out of Minnesota within hours. The county attorney's office says ICE does not notify prosecutors when it deports a defendant.

Prosecutors presented ICE with state court orders directing the return of 20 defendants to the Hennepin County Sheriff's Office. ICE returned eight to be prosecuted, the report says. It says ICE refused to return nine, disregarding the orders, and claimed to be unable to return the other three.

The report says nearly two out of three immigrants arrested by ICE during the operation had no prior U.S. criminal history, citing a Human Rights Watch report. Dozens of those arrested were crime victims themselves, the report says.

The county attorney's office says armed and masked federal agents raided county courthouses during the operation. Hennepin County prosecutors and law enforcement partners, including the Minnesota Attorney General's Office, sent two letters asking then-Chief Justice Natalie Hudson to prohibit civil enforcement actions, including immigration enforcement, in courthouses. Connecticut and Oregon already had such policies. Hudson declined, most recently on March 6.

Federal agents shot three Hennepin County residents between Jan. 7 and Jan. 24, killing two, Renee Good and Alex Pretti, the report says. It says federal agencies barred state investigators from shooting scenes and withheld evidence. The county attorney's office and state partners have sued the federal government twice. The office announced July 13 that it had obtained some withheld evidence, but the report says federal cooperation soon halted again and litigation continues.

The county attorney's office has charged two ICE agents. Gregory Donnell Morgan Jr. was charged April 16 with two counts of second-degree assault for allegedly pointing a weapon at two people while driving alongside them. Christian Castro was charged May 18 with four counts of second-degree assault and one count of falsely reporting a crime for allegedly firing through the front door of a home.

The county attorney's Transparency and Accountability Project, launched March 2, is investigating more than 30 federal actions. Its investigator has conducted more than 100 witness interviews and collected more than 1,100 photos and videos. Prosecutors say identifying agents is difficult because most wore face coverings and the federal government has not shared evidence.

WCCO has reached out to ICE and the Department of Homeland Security for comment and is awaiting responses.

title: Weingarten v. McMahon: Major Class Action Lawsuit Launched Against Education Secretary ...
description:

It enables qualifying public service workers—among them teachers, nurses and first responders—to discharge their student loan balances after 120 monthly repayments.
Public service workers and the communities they serve deserve better than more dysfunction and broken promises.
The law guarantees public service workers certain rights, and we will enforce those rights wherever and whenever they are violated.” Weingarten is the lead named plaintiff, alongside AFT members and public service workers.
In AFT v. McMahon, filed in March 2025, the union sued after McMahon blocked access to more affordable repayment plans.
text:
WASHINGTON—A landmark class action lawsuit filed today in federal court documents how Education Secretary Linda McMahon systematically prevented tens of thousands of public service workers from securing millions in student debt relief they are owed under federal law.

The nationwide suit, Weingarten v. McMahon, lays bare the gross mismanagement of the buyback and other key provisions of the Public Service Loan Forgiveness program by McMahon and her Department of Education. Borrowers who have applied for debt relief have had their applications are stuck in limbo, with no updates for months on end.

The case, filed Friday in federal District Court for the District of Columbia, is brought as a class action and is seeking relief for all similarly situated borrowers, not just the named plaintiffs.

“Secretary McMahon has flagrantly ignored her responsibility to help teachers, nurses and first responders under the buyback provision her department is required to honor,” said AFT President Randi Weingarten, the lead plaintiff. “This provision was adopted to help people hurt by the first Trump administration’s mismanagement of student debt. Instead of processing applications in good faith, McMahon has left 90,000 dedicated public employees in the lurch, forcing them further into debt while their applications just sit there. This lawsuit demands that McMahon stop stalling and do her job—to help, rather than hurt, the people she is sworn to serve.”

McMahon has made it her “final mission” to “put herself out of a job” by abolishing the department she runs. She has hobbled its key functions by trying to move them elsewhere, adding to the red tape and bureaucratic dysfunction she claims to want to eliminate.

PSLF is a bipartisan loan forgiveness plan signed into law by President George W. Bush. It enables qualifying public service workers—among them teachers, nurses and first responders—to discharge their student loan balances after 120 monthly repayments.

In recent years, following changes to federal repayment plans and during the COVID-19 pandemic, loan servicers and the department often placed borrowers into forbearance or deferment for several months at a time. Under the buyback provision, borrowers can elect to pay now the amount that they would have paid during those months, have them retroactively credited to their 120-payment total, and then have their remaining debt discharged. This opportunity builds on PSLF account review opportunities negotiated by the AFT as part of a previous legal settlement.

However, by April of this year, the buyback backlog had reached nearly 90,000 applications, from the previous total of 49,000 a year earlier, with the department refusing to give an updated processing timeline. The suit alleges that as a direct result of McMahon’s mismanagement, those applications have been shelved, with little or no communication with borrowers about when they might be processed. Because borrowers can only apply for a buyback when they have already worked in public service for 10 years, the department’s actions are all that is standing between these borrowers having their outstanding loan balances—often totaling hundreds of thousands of dollars—forgiven through PSLF.

The complaint also details a raft of other PSLF issues, including the department clawing back previously granted PSLF credit: In August, some borrowers saw their PSLF payment counts mysteriously drop, some by 15 months or more. The department initially dismissed the error, then admitted that some earlier waiver and account-adjustment credits were being purposely rolled back. The complaint details how, in addition to the department clawing back PSLF credits, it has withheld, without explanation, recently earned qualifying payments.

“I’ve dedicated my career to improving the lives of children in my community. I did everything right to earn relief from my student debt,” said Elizabeth Schoepflin, a speech-language pathologist, AFT member and co-plaintiff from New York. “Meanwhile, the Department of Education has ripped away the loan forgiveness credit I earned without any explanation. Every month this drags on is another payment I shouldn’t have to make. I kept my end of the deal. It’s time for the department to keep theirs.”

The suit cites repeated violations of the Administrative Procedure Act. Plaintiffs are seeking permanent injunctive relief compelling the department to comply with its statutory obligations under the Higher Education Act to forgive the loans of all borrowers who satisfy the PSLF requirements.

“PSLF is not a handout. It is a commitment to people who dedicate their careers to public service,” said David Petley, a co-plaintiff and associate AFT member from Oregon. “As a rural Oregon hospital pharmacist, I have seen firsthand how this program helps bring skilled professional public servants to communities that need them. But now, after 10-plus years of public service, I have waited a year and a half for a response to my PSLF buyback request, with no information about when it will be resolved. I am expected to keep making more expensive monthly payments in the meantime. That is unacceptable. Public servants deserve better.”

“The teachers, nurses and public service workers of this country deserve the debt relief Congress promised to them, and the AFT will fight to deliver on that promise,” said Protect Borrowers Senior Counsel Laura C. Dismore. “The AFT is, once again, stepping up to hold Linda McMahon accountable in court for her blatant defiance of the law. From President Trump on down, this administration is so focused on destroying what’s left of the Department of Education—and blaming borrowers for the consequences—that it has lost sight of its basic obligation to the American people: lower costs and fix the economy. Public service workers and the communities they serve deserve better than more dysfunction and broken promises. The law guarantees public service workers certain rights, and we will enforce those rights wherever and whenever they are violated.”

Weingarten is the lead named plaintiff, alongside AFT members and public service workers.

“This is our third case in less than two years against the Trump administration, and the AFT will not stop fighting until every teacher, nurse and public worker gets the loan forgiveness they were promised,” she said. “People who dedicate their careers to serving the public should be helped by the federal government; instead, McMahon has waged a war on affordability and retied the Gordian knot we forced Betsy DeVos to unravel. That’s why we’re suing again.”

Today’s filing marks the AFT’s eighth lawsuit over a decade to protect student loan borrowers from predatory loan servicers and politicians determined to make it harder for young people to pay for college. The case is effectively a successor suit to 2019’s Weingarten v. DeVos, settled in October 2021, that gave applicants who had been denied a path to re-review through a PSLF reconsideration process that was ultimately codified by the Biden-era Education Department, leading to over 1 million public workers receiving $78 billion in forgiveness. In AFT v. McMahon, filed in March 2025, the union sued after McMahon blocked access to more affordable repayment plans. In November 2025, the AFT joined the National Council of Nonprofits to restore access to PSLF for work that the administration disagreed with politically.

Weingarten v. McMahon seeks to be certified as a class action to represent the interests of borrowers across the country with pending buyback applications, whose PSLF credits have been clawed back, or whose recent payments are not being counted toward PSLF.

All plaintiffs and the proposed class of borrowers are represented by Protect Borrowers and Berger Montague.

The outcomes demonstrate the administration’s failure to acknowledge dangerous circumstances facing many TPS holders, immigrant advocates say.
“The harms are overwhelming for Venezuelan TPS holders,” said Emi MacLean, senior staff attorney at the ACLU of Northern California.
Looming Decisions Other immigrant advocacy organizations also gathered anecdotal evidence of the effects of TPS terminations on their members.
VanDiver said many Afghan TPS recipients helped American troops in Afghanistan and were brought to the US, or escaped to the US, after the fall of Kabul.
text:
Venezuelan immigrants whose Temporary Protected Status was voided in the first year of the Trump administration faced ejection to third countries, underwent torture from their home governments, and lost critical healthcare.

Those experiences detailed in recent court filings underline ongoing threats to TPS holders, immigrant advocates say, with decisions on protections still looming for several hundred thousand people from Ukraine, El Salvador, and Sudan.

Whether TPS recipients from those countries keep their status is unclear after the Department of Homeland Security punted on deadlines to renew or terminate those designations. But over 1 million foreign nationals have already been stripped of the protections as DHS advances a mass deportation campaign that’s led to the removal of more than 660,000 people.

Plaintiffs challenging the termination of TPS for Venezuelans — the first to lose that status under Trump’s second term — told an appellate court this month that experiences of individual immigrants demonstrate the irreparable harm that will result if protections aren’t restored.

Court declarations detail stories of pregnant women fleeing to third countries after being deported to Venezuela, incarceration in a government prison and “known torture site” in Caracas, and even deaths in US immigration custody and in their home country.

Others, including Carlos Ernesto Sánchez Villa, were sent to third countries after being detained. He contracted malaria and was hospitalized for a week after his deportation to Liberia.

“Even if I somehow manage to get out of this situation, the psychological harm that this has done to me and my family can never be undone,” he wrote. “This will mark me and my family for the rest of our lives.”

TPS, established by Congress in 1990, allows immigrants to remain in the US for up to 18 months when DHS determines that conditions like armed conflict or natural disasters prevent a safe return. The outcomes demonstrate the administration’s failure to acknowledge dangerous circumstances facing many TPS holders, immigrant advocates say.

“How many people have to be killed when they’re deported back?” said Todd Schulte, president of FWD.us.

Numerous lawsuits added roadblocks to TPS termination efforts. But the Supreme Court has allowed the Trump administration to move forward with lifting protections, and in a June decision endorsed government arguments that those decisions can’t be challenged in court.

DHS said in a statement to Bloomberg Law that it’s restoring TPS to a limited form of relief, rather than a “de facto amnesty program.” Some conservatives have long criticized the program for providing status for years longer than they say Congress intended.

Venezuela Terminations

Earlier this month, another tranche of Venezuelan TPS recipients lost their legal status and work authorization, including an accountant who was preparing to seek an employment-based green card after a decade in the US.

“All the effort that I put into securing a more permanent immigration status went up in smoke,” she wrote.

The Trump administration moved swiftly last year to eliminate deportation protections for Venezuelans. But its plans to cancel Biden-era TPS extensions were tied up in court challenges with a district court judge ruling that the early termination of those protections was unlawful.

The Supreme Court later granted a DHS request to go forward with stripping protections while litigation continued, meaning thousands became vulnerable to detention and deportation.

Although lower court rulings continued to stymie TPS terminations, justices in June backed government arguments that those decisions are off limits to court review. Since then, DHS has lifted protections for people from 13 countries, including Haiti, Afghanistan, and Yemen.

The National TPS Alliance told the US Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit this month that the Supreme Court hasn’t addressed the lawfulness of vacating a prior TPS decision, which sets the case apart from other litigation. Court declarations show the ongoing risks to recipients, including family separation and removal to countries where they have no ties, the group said.

Legal counsel for the group surveyed Venezuelan members earlier this year about the impact of losing the protections. Out of more than 600 responses, the overwhelming majority reported subsequent arrests.

“The harms are overwhelming for Venezuelan TPS holders,” said Emi MacLean, senior staff attorney at the ACLU of Northern California.

Although many in detention were released after filing habeas petitions, others who claimed fear of persecution back home were sent to third countries, she said.

“If an illegal alien chooses to file a claim in court refusing to go to their home country, they should not be surprised when we find a safe and secure nation for them to go to,” a DHS spokesperson said.

Looming Decisions

Other immigrant advocacy organizations also gathered anecdotal evidence of the effects of TPS terminations on their members. Shawn VanDiver, president of AfghanEvac, said that after TPS was terminated for over 8,000 Afghans, his organization has been tasked with filing habeas petitions for those detained.

VanDiver said many Afghan TPS recipients helped American troops in Afghanistan and were brought to the US, or escaped to the US, after the fall of Kabul. Others included students or other visitors who were already here when the Taliban took control of the country.

“They’ve had all of their dignity stripped from them,” VanDiver said, adding that some were deported to third countries. “They’ve been sent or are in the process of being sent either back to Afghanistan where they face certain death or to countries where it’s untenable.”

Protections for Salvadorans, who hold the longest-running TPS status, were set to lapse last month. Rather than terminate or extend them, DHS said in a Sept. 9 website update that an announcement “will be made at the appropriate time.”

The agency offered the same reprieve for Ukrainian and Sudanese TPS recipients when protections expired this month. That’s left them, employers, and US citizen relatives without clarity over their continued presence in the country.

“The idea that it is safe to return people to many of these countries is just patently ridiculous,” Schulte said.

title: New federal lawsuit accuses feds, Indiana of human rights abuses in “Speedway Slammer ...
description:
“All our litigation is aimed, first and foremost, at ending the existing human rights abuses taking place [at the Miami facility].
She said immigration detention at the Miami facility is essentially run “like a high-security prison,” noting the Miami facility also still functions as an Indiana state prison.
The Miami facility contracts with private healthcare provider Centurion Health for its medical needs.
As of press time, Centurion is still advertising for nursing positions at the Miami facility.
But the Broadview ICE facility is run directly by federal authorities and is much smaller, meant to operate only for short-term processing of recent detainees.
text:
Denial of medication. Beatings. Cells flooded with human waste. Sexual assault.

Hundreds of people held in immigration detention at the Miami Correctional Facility in Bunker Hill, Indiana, have suffered these and other abuses, according to a federal class action lawsuit filed by attorneys with multiple civil and immigrant rights advocacy groups in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Indiana, South Bend Division, on Thursday afternoon. And federal and state authorities, the suit further alleges, knew and didn’t do much to stop them. The suit names the U.S. Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) as defendants, along with the Miami facility’s interim warden Christopher Lee Dixson; Indiana Department of Corrections (IDOC) Commissioner Lloyd Arnold; and IDOC Chief Medical Officer Dr. Adrienne Bedford.

“All our litigation is aimed, first and foremost, at ending the existing human rights abuses taking place [at the Miami facility]. That is the emergency goal and there are some horrific ones in Miami.” said Alexa Van Brunt, director of the Illinois office at the civil rights legal nonprofit MacArthur Justice Center, and one of the attorneys representing the plaintiffs in the case.

Sergei Vasenin, Kemoye Muslar and Cynthia Acevedo, three plaintiffs detained in the Miami facility, represent a proposed class of “all civil immigration detainees who are currently detained, or who will be detained” there. They seek a court declaration that immigration detention conditions at the facility—dubbed the “Speedway Slammer” by the Department of Homeland Security—violate the due process protections of the Constitution’s Fifth and Fourteenth Amendments, and injunctive relief compelling the state and federal defendants to address their injuries.

According to the complaint, Muslar—an immigrant from Jamaica reportedly held in the facility for ten months—spent three days of a ten-day lockdown with sewage flowing into his cell. Vasenin, a Ukrainian-born immigrant from Russia who has reportedly spent a year there, endured a total of nine weeks of solitary confinement—one three-week stint followed by another six-week stint, per his declaration to the court—and contemplated suicide. Lawyers claim he spent 23 to 24 hours a day in a “tiny, frigid cell.” (The United Nations defines 15 consecutive days with fewer than two hours of meaningful human contact as torture.) Acevedo, a transgender woman and Guatemalan immigrant brought to the Miami facility in July, was allegedly sexually assaulted by another detainee, and was not immediately provided with HIV testing or medication to prevent HIV transmission.

The suit claims none of the three named plaintiffs have any criminal convictions.

Van Brunt and the MacArthur Justice Center are joined by attorneys from other civil rights groups like the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU) and the National Immigrant Justice Center. She said immigration detention at the Miami facility is essentially run “like a high-security prison,” noting the Miami facility also still functions as an Indiana state prison. Even before the facility began holding people for civil immigration enforcement last year, it had its own history of inmates alleging abuses and inhumane conditions.

“It’s the same correctional officers on the state prison side as on the immigration side, and they’re even using state prison tiers, like solitary cells, for the immigrant detainees,” Van Brunt said. “So it’s really no different.”

Samuel Cole, a former immigration judge in Chicago and now the ACLU of Illinois’s Chief Immigration Litigation Counsel, is another attorney representing the plaintiffs in the suit.

“This is a state penitentiary and they’re treating these people who have done nothing wrong like criminals,” he said.

In August 2025, DHS announced plans to add 1,000 beds for immigration detention at the pre-existing Miami Correctional Facility, in cooperation with the state of Indiana. The following month, Indiana legislators approved nearly $16 million in funding to prepare the facility for the expansion. Deemed the “Speedway Slammer,” a cruel, sophomoric nickname in the same vein as the now-closed “Alligator Alcatraz” detention facility in Florida, it is part of the multibillion dollar buildout for the Trump administration’s mass deportation machine.

That buildout, codified in July 2025 by the so-called One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA), funds ongoing ICE operations across the country, new immigration detention contracts for private prison operators like GEO Group, which runs 52 “secure facilities and processing centers,” according to its website, and the expansion of 287(g) programs, which allow local police to carry out immigration enforcement on feds’ behalf, in multiple states, including Indiana but not Illinois.

Unlike privately managed immigration detention sites like Delaney Hall in New Jersey and the Dilley Immigration Processing Center in Texas, IDOC manages the Miami facility in conjunction with federal authorities. According to a 2025 intergovernmental service agreement between DHS, ICE, and the Miami facility, the feds agreed to pay the facility over $291 per day per immigration detainee, as well hourly pay for on-call guards and by-the-mile reimbursement for transportation. According to the suit, these payments “guaranteed the state defendants at least $80 million in only two years.”

The suit claims the facility fails “to provide adequate medical care at every level,” with reports of insufficient medical staffing, detainees not getting necessary medications, and requests for urgent medical attention going ignored.

Two people have died in immigration detention at the Miami facility since the start of 2026—59-year-old Lorth Sim in February and 55-year-old Tuan Van Bui in April—which the suit attributes to the allegedly poor healthcare. According to a separate lawsuit filed by Lorth Sim’s son, Viccheat Sim, this August, Lorth died of cardiovascular disease with diabetic complications. Viccheat alleges his father did not receive his diabetes medication while in ICE custody. Van Bui’s death was also reportedly linked to heart disease.

The Miami facility contracts with private healthcare provider Centurion Health for its medical needs. Centurion is not a named defendant in the suit filed Thursday, but another former immigration detainee at the Miami facility sued the company in July over allegations of neglect and insufficient medical staffing. As of press time, Centurion is still advertising for nursing positions at the Miami facility.

“There’s a lot of knowledge by ICE and the state of Indiana that Centurion is not fit to be providing care,” Van Brunt said.

Thursday’s suit resembles last year’s federal class action which the MacArthur Justice Center and ACLU filed against ICE and DHS over alleged inhumane conditions at the ICE processing facility in Broadview, Illinois. Van Brunt also represented plaintiffs in that complaint, which similarly alleged inhumane conditions and abuse of detainees inside the facility. During one hearing in the case in Chicago, District Judge Robert Gettleman even drew a comparison between the Broadview facility and Auschwitz.

That case resulted in the court ordering a number of reforms at the Broadview facility, which during open hearings, an attorney for the federal government argued would effectively shut down operations there. (Gettleman’s reforms remain in place as settlement talks continue.)

Van Brunt acknowledged the similarities, and Cole remarked that many people ICE take to Broadview end up in the Miami facility. But the Broadview ICE facility is run directly by federal authorities and is much smaller, meant to operate only for short-term processing of recent detainees. The Miami facility is meant for longer-term incarceration.

Noting the government’s complaints during the Broadview case, Van Brunt remarked people shouldn’t be held at the facility if the state or federal government can’t improve conditions there.

“Just as with Broadview, if the state of Indiana and the feds cannot operate this facility in a way that protects people’s rights, then it should not be operated at all,” she said.

text:
A federal appeals court has temporarily blocked an order requiring the Trump administration to reopen the Diversity Visa lottery, allowing the government to keep the program paused while it pursues an appeal.

A three-judge panel of the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals on Thursday granted the government's emergency request to stay a preliminary injunction. This would have required the State Department to open registration for the fiscal year 2027 Diversity Visa Program by Sunday, November 1.

Red Eagle Law is a California-based immigration law firm that represents Diversity Visa selectees. It sued Secretary of State Marco Rubio in August over the State Department's failure to open registration for the Diversity Visa Program for fiscal year 2027.

Read More on News

The court's decision does not resolve the government's underlying appeal. Instead, it puts the lower court's order on hold while that appeal moves forward.

"Red Eagle will be moving forward quickly with other litigation to challenge the State Department's failure to carry out the DV program," Curtis Morrison, owner of Red Eagle, told Newsweek.

Newsweek has contacted the State Department for comment via contact form outside office hours and is awaiting a response.

"We do not endorse the Department’s failure to open the lottery registration period. Nevertheless, Red Eagle has not shown a likelihood of success on the merits because it is not within the zone of interests of the statute and does not have a cause of action," the court wrote.

The Diversity Visa Program makes available up to 55,000 visas annually to people from countries with low rates of immigration to the United States. The appeals court said the State Department had failed, without explanation, to open the registration period for fiscal 2027, "effectively canceling" the program.

The Diversity Visa Program, commonly known as the green card lottery, grew out of congressional efforts in the 1980s to create immigration opportunities for people from countries underrepresented in the U.S. immigration system.

Congress established the permanent program through the Immigration Act of 1990, signed by former GOP President George H.W. Bush on November 29, 1990. It was set up to encourage immigration from countries that had historically sent relatively few immigrants to the United States.

The failure to open the Diversity Visa Lottery could have serious consequences for thousands of people worldwide, particularly those from countries with historically low immigration rates to the United States. It effectively denies eligible applicants an opportunity to pursue permanent residency.

The Trump administration has also moved to tighten legal immigration: expanding scrutiny of some green card applicants under the "public charge" test; imposing new or higher fees for asylum, work permits, parole and other immigration benefits; and pursuing restrictions on the H-1B skilled-worker program. It has also sharply limited the broader refugee program while giving priority to Afrikaners and other racial minorities from South Africa.

On October 14, a federal-district court granted Red Eagle a preliminary injunction and ordered the State Department to reopen the program. Under that ruling, the department was required to announce the registration period by October 29, begin accepting registrations by November 1, and notify those selected of their eligibility to apply by December 3.

The government appealed and sought an emergency stay of the injunction. On October 29, Circuit Judges M. Margaret McKeown, N. Randy Smith, and Holly A. Thomas granted that request.

The panel said the government was likely to prevail; Red Eagle’s financial interest in representing Diversity Visa applicants was not sufficiently connected to the program, which "was enacted to encourage immigration, not generate revenue for law firms," the court said.

Judge Smith separately concurred and argued that Red Eagle also lacked constitutional standing.

Morrison said the firm planned further litigation. It was looking for a noncitizen living in the United States on an F-1, H-1B or other nonimmigrant visa who was willing to challenge the Trump administration as a plaintiff and was not fearful of potential retaliation.

The 9th Circuit said its clerk would issue a briefing schedule for the appeal.

This is a developing story and will be updated.

Newsweek’s reporters and editors used Martyn, our AI assistant, to produce this story. Learn more about Martyn here.

text:
Immigration detainees held at Indiana’s Miami Correctional Facility are suing state and federal agencies for what they say are inhumane and unconstitutional conditions.

The 72-page court filing details medical neglect, cells flooded with human waste, and abusive punishments detainees claim to have experienced at the maximum security prison used by the Trump administration for its immigration enforcement policies.

The lawsuit also alleges conditions at the facility violate the Fifth and Fourteenth Amendment due process clauses because the detainees are civil detainees, not under criminal convictions, and are facing punitive punishments like lockdowns and solitary confinement.

The ACLU of Indiana and Illinois filed a class action lawsuit Thursday, Oct. 29, in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Indiana. The lawsuit covers the three named plaintiffs and all other detainees at the correctional facility north of Kokomo.

“Frankly, they are experiencing physical decline, potential long-term medical consequences, and, like, severe emotional distress and suffering,” said Katie Hickey, an attorney with the ACLU of Illinois representing the plaintiffs.

Officials with the U.S. Department of Homeland Security, ICE and Indiana Department of Correction are listed as plaintiffs. Representatives for the agencies did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The lawsuit comes after continued reports from detainees, lawyers and advocates about the conditions at the prison. This summer Gov. Mike Braun called for an audit to review the private healthcare provider the state contracts to work in the facilities after reports from the IndyStar on delays in medical care for detainees.

Indiana began housing Immigration and Customs Enforcement detainees at Miami Correctional in October 2025 through a two-year contract with the U.S. Department of Homeland Security. Miami Correctional is a maximum security facility for men.

Since detainees began to arrive, there have been two reported deaths.

In the lawsuit, plaintiff Cynthia Acevedo said healthcare providers at the facility switched her to a different seizure medication that is ineffective at preventing seizures. Even then, Acevedo, a transgender woman, does not regularly receive the medication and has multiple seizures a week. When she goes to get medical treatment, no Spanish translator is made available.

Sergei Vasenin and Kemoye Muslar, the other plaintiffs, share their experiences of slow and limited medical care and regular solitary confinement and lockdowns.

During a 10-day lockdown, Muslar said his cell flooded over with sewage for three days. He was not provided cleaning supplies or hygiene products.

The detainees also allege guards call them racial slurs, threaten death and physically beat them without any reason.

The lawsuit details a case of a recent suicide attempt by a detainee. It alleges, staff were notified of concerns for the man’s mental health. It goes on to say that guards locked him alone in his cell where he went on to use a cable and hang himself according to witnesses. The lawsuit says the condition and whereabouts of the detainee remain unconfirmed.

The plaintiffs are asking for the court to declare the facility’s medical and mental health care and conditions inadequate and in violation of the the Fifth Amendment and Fourteenth Amendment due process clause.

‘Further litigation forthcoming’

Hickey said she hopes this lawsuit forces changes but also gets answers to what has occurred at Miami Correctional Facility.

“The people who have died, the recent suicide attempt. There’s been no transparency from the government about all of that, so we hope that we can learn a lot more about all of these things in Miami over the next; over the coming months,” Hickey said.

For more than a year religious leaders have gathered monthly at or near the prison to pray for the detainees being held there and their families. André Carson visited Miami Correctional in April demanding answers to the deaths in the facility. After speaking with people held at the prison he said the state needed to end its holding of ICE detainees there.

Other groups including the Indiana Organizing Project have held events across the state calling on the governor to end the contract with ICE or at least not renew it.

Indiana Organizing Project Executive Director Stuart Mora said nothing in the lawsuit surprised him and it comes as conditions fail to improve.

“I think that there will be further litigation forthcoming,” said Mora. “Our team has not seen significant changes in Miami Correctional, since the governor called for an investigation several months ago.”

The ACLU was joined by the National Immigrant Justice Center, Macarthur Justice Center and law firm Dunn Issaacson Rhee in filing the lawsuit on behalf of the detainees.

SOUTH BEND, Ind. — The American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU) has filed a federal lawsuit in South Bend, claiming the Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detention center at the Miami Correctional Facility in Bunker Hill, often referred to as the “Speedway Slammer,” is holding detainees in unconstitutional conditions.

The class action lawsuit called the Miami Correctional Facility “Indiana’s largest and most dangerous high security prison.” The lead plaintiff said the facility provides inadequate health care, uses abusive punishment and provides inhumane conditions.

The lawsuit said he facility is dangerously understaffed and delays and denies urgently needed medications and treatments. It said one of the plaintiffs has been treated for epilepsy for years but is being denied proper medication. Another plaintiff has been denied healthcare for weeks, the lawsuit claimed.

The abusive punishment includes forcing people into solitary confinement for 23 and 24 hours each day with “little or no justification,” the suit claimed.

The plaintiff in the case said staff have degraded detainees by using racial and xenophobic language, including calling the detainees a “plague.”

Mark Feldman, the senior litigation attorney at the National Immigrant Justice Center, said the conditions at the facility are emblematic of ICE facing no accountability for its actions.

“ICE turned to Miami Correctional Facility to detain people at the height of its violent arrest operations in Chicago and Minnesota, and since then, has disappeared hundreds of people into this isolated prison where they are forced to either endure deadly conditions or abandon heir immigration cases and their loved ones in the United States and ‘voluntarily’ depart the country,” Feldman said. “No one should have to choose between their safety and their right to seek immigration relief in this country. ICE’s use of Miami Correctional as a tool of coercion and abuse must end.”

in its announcement, the ACLU said last year, at least two people died while detained at Miami Correctional, and another person attempted suicide.

The three named plaintiffs in the lawsuit, Sergei Vasenin, Kemoye Muslar and Cynthia Acevedo, are from Jamaica, Russia and Guatemala. The announcement said they are being denied adequate medical care and have inadequate access to food, water, clothing, essential medications and hygiene items.
