text:
A year ago, the Trump administration said the city of Portland was being ravaged by protests. So much so, U.S. Department of Justice attorneys argued they needed to deploy the National Guard.

The city and state quickly sued. What followed was an unprecedented trial that tested the power of the presidency. Attorneys for the city of Portland argued the administration falsely labeled the city as “war-ravaged,” and that the protests were under control.

U.S. District Court Judge Karin Immergut ultimately agreed with Portland. Legal experts say the three-day trial between the clashing governments became a rare test of federal power.

“If there’s a crisis, then it makes sense to give the government more powers to handle it,” said Juliet Stumpf, a law professor at Lewis and Clark. “If things had gone the other way, and the judge had said ‘It’s OK to bring the military in, it’s OK to federalize the National Guard’ — I think things would have looked very different.

“And that almost happened,” Stumpf added.

Related: Watch the first episode of “The Crackdown”

Related: Watch the second episode of "The Crackdown"

The third episode of OPB’s documentary series “The Crackdown” explores how the dueling narratives around Portland’s anti-deportation protests played out in federal courts. It also explores how the executive branch’s ambitions to rev up immigration enforcement led to that courtroom showdown.

President Donald Trump began his second term signing executive orders on immigration policy. Officials in his administration called migration from the southern border an “invasion.” With a stroke of his pen, the president tightened security at the borders and began to undo legal protections that had historically allowed immigrants to remain in the country.

Portland resident Jackie Merlos offers a case study. Her pending U visa application — a humanitarian visa given to people who were victims of crimes — historically protected immigrants from deportation. But it provided no protection when Merlos and her four children, who are all U.S. citizens, were detained last summer.

The family was detained in late June shortly after a visit to a park at the U.S.-Canada border. At the time, U.S. Customs and Border Protection officials accused Merlos of “attempting to smuggle illegal aliens into the U.S.”

Merlos’s children were eventually freed. After decades in the U.S., her husband was quickly detained and deported to Honduras. She spent roughly four months at the Northwest ICE Processing Center in Tacoma, Washington.

“It was a cell. Prison,” Merlos told OPB in a recent interview. “A sink and a bathroom. And cement floors.”

While Merlos was detained, stories like hers fueled the anti-deportation protests across the country. On the streets outside the Portland ICE facility, protests led to clashes with federal law enforcement officers.

While property damage and violence spiked at Portland protests during the first “No Kings” rally in June, protest numbers dwindled in August and September. Whatever skirmishes did break out during the late summer saw protesters, counter-protesters and federal law enforcement blame each other.

On Sept. 27, Trump posted on Truth Social that he would federalize and deploy the Oregon National Guard to the city. The official order came the next day.

The administration had successfully deployed National Guard forces to Los Angeles, Memphis and Washington, D.C., and had been threatening to send troops to cities like Portland and Chicago.

Attorneys with the city of Portland and the state of Oregon pushed back against the deployment. They argued there was no need for the military.

“We’re not on fire. We’re not war-ravaged,” Senior Deputy City Attorney Caroline Turco told OPB. “So to have to go into court and prove that felt ridiculous.”

Administration officials such as Stephen Miller, long described as the architect of the second Trump administration’s immigration policies, argued the president had “undisputed authority” to deploy troops into Portland.

“The argument that the Department of Justice was making, on behalf of the Trump administration, was ultimately frightening,” Turco said. “Essentially, that President Trump was above reproach.”

Justice Department attorneys cited a seldom-used federal law that allowed the president to deploy National Guard troops to fight a foreign invasion, quell a rebellion or to enforce federal laws.

Barely a month after Trump announced his plan, Judge Immergut oversaw a three-day trial. She focused on the question of whether Portland’s protests had created such dangerous conditions on the ground that federal troops were needed.

Immergut ultimately issued a sweeping, 106-page opinion determining that the president didn’t have the legal authority to co-opt National Guard forces and deploy them in the city. She ruled that the protests could be effectively managed by the Portland Police Bureau.

“Since that brief span of a few days in June, the protests outside the Portland ICE facility have been predominantly peaceful, with only isolated and sporadic instances of relatively low-level violence,” Immergut wrote. “The President did not have a lawful basis to federalize the National Guard.”

While the president’s authority was checked, the legal challenges continue.

Two cases, one brought by protesters and the other by residents of an apartment complex across the street from the Portland ICE facility, argued the federal government’s response to protests violated their constitutional rights.

Likewise, Merlos and other detainees have begun to push back. Merlos is a lead plaintiff in a class action lawsuit that accuses the Trump administration of unlawfully disregarding U visas. She’s also exploring filing a personal injury lawsuit related to her detention.

text:
Friday’s A Closer Look is typically a judicial biography. This week we cover Justice John McKinley, who served on the court from 1838 to 1852.

With the Eighth and Ninth Circuits Act of 1837, Congress added two more seats to the court. The first went to Justice John Catron, and the second went to Justice John McKinley, whose confirmation created a nine-justice court. While the seat itself was an honor, its duties were less so, as McKinley would discover.

McKinley was born in May 1780 in Culpeper County, Virginia. His family soon moved to Kentucky, where he taught himself law, passed the bar in 1800, and practiced in both Frankfort and Louisville. After moving to Alabama around 1818, McKinley grew wealthy from land speculation, partnered with Andrew Jackson in the Cypress Land Company, and helped found the city of Florence, Alabama. Jackson himself called McKinley “the most prominent man” in the state.

McKinley entered the Alabama Legislature in 1820, and, after backing Jackson for the presidency (he had previously supported Henry Clay), won a U.S. Senate seat in 1826. In the Senate, McKinley advocated for bankruptcy policies “favorable to small farmers.” However, his vote to override Jackson’s Maysville Road veto (the Maysville Road Bill essentially proposed federal stock purchases for internal improvements, like state roads) raised doubts about his loyalty, and he was not reelected in 1830. After one term in the U.S. House and another in the state legislature, he won a second Senate term in 1836, only to leave the seat within two months due to his Supreme Court appointment.

In 1837, the Eighth and Ninth Circuits Act expanded the court to nine justices, and Jackson’s advisers pushed McKinley for one of the new seats, but Jackson preferred his friend William Smith instead. When Smith declined, the pick then fell to the newly inaugurated President Martin Van Buren, who went with McKinley. Van Buren gave McKinley a recess appointment in April 1837, and the Senate confirmed him by voice vote that September.

After his nomination, McKinley wrote to then-House speaker James Polk that he had “accepted the appointment, although it is certainly the most onerous and laborious of any in the United States.” The new 9th Circuit included Alabama, Arkansas, Mississippi, and eastern Louisiana and required eight circuit terms a year. McKinley told Polk he would travel more than 5,000 miles annually, although McKinley later reported a figure closer to 10,000. The duties also likely ate into his finances (the justices were required to personally pay for their own circuit court duties) and took a toll on his health (he later had a paralyzing stroke on his way to Jackson, Mississippi).

Even before his first term started, McKinley asked Van Buren in person about changing the new 9th Circuit, but the president left the issue out of his next annual State of the Union, upsetting McKinley. Following McKinley’s first full term, the justices disbanded in March 1838 to “confront some 6,000 cases on their cumulative circuit dockets,” according to Steven Brown, who wrote McKinley’s first full-length biography. McKinley’s share from the 9th Circuit alone made up 4,700 of those.

Brown detailed one of the more interesting stories from McKinley’s extensive circuit duties in a 2011 Journal of Supreme Court History article. In April 1839 while holding circuit court in Jackson, a fight spilled into the courtroom and an officer of the court (who had been called “a stupid jackass” by McKinley for not bringing in the court marshal) pulled McKinley’s nose. Newspapers reported that the justice swore never to return to Jackson, and McKinley referenced the “gross personal indignity” in a letter to Van Buren.

In his 1839 State of the Union address, Van Buren told Congress that the circuit’s schedule and distances made it “impossible” for its judge to keep up. McKinley missed much of his circuit duties, along with the entire 1840 term, due to illness. Combined with his failure to hold court in Arkansas for almost five years, states in his circuit felt “neglected,” and the Mississippi Legislature called for McKinley’s impeachment. Congress eventually reorganized the circuits in August 1842, relieving McKinley of Mississippi and Arkansas; beginning in 1843 he rode the reconstituted 5th Circuit, which covered Alabama and Louisiana.

As for McKinley’s actual approach to cases, he was strongly for states’ rights, supporting them “over the authority of the federal government.” During his time on the court, McKinley wrote 19 majority opinions, four dissents, and two concurrences by one count, 22 opinions by another, and 23 by a third, the lowest per-term rate of his era. One of his opinions for the court was in 1845’s Pollard’s Lessee v. Hagan, where he held that new states enter the union on equal footing with the original 13, including ownership of the lands beneath navigable waters. Four years later in the 1849 Passenger Cases, McKinley argued in his concurrence that the federal government, not the states, controlled immigrants arriving from overseas until they became permanent residents of the states.

title: ICE continues to arrest dozens of illegal aliens in nationwide crackdown on voter fraud
description:
“We have uncovered hundreds of cases of election fraud and the extent of this problem continues to expand.
Each vote by a criminal illegal alien cancels out a vote of an American citizen.
Lawrence Cole, of Jamaica, is a criminal alien convicted of a felony for selling drugs during the Clinton administration.
Carlos Javier Alamo-Sorino, of Cuba, is a criminal illegal alien currently in custody.
Gerardo Nieves-Borja, a criminal illegal alien from Mexico who illegally voted in the 2024 election.
text:
WASHINGTON — ICE announced Oct. 28 another round of illegal aliens who have been arrested in connection with alleged voter fraud and election related offenses, including numerous cases of illegal aliens admitting to unlawfully registering to vote and casting ballots in American elections. This is part of a larger, governmentwide crackdown on illegal voting.

“Secure elections protect our nation’s sovereignty and Americans’ sacred right to vote,” said ICE Public Affairs Assistant Director Micah Bock. “We have uncovered hundreds of cases of election fraud and the extent of this problem continues to expand. Each vote by a criminal illegal alien cancels out a vote of an American citizen. This nationwide crackdown shows that President Trump, Secretary Mullin and acting ICE Director David J. Venturella are committed to fixing the failed immigration policies of the Biden administration that enabled this mess.”

Federal officials are working to restore integrity to our nation’s elections. This administration will continue to pursue cases of voter fraud to further that end.

The following 17 cases are just SOME of ICE’s ongoing investigations and arrests:

Jose Zapete-Quinonez, a Guatemalan national who illegally entered the country and has a final order of removal. He illegally voted in an election in 2021.

Puja Bagga, a lawful permanent resident from India, who unlawfully registered to vote and illegally voted three times — once in a local election in 2015 and in state elections in 2022 and 2024.

Christian Lawrence, of Liberia, was convicted in 2013 for failure to register as a sex offender and charged with failure to appear in court. Lawrence illegally voted in 2012 and 2016.

Lawrence Cole, of Jamaica, is a criminal alien convicted of a felony for selling drugs during the Clinton administration. He illegally voted in the 2004 and 2008 general elections and the 2008 presidential primary.

Lise Johnson, of Canada, was arrested for felony voter fraud. She voted in an election in 2022.

Vladislav Vaska, of Russia, is a lawful permanent resident arrested for illegally voting in the 2024 election.

Carlos Javier Alamo-Sorino, of Cuba, is a criminal illegal alien currently in custody. He was paroled into the U.S. by the Obama administration and was convicted of sexual assault and another sexual offense, robbery, larceny and harassing communication. Sorino admitted to illegally voting in an election.

Ramiro Daniel Cuarezma Aleman, of Nicaragua, is an illegal alien in custody who voted in the 2024 election.

Joshua Edzie, of Ghana, is a lawful permanent resident who voted in elections in November 2024 and August 2025.

Cliff Medgy Sanon, a citizen of Haiti and criminal illegal alien, has been convicted of receiving stolen property and has a final order of removal. He voted in the 2022 election.

Karl Stephen Branzon Pau, a citizen of the Philippines, has been in the U.S. illegally for 22 years. He overstayed his term of admission and voted in the 2024 election.

Mariana Alexandra Dewey, a lawful permanent resident and criminal alien from Peru, voted in the 2024 election and has been convicted of disorderly election conduct.

Gabriel Mendoza Vicente, a criminal illegal alien from Guatemala, has been convicted of a licensing violation and reckless driving under the influence of alcohol or drugs. He voted in the 2024 election.

Anthony Tyrone Higgs, a lawful permanent resident originally from the Bahamas who illegally voted in a 2020 election. Higgs has a lengthy rap sheet that includes convictions for armed robbery with a deadly weapon, grand larceny, domestic violence, simple assault and resisting arrest.

Omar Ponce-Juarez, an illegal alien from Mexico with no legal basis to remain in the United States, who illegally voted in a 2022 election.

Julio De La Rosa, a criminal illegal alien from Mexico with a final order of removal who illegally voted in the 2020 election. De La Rosa has been convicted of strangulation, assault, violation of a court order and a probation violation.

Gerardo Nieves-Borja, a criminal illegal alien from Mexico who illegally voted in the 2024 election. Nieves-Borja has been charged with DUI.

You can report crimes, including voter fraud, by calling (866) DHS-2-ICE (3472423) or completing the online tip form.

title: ICE should have no role in Georgia elections. There is a role for each of us.
description:
Most of my community members are worried about encountering U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement at the polls, and I can’t blame them because of what we’ve seen take place at the ballot box this year.
When the Trump administration threatens to deploy ICE agents near polling locations leading up to Election Day, immigrants become afraid to leave their homes to vote.
Authoritarianism is on the rise and on the ballot as the Trump administration spreads disinformation, refuses international poll monitors and encourages states to purge voter rolls.
There is no role for ICE in our elections.
For years, ICE has been harassing our neighbors at their doorsteps, threatening our colleagues at their workplaces and gunning us down in the streets.

title: The Real Stakes of the Ilhan Omar Case | The New Yorker
description:
The Trump Administration insists that this is not a political move, but the timing of the raid—a few weeks before a heated midterm election—suggests otherwise.
For ten years, Trump and Omar, who were first elected to public office on the same night, have sparred with open disdain.
Among those, only a quarter of one per cent revealed potential fraud: people who had been ordered deported and seemed to have used different identities to gain U.S. citizenship.
The case of Ilhan Omar is far less clear.
Still, few legal experts believe that the Administration will succeed in unearthing definitive evidence against Omar.
text:
All the way back in 2015, as Donald Trump was ascending onto the political stage, he proposed a “total and complete shutdown of Muslims entering the United States.” Islamophobia featured prominently in that first campaign for the Presidency. “If you have people coming out of mosques with hatred and death in their eyes and on their minds,” he said, on CBS News, “we’re going to have to do something.” A few months after pressing for the ban, Trump declared, simply, “I think Islam hates us.”

A complete prohibition on immigration by Muslims was blatantly unconstitutional, but that did not stop Trump, during his first week in office, from signing an executive order that banned travel from a list of Muslim-majority countries. After several legal challenges, Proclamation 9645, the third iteration of the policy, which the White House had expanded to include two non-Muslim countries—Venezuela and North Korea—was upheld by the U.S. Supreme Court. Chief Justice John Roberts, in his 5–4 opinion, noted that the Court must consider not only the President’s contentious statements but also the executive’s “authority” on matters of immigration and national security.

Meanwhile, in a scathing dissent, Justice Sonia Sotomayor argued that the Court could not disregard the President’s racist intentions. “What began as a policy explicitly ‘calling for a total and complete shutdown of Muslims entering the United States’ has since morphed into a ‘Proclamation’ putatively based on national-security concerns,” she wrote. “But this new window dressing cannot conceal an unassailable fact: the words of the President and his advisers create the strong perception that the Proclamation is contaminated by impermissible discriminatory animus against Islam and its followers.”

Questions of contamination and concealment appear newly relevant in light of a raid by more than a dozen federal agents on Representative Ilhan Omar’s home in Washington, D.C., earlier this month. It was six o’clock in the morning when Omar, who had just returned from a trip a few hours earlier, awoke to sounds of banging on her front and back doors. As Omar relayed in a recent interview with MS NOW, she was confused and disoriented: She and her husband were presented with a search warrant by officers with Homeland Security Investigations, an immigration-enforcement agency that typically pursues crimes such as drug or child trafficking. Over the next several hours, the agents scoured each room of Omar’s home, taking with them seventeen items, including her phones, a daughter’s old cellphone, and her husband’s camera, as well as a Somali-language phrase book.

The following day, anonymous government officials confirmed to reporters that the raid was part of an investigation into potential immigration fraud. The government was building a case to denaturalize and ultimately deport Omar, who was born in Somalia and arrived in the U.S. as a child refugee in 1995 with her family, and who obtained citizenship five years later. The Trump Administration insists that this is not a political move, but the timing of the raid—a few weeks before a heated midterm election—suggests otherwise. Trump claimed that the investigation was spearheaded by the Justice Department and had “nothing to do with me.”

This strains the imagination. For ten years, Trump and Omar, who were first elected to public office on the same night, have sparred with open disdain. Omar described her 2018 congressional victory, in Minnesota’s Fifth District, as “a rejection of Donald Trump’s way of thinking.” The following year, she began to call for his impeachment. Trump, for his part, has accused her of praising Al Qaeda; of launching “vicious antisemitic screeds”; of marrying her brother; of being an “America-hating socialist,” a “disgrace,” a “sick woman,” a jihadist, a piece of human “garbage.” She should be “sent back to Somalia,” he has said.

Perhaps these statements by the President of the United States are incidental to current efforts by the Departments of Justice and Homeland Security to tackle a possibly fraudulent immigration application from more than thirty years ago. Perhaps they are coincidences, as prosecutors build a legitimate case against a sitting congresswoman, who happens to be a Black, Muslim woman in a hijab. But it would not be the first time that Trump has issued a racist threat, and then used the levers of power to make it reality.

Trump began his first term with a clear intent to restrict immigration. It wasn’t difficult to discern his underlying motives. In a major immigration-policy speech ahead of the 2016 election, he promised to “get the right people” by calling for new screening tests—an “ideological certification to make sure that those we are admitting to our country share our values.” He has pursued this mission with furious determination in his second term, too. The number of migrants crossing the southern border has plunged. One of the first executive orders that he signed in January of 2025 effectively ended the U.S. refugee resettlement program. (Later, the Administration made an exception for white South Africans.) Although Joe Biden repealed the Muslim ban when he was in office, Trump announced more expansive restrictions; a recent analysis by the Cato Institute found that visa grants to people from Muslim-majority countries have reached nearly zero.

With the major immigration pipelines blocked off, the Administration turned its attention inward. Somali Americans became a repeated target. They “contribute nothing,” Trump told reporters, this past December, during a Cabinet meeting. “I don’t want them in our country.” Two days later, D.H.S. launched Operation Metro Surge, an aggressive and violent incursion in Minnesota, where much of the Somali diaspora lives. The official rationale was to clamp down on unauthorized immigration and to combat fraud. Greg Bovino, the former U.S. Border Patrol commander who has reportedly described undocumented immigrants as “filth,” “trash,” and “scum,” oversaw the operation; recently, he appeared at an anti-Muslim protest in Michigan alongside the far-right activist Jake Lang, where demonstrators called for the deportation of the Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed (who was born in the United States).

The Trump Administration’s animus has not been limited to the Somali community. On the campaign trail, in 2024, then Senator J. D. Vance claimed that Haitian migrants in Ohio ate pets; this year, the Administration revoked Temporary Protected Status for about three hundred and fifty thousand Haitians. In September, D.H.S. posted (and then deleted) an A.I.-generated image of a “Transformers” character facing off against an Indian Sikh man, with the phrases “America for Americans” and “Self-deport or find out.” But many Indians, like many Somalis, are U.S. citizens, as the Administration discovered during its crackdown in Minnesota.

Even for an agency that has been accused by multiple federal judges of flagrantly violating the law, actually deporting American citizens isn’t so easy. But there is a way to do so: by revoking their citizenship.

This isn’t entirely fantastical. There is considerable precedent for such a policy. In the first half of the twentieth century, as citizenship became a defining feature of nation-states, the U.S. stripped nearly twenty-two thousand people of that privilege. According to the scholar Patrick Weil, this was the most of any democratic country in that era. Political dissent spurred these efforts, as in the case of the activist and anarchist Emma Goldman. So, too, did straightforward racism—a series of exclusionary immigration laws ushered in an official, nativist reading of citizenship. In 1923, several years after a ban on most Asian immigration, the Supreme Court ruled that an Indian man seeking citizenship was racially ineligible for naturalization, in part because of the ban: how could Indians be American citizens if they weren’t even allowed to enter the country anymore? The government went on to denaturalize dozens of Indians living in the U.S.

The Civil Rights era led to the abolition of nationality-based immigration quotas. In 1967, the Court ruled that the Constitution protects “every citizen of this Nation against a congressional forcible destruction of his citizenship, whatever his creed, color, or race.” When denaturalizations did occur, they often involved egregious offenses, such as Nazism, war crimes, or espionage. Denaturalization was a dramatic punishment, and the legal and political consensus was that it must be predicated on a dramatic crime.

The War on Terror moved away from that precedent. In 2010, the government launched a program to find people who may have misrepresented their identities to obtain permanent residency or citizenship. The program, named Operation Janus, initially uncovered three hundred and fifteen thousand instances of missing fingerprint data in immigration files, which were flagged for further investigation. Among those, only a quarter of one per cent revealed potential fraud: people who had been ordered deported and seemed to have used different identities to gain U.S. citizenship.

It was hardly a widespread problem—but it provided an opening for Trump. In 2018, his Administration expanded these efforts, announcing a task force to actively search for people who may have lied on citizenship applications; the following year, he launched his own program, calling it Operation Second Look. The move was relatively quiet, but critics voiced concerns that the effort seemed less like an attempt to protect national security than an attack on naturalization itself. A former D.O.J. attorney warned, in the Times, that “if we’re going after people who did nothing of note, or whose wrong caused no harm, it means they’re going after citizenship.” Fear pervaded immigrant communities, where naturalization was believed to offer irrevocable protection. As reported in The Nation, many immigrants reconsidered getting naturalized at all, afraid of “being targeted or tripped in a lie.” By the end of Trump’s first term, the Justice Department had filed an average of twenty-five denaturalization cases a year.

In the summer of 2025, soon after Trump settled back into Washington, senior officials at the D.O.J. directed their attorneys to make denaturalization a priority. The White House outlined target goals: no fewer than a hundred new cases per month. After a slow start, efforts are ramping up. This past May, there were fifteen cases filed. In early October, the D.O.J. announced that it was moving to strip forty people of citizenship, what it boasted was the “largest denaturalization effort in modern history.” The Attorney General, Todd Blanche, claimed that the objective was to “maintain our national security and protect the American people.”

Trump is not the first President in recent decades to have enacted discriminatory national-security policies. In the aftermath of September 11th, the Bush Administration implemented a national registry that required immigrant boys and men from twenty-four Muslim-majority countries to register with the government. The aim was to search for ties to terrorism; the government ended up funnelling thousands of Muslims into deportation proceedings on mostly minor visa infractions. Later, the Obama Administration excluded dual nationals of four Muslim-majority countries from a visa waiver program, restricting their entry to the U.S.

Cassandra Burke Robertson, a professor of law at Case Western Reserve University who studies citizenship, told me that recent denaturalization efforts are nevertheless a departure from modern Presidencies, even from the veneer of Trump’s attempt, in his first term, to ban Muslim immigrants for the ostensible reason of keeping the nation safe. There is no window dressing this time. “The Trump Administration is the first that we’ve seen using denaturalization as an end goal in and of itself, not as a means of something else,” Robertson said.

In December, 1991, Parvez Manzoor Khan, a man in his thirties who hardly spoke English, journeyed from Pakistan to the United States to visit his brother. He presented a doctored passport at the border, which he acknowledged bore a name that was not his. He was briefly detained, then released on bond. He later found work as a truck driver, in Florida; married a U.S. citizen; and became a citizen himself, in 2006. When Operation Janus revealed a discrepancy between the fingerprints in his immigration files, authorities questioned Khan, and he again admitted that he had entered through fraudulent means. In 2017, the Trump Administration brought a denaturalization suit against Khan, who by then had been living in the U.S. for nearly three decades, and had become a grandfather.

A federal court eventually sided with the government, allowing it to strip Khan of his citizenship. James LaVigne, an immigration lawyer who defended Khan in court, told me that the government was successful in part because it had such strong evidence of misconduct, including a copy of the doctored passport, which Khan confessed to using, and the fingerprint discrepancy. Khan also had been ordered deported not long after he arrived, for missing an asylum hearing. (He never got the notice to appear for it, nor was he made aware of a deportation order.)

The case of Ilhan Omar is far less clear. No evidence has yet been presented to the public that she used a false identity to enter the United States, or that she has ever been ordered deported. According to initial reports, the case hinges on the possibility that, when Omar received U.S. citizenship through her father, she was not seventeen years old, as she claimed, but eighteen, which would’ve meant that she needed to pursue a citizenship application on her own. Trump allies have dredged up another allegation, too, long peddled by the MAGA crowd: that she may have later married her brother to help him secure permanent residency. A recent Times story quotes several anonymous former and current government officials who attribute some credibility to this claim, though they did not offer any specific evidence, and Omar has denied the allegation. (How this relates to her own citizenship status, if it does at all, remains hazy.) Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin intimated, in an interview on “The Charlie Kirk Show,” that the government could bring racketeering charges against Omar and anyone who abetted her if it is found that she procured citizenship through fraud. Increasingly, the Administration appears to be hunting for a crime to punish.

Even in cases where fraud is clear, denaturalization does not automatically result in deportation. LaVigne, for example, was able to fight for Khan to retain his permanent residency and remain in the U.S. after his citizenship was stripped, in part because the government chose not to pursue deportation. As for Omar, the President and his circle have openly called for expelling her from the country. Recently, Trump suggested that she could even go to prison. “I have some serious issues with the constitutionality of what is going on,” LaVigne told me. “I say that as a registered Republican. I don’t like what I see. It’s supposed to be a nation of law, not of men.”

The government continues to expend financial resources and manpower on the case. As the writer M. Gessen noted, in The New Yorker, in 2018, “just about every naturalized citizen might look like an outlaw, or a liar,” if inspected closely enough. Still, few legal experts believe that the Administration will succeed in unearthing definitive evidence against Omar. Her father is dead. And establishing that Omar or her family deliberately lied about her age would be complicated, because birth records are practically nonexistent in Somalia.

Even if the investigation fails to result in Omar’s denaturalization, it may provide Trump a victory of a different kind. Among the President’s many allegations against Omar—that she is a jihadist, or married to her brother, or guilty of fraud—is one underlying theme: that she is not really an American. According to Trump, Omar’s disgust with him, and with Republican policies, suggests that she “hates our country.” In this view, the parameters for citizenship are not national security or public safety but loyalty.

No wonder, then, that at a recent rally in Michigan to campaign for Mike Rogers, the Republican candidate for Senate, Trump stood alongside David Beamer, whose son died on one of the hijacked planes on September 11th, as he excoriated Rogers’s opponent, Abdul El-Sayed. “The enemy is right here among us—local terrorists, local citizens that want to demolish our country,” Beamer said. “Abdul has a birth certificate. The birth certificate says he’s a citizen of America. You know what? A birth certificate doesn’t make you an American.” ♦

title: ACLU requests investigation into claim that ICE officer slashed tire - USA Today
description:
"We observe and record public ICE activity in order to shine a light on their abusive behavior and to create a record of what our government is up to.
The ACLU in filing the complaint asked DHS and ICE to investigate, preserve all evidence of the incident and discipline the officers involved.
USA TODAY has reached out to DHS and ICE for comment on the incident and the ACLU complaint.
According to the ACLU complaint, the observers had been following the ICE officers and alerting the neighborhood to their presence.
"Like many people across the country, our clients have been observing and recording ICE activity in their community.
text:
The American Civil Liberties Union on Thursday, Oct. 29, filed a complaint with the Department of Homeland Security on behalf of a pair of people who said an ICE officer slashed their tire while they were acting as legal observers.

The ACLU also released video footage of the Oct. 7 incident in the suburbs of Portland, Oregon. Footage recorded by the legal observers shows ICE officers drive up alongside their stopped car, and a masked officer hops out and quickly uses a knife to stab multiple holes in the wall of one of the car’s rear tires before driving away without speaking to the observers. The complaint says the observers were stopped at a traffic light.

"What happened to us is not unique, and that is what is so terrifying," the legal observers, who were in the car together, said in a statement shared by the American Civil Liberties Union. "We observe and record public ICE activity in order to shine a light on their abusive behavior and to create a record of what our government is up to. Because of that, they are terrorizing us and anyone else who dares to exercise their First Amendment right to hold our government accountable."

The ACLU in filing the complaint asked DHS and ICE to investigate, preserve all evidence of the incident and discipline the officers involved. The prominent constitutional rights group did not share the names of the people involved in the incident.

USA TODAY has reached out to DHS and ICE for comment on the incident and the ACLU complaint.

The incident out of Oregon came amid a surge of immigration enforcement activity in the area in early October. According to the ACLU complaint, the observers had been following the ICE officers and alerting the neighborhood to their presence. The ACLU said both actions are protected by the Constitution.

According to the ACLU, the incident is not unique but part of a host of actions by ICE officers aimed at scaring people from recording their enforcement activity. The ACLU has brought cases against DHS over their tactics in courts from Memphis, Tennessee, to Los Angeles.

"The right to record publicly visible law enforcement activity is fundamental to our democracy," said Scarlet Kim, an ACLU senior staff attorney. "Like many people across the country, our clients have been observing and recording ICE activity in their community. These videos have proven critical to exposing ICE’s abuses. If we cannot see and document what our own government is doing on our streets, we cannot hold it accountable for running roughshod over our rights."

title: Congressional Democrats send scathing letter to ICE and DHS decrying treatment of hunger strikers
description:
Detained immigrants on hunger strike say the facility has substandard medical care, undrinkable water and guards that mistreat them.
“Whether they arose through indifference or inability, such conditions violate the … DHS and ... ICE documented detention standards,” the letter said.
In past weeks, senators from Georgia have similarly expressed concern about an ongoing hunger strike at the Folkston ICE detention center complex in their state.
The DHS denies the hunger strikers in Georgia have been threatened.
One of the hunger strikers is Inna Eremeeva, an asylum seeker from Russia.
text:
Members of Congress sent a scathing letter to federal immigration officials this week demanding answers about conditions inside a Texas immigration jail, as detained immigrants on a prolonged hunger strike claim officials are retaliating against them and threatening them with force-feeding.

A group of seven congressional Democrats sent the letter earlier this week to Markwayne Mullin, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) secretary, and David Venturella, the Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) acting director, protesting about the treatment of hunger strikers.

The El Valle detention facility in Raymondville, Texas, detaining men and women, has fallen under scrutiny in recent weeks for allegations of harsh conditions. Detained immigrants on hunger strike say the facility has substandard medical care, undrinkable water and guards that mistreat them. Some hunger strikers are also protesting against their prolonged detention and are asking for their cases to move more quickly or to be transferred closer to loved ones in other parts of the country.

“It is abundantly clear that DHS continues to demonstrate gross disregard for the health, dignity, personhood, and safety of our communities,” the group of lawmakers, led by the Illinois representative Delia Ramirez, said in their letter to the DHS and ICE. “However, we remain committed to conducting oversight, advocating for our constituents, and pursuing accountability.”

The representatives “unequivocally condemn” conditions reported at the facility.

“Whether they arose through indifference or inability, such conditions violate the … DHS and ... ICE documented detention standards,” the letter said.

“It’s clear that DHS continues to demonstrate gross disregard for our health, dignity, personhood, and the safety of our communities,” Ramirez posted on X.

The congressional letter comes as the number of people detained by ICE increases amid the Trump administration’s aggressive but quieter anti-immigrant crackdown.

In past weeks, senators from Georgia have similarly expressed concern about an ongoing hunger strike at the Folkston ICE detention center complex in their state. The Guardian reported last week that a man detained there died, even as allegations surfaced of force-feeding threats. The DHS denies the hunger strikers in Georgia have been threatened.

The latest letter, signed by Representatives Ramirez, Texas’s Greg Casar and Jasmine Crockett and others, also demands details about the detainee population, the quality of medical care and more.

“People should not be detained in these horrific detention centers – the hunger strikers should be released to their families and we demand that they receive protection from further detention and deportation,” the representatives wrote. “We also demand that you refrain from force-feeding any person in your custody.”

In a statement, a DHS spokesperson said that the department responds to official correspondence through official channels and added that the representatives “should be thanking our law enforcement for removing these dangerous criminals from their districts – NOT vilifying law enforcement”.

The DHS did not provide proof that the detainees participating in the strike, whose relatives spoke with the Guardian, have any criminal history.

El Valle is owned by the Willacy County Local Government Corporation and operated by the private prison company Management and Training Corporation (MTC). The local government corporation did not respond to a request for comment. MTC referred all questions to ICE.

The Guardian spoke with three relatives of asylum seekers detained in El Valle, who have all been detained for nearly a year and are participating in the strike, which is approaching three weeks.

On 11 October, detained immigrants inside the El Valle facility launched the hunger strike. More than two dozen immigrants, from Russia, Cameroon and other countries, first participated, according to family members and advocates.

There are now four women and 10 to 20 men still participating in the strike, family members said.

One of the hunger strikers is Inna Eremeeva, an asylum seeker from Russia.

While in detention, “she started having serious pain in her legs and her hips”, Eremeeva’s husband, Alexei, said through an interpreter. “She feels a growth in her private areas. She has been declined any medical care to figure out what is going on.”

Alexei also said that officials earlier told hunger-striking women they would be transferred to another ICE facility to be force-fed. Other ICE detention centers in Texas have been used to force-feed detainees.

In a statement, an ICE spokesperson said that “allegations that detainees are being threatened are FALSE. No detainees are being force fed or threatened with force feeding.

“During hunger strikes, ICE continues to provide three meals a day, delivered to the detained alien’s room, and an adequate supply of drinking water or other beverages,” ICE added. “ICE is committed to ensuring the safety, security, and well-being of all individuals in its custody.”

Eremeeva arrived in the US in 2024 and requested asylum. In November 2025, during one of Eremeeva’s work trips as a truck driver, she was stopped at a border patrol checkpoint in Texas and arrested by officials. She has been in detention since.

The DHS said in a statement that Eremeeva entered the US “using the disastrous Biden administration CBP One app”, which was used to process asylum seekers and “released in the country completely unvetted”. Eremeeva remains in detention as she challenges ICE’s attempts to deport her.

“People are feeling hopeless and desperate in the black hole of ICE detention,” said Savannah Kumar, a staff attorney at the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU) of Texas. “People in immigration detention centers across the country have had to resort to hunger strikes because they are caged in conditions that feel unsurvivable.”

Amaliia Gilmutdinova’s husband, Shokhrukh Abdullaev, is also detained and participating in the strike. Abdullaev also worked as a truck driver and was arrested in November 2025 at a checkpoint in Texas. He entered the country in September 2021 using the CBP One app, the DHS said.

“He is very afraid to say anything,” Gilmutdinova said about her husband through an interpreter. “He is very much afraid of being put back in isolation.”

Another man, whose daughter requested their names not be shared for fear of retaliation, is 63 years old and struggles with various health problems. He is participating in the hunger strike. The man calls his daughter frequently with panic attacks and she guides him through breathing exercises to calm him down, she said.

Kumar from the ACLU of Texas added that ICE “essentially locks people up away from their families indefinitely”, pointing to a recent fifth circuit court decision that ICE detainees in Texas, Louisiana and Mississippi do not have the right to seek release on bond.

According to the 63-year-old man’s daughter, “the only thing he wants is to be able to see his family. He wants to be transferred.

“He is like a child, asking: ‘Why am I here? I didn’t do anything’,” she added.

After the deaths of protesters Renee Good and Alex Pretti, who were shot by federal agents just weeks apart in Minneapolis, nine progressive prosecutors formed the Fight Against Federal Overreach to support prosecution of immigration officers who may have violated state law.

text:
The prosecutor overseeing Utah’s largest county led a national conversation this summer on bringing charges against federal immigration officers who violate state laws as U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement arrests soar across the country.

Salt Lake County District Attorney Sim Gill, a first-generation immigrant from India, delivered a presentation to the Major County Prosecutors Council in July with legal guidance on how to hold ICE agents accountable for alleged infringements of citizens’ rights.

This is a key issue for the reform-oriented attorney running for a fifth term. While his Republican opponent, Kent Davis, has framed the race in terms of restoring trust in the rule of law, Gill believes that one way to do this is upholding constitutional limits on federal power.

“Here’s the bottom line: ICE does not get to violate rights of our citizens,” Gill told the Deseret News. “We’re still living in America, which is ruled by the Constitution and the law, and I am committed to that.”

Gill’s workshop answered questions about when immunity applies to federal agents carrying out administrative functions. States cannot impede legitimate exercises of federal authority, he outlined. This depends on whether an officer has acted on an objectively reasonable basis.

After the deaths of protesters Renee Good and Alex Pretti, who were shot by federal agents just weeks apart in Minneapolis, nine progressive prosecutors formed the Fight Against Federal Overreach to support prosecution of immigration officers who may have violated state law.

The elected prosecutor in Minneapolis, Mary Moriarty, a member of the organization, filed charges against two agents earlier this year.

Gill is not a member of the coalition, but he said he plans to continue discussions on the topic with a collection of county prosecutors during their January meeting. Gill’s concern about the impact of ICE operations on his jurisdiction has only increased since the July seminar.

ICE arrests surge in Utah

Utah ICE apprehensions spiked to a record 613 in June, following a brief decline since a December high of 511, according to totals published by the Deportation Data Project, which calculates state-by-state arrests based on government responses to public information requests.

The number of Utah arrests conducted by the Trump administration in July, 548, is roughly five times the average monthly figure under President Joe Biden. Nationwide, the number of monthly arrests has rocketed from 8,603 in December 2024 to 49,571 in July 2026.

Around half of July arrests were of immigrants with no criminal charges. In Utah, where a dozen police agencies have 287(g) agreements with ICE to facilitate the deportation of immigrants in the country illegally who broke additional laws, the ratio was closer to one-third.

While public deportation data only extends through July, there are signs the rate continues to speed up. ICE deportation and transfer flights from Salt Lake City have nearly tripled since June, the Human Rights First tracker found, with more than three flights occurring weekly.

Gill does not seek to obstruct President Donald Trump’s deportation of immigrants in the country illegally, he said. But he fears that surging ICE activity creates a chilling effect among immigrant residents, including citizens, who are now afraid to come forward with criminal complaints.

“My fundamental concern is the safety of my community,” Gill said. “Our goal is not to interfere with anyone, but nor turn a blind eye to a blatant violation of constitutional rights of all our citizens.”

In a statement to the Deseret News, Davis said ICE agents should be treated equally under Utah law. The district attorney has no place in civil immigration enforcement, he said, expressing a similar focus on ensuring victims report crimes regardless of their status.

Differences between the two candidates hinge on how best to address criminal recidivism in the county.

Do DAs address homelessness?

As Gill’s deputy district attorney from 2017 to 2021, Davis has focused his attacks on the inner workings of the office, not on partisan disagreements over whether Gill is “soft on crime.” But a recent audit, which Davis said inspired his bid, suggests the two may be linked.

In December 2025, state legislative auditors released a report finding around half of the felony cases declined by Gill’s office lacked a detailed explanation for the dismissal. A similar pattern was observed among plea deal agreements where charges were reduced.

The biggest takeaway from the audit for Davis was that the diversion programs created by Gill as alternatives to incarceration do not keep track of criminal recidivism for participants who later reoffend. This can contribute to a “revolving door” of criminal activity, according to Davis.

“I want written standards, documented decisions and regularly published performance metrics,” Davis said.

The criticism is outweighed by outcomes under his watch, according to Gill. His dedication to reforming the criminal justice system without compromising safety is vindicated, he said, by Salt Lake crime falling to the lowest level in a decade, though some violent crime is up.

These results blow through the false binary between building alternatives to prison and being “tough on crime,” Gill said, pointing out that his office has a higher than average filing rate and claiming that violent offenders are never referred for pre-filing diversion.

During his 16 years in office, Gill has led out on finding solutions to the persistent problem posed by “high utilizers,” individuals who are often chronically homeless and who take up the majority of police resources, according to Salt Lake City Mayor Erin Mendenhall.

“He’s been, not only key, but instrumental in rethinking the approach,” Mendenhall told the Deseret News.

In stark contrast to the characterizations found in the audit, Mendenhall said Gill has been more “hands-on” with dangerous felons than other prosecutors, even as he helps the city to brainstorm ways to coordinate services to help those with underlying disorders.

A search warrant aimed at obtaining evidence following the Oct. 10 crash in which an ICE agent hit a Houston immigrant with his SUV during a chase has revealed the range of charges Harris County prosecutors could pursue with a grand jury in the case.

Prosecutors could seek aggravated assault — which District Attorney Sean Teare already said he thought the northwest Houston incident amounted to — or a misdemeanor offense of reckless driving against the ICE agent who struck 48-year-old Miguel Parra Hernandez as he fled on foot, according to an investigator's Oct. 15 sworn affidavit.

Teare has openly discussed aspects of the Harris County Sheriff's Office investigation detailed in the search warrant during an array of media interviews, even saying the agent ran Parra Hernandez down and hit him. The agent, whom Teare's office identified by his first initial and surname, was behind the wheel of an unmarked Jeep Grand Cherokee as he gave chase to Parra Hernandez and another man around 7:30 a.m., near the intersection of state Highway 6 and Clay Road. Parra Hernandez was hit in a strip mall parking lot. One of his legs was broken as the agent drove over him. The other man escaped on foot.

The warrant was signed by a state district court judge days after Harris County investigators failed to obtain evidence from the agent's Jeep in the form of event data recorders — which track information such as GPS coordinates and the vehicle's speed and direction at any given time — before federal authorities drove the vehicle back to their field office "without authorization."

A sheriff's office captain contacted Houston's ICE field director, Gabriel Martinez, only to be told the vehicle would remain at their field office — which the captain said was behind a "secured locked gate."

COURTHOUSE NEWS: Key witness in ICE shooting of Lorenzo Salgado seen entering grand jury room

The district attorney's office sent the warrant to the Department of Homeland Security. Although the federal office acknowledged the warrant and their plan to forward it to their legal team, Teare's office never heard back.

"Access to 2025 Jeep Grand Cherokee has not been provided — no search of vehicle," the investigator wrote Oct. 23 in the search warrant's return and inventory.

The basis of the warrant contends a Harris County Sheriff's Office deputy dispatched to the crash site learned from the agent that he was looking for "Jose Mendoza," whom he was following on Highway 6. The agent said the truck turned "the wrong way" onto Clay Road and came to a stop. The occupants then fled on foot into a parking lot.

The agent said he drove over the median, crossed the street and went toward them. He then "struck Mr. Hernandez with the front driver side of the Jeep and rolled over" him, according to the search warrant.

The agent's account of what happened makes no mention that he was chasing the truck's occupants.

After watching surveillance footage of the crash from a nearby business, Teare's investigator observed that the agent accelerated toward Parra Hernandez, made a "clear turn to the left" and lined up his vehicle straight toward Parra Hernandez.

The agent then struck Parra Hernandez, who had his back to the Jeep as he was running away, the investigator wrote.

At the time of the crash, Teare's office was already reviewing the July 7 shooting death of Lorenzo Salgado Araujo during an East End chase that remains before a grand jury. The term for the grand jury hearing evidence in that case ends Friday, but Texas statutes allow the grand jury to extend their time.

text:
U.S. Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin announced Thursday in Dallas that a 10-day statewide immigration enforcement operation in Texas resulted in 4,170 arrests.

The operation, called Lone Star Mission, involved partnerships between federal immigration officers and Texas sheriff’s offices and police departments. Mullin said more than 60% of those arrested had criminal backgrounds, including convictions involving murder, sexual assault, drunken driving and immigrant smuggling.

“They should have never been on our streets. We were able to make the Lone Star State safer,” Mullin said.

Flanked by Enforcement and Removal Operations field office directors from Dallas, Houston, San Antonio, El Paso and Harlingen, Mullin said the operation allowed officers to locate people they had been trying to find for some time.

“Most of these individuals are looking for, for quite some time, but we just didn't have the resources to be able to go in and do a pattern of life on the individuals, make sure we know where they live, know where they work out,” Mullin said.

879 arrests in North Texas

Of the 4,170 arrests statewide, 879 occurred in North Texas.

One person arrested in Dallas was Orlando Aguilar, a Mexican national taken into custody by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement on Saturday. His convictions include felony intoxication assault involving a vehicle that caused serious bodily injury and driving while intoxicated.

Mullin said officers worked with local law enforcement agencies to carry out arrests involving people with outstanding warrants.

He also said 40% of those arrested did not have criminal records. Mullin referred to those individuals as “collateral criminals,” explaining that they were not necessarily the intended targets of the enforcement actions.

“They may not been the target, but they were in the vehicle, they were in a house, or wherever the warrant was served at,” Mullin said.

Homeland Security secretary says enforcement will continue

Mullin said Texas Enforcement and Removal Operations officers took more than 136,000 criminals into custody from October 2025 through Sept. 30, 2026.

Asked whether North Texans and Americans should expect increased immigration enforcement over the next couple of years, Mullin said targeted enforcement would continue, while noting that officers are working within available resources.

“So that type of target enforcing you're going to continue to see but we work as hard as we can with the resources we have, so increase, we're working as hard as we can,” Mullin said.

text:
Nearly 40 House Democrats appear to have shunned an effort by their colleagues to end the federal probe into Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn.

House Democrats led by Rep. Pramila Jayapal, D-Wash., sent a letter to the Trump administration earlier this week demanding a stop to the investigation into Omar’s immigration paperwork, arguing it was a bid to sway her re-election campaign ahead of Tuesday’s midterm Election Day.

The letter was backed by some 175 House Democrats, more than two-thirds of the caucus — though some notable names were left off.

Two of three of House Democrats’ previous senior leadership did not sign the letter. Former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif., and former House Majority Leader Steny Hoyer, D-Md., did not sign on. Rep. Jim Clyburn, D-S.C., who previously served as House majority whip, was among the signatories, along with all three current members of House Democratic leadership.

175 DEMOCRATS DEMAND TRUMP ADMIN STOP ILHAN OMAR INVESTIGATION, WARN IT COULD HURT HER RE-ELECTION BID

Both Pelosi and Hoyer are retiring, but it’s worth noting that nearing the exit did not stop other outgoing members like Rep. Nydia Velazquez, D-N.Y., from signing the letter.

THE HITCHHIKER’S GUIDE TO WHY REMOVING ILHAN OMAR FROM CONGRESS COULD BE HARDER THAN TRUMP EXPECTS

Democrats running in tight races also kept their distance from the public condemnation of the probe. Reps. Henry Cuellar, D-Texas, Tom Suozzi, D-N.Y., Marie Gluesenkamp Perez, D-Wash., and Don Davis, D-N.C., are among the names left off the letter as well.

Fox News Digital reached out to each of them for comment but did not immediately hear back.

ILHAN OMAR BELIEVES TRUMP RAID ON HOME WAS MEANT TO ‘INTIMIDATE AND SCARE PEOPLE’ FROM VOTING

“Congresswoman Omar is seeking reelection in Minnesota’s 5th congressional district in just one week. News of the search warrant, whether properly predicated or not, could affect voters’ decisions, which is exactly why federal law enforcement should not engage in such conduct when voters are casting their ballots. This type of interference strips Minnesotans of their right to a free and fair election guaranteed to them under the Constitution,” the letter said.

“We stand with Congresswoman Omar and condemn the weaponization of law enforcement against her. You have already disgraced the offices you hold, and we demand you refrain from taking any further actions that could affect the outcome of the upcoming election.”

ILHAN OMAR SHOULD BE JAILED, DEPORTED IF CITIZENSHIP FRAUD PROVEN, TOP HOUSE REPUBLICAN SAYS

Omar is under federal investigation over allegations she or her father lied about her birth year on immigration paperwork to obtain her citizenship when her family fled Somalia in the late 1990s. If she was 17 when her father obtained citizenship, as previously thought, she would have automatically qualified along with him. If she was 18 or older, which federal officials now suspect, she would have had to make her own application.

Her fellow House Democrats recounted the allegations in their letter, saying, “Your probe into the congresswoman reportedly concerns her late father’s filing of immigration paperwork after she fled Somalia’s civil war at age eight, making her a U.S. citizen at age seventeen.”

But they argued it does not justify “a pre-dawn raid on her home for paperwork her father filed when she was a minor.”

Federal agents executed a judicially authorized search warrant on Omar’s home on Oct. 12, seizing multiple phones and notebooks, among other items.

text:
KUALA LUMPUR: Malaysia must adopt a more comprehensive approach to tackle illegal immigration, as repatriating undocumented foreign nationals alone will not provide a lasting solution, says Tan Sri Lee Lam Thye.

The Alliance for a Safe Community chairman said repatriating 45,597 foreign nationals in the first nine months of this year was a significant step that would help ease overcrowding at immigration detention depots.

However, he said the focus must also be on preventing the problem from recurring by dismantling human smuggling syndicates and taking action against those who facilitate and profit from illegal immigration.

"If the syndicates, middlemen, unscrupulous recruitment agents and employers who facilitate and profit from illegal immigration are not effectively dealt with, undocumented migrants will continue finding ways to enter and remain in the country," he said when contacted on Friday (Oct 30).

Lee said Malaysia needed an integrated strategy involving stronger enforcement, improved border security, better detention depot management, a review of foreign worker recruitment practices and greater regional cooperation.

He said enforcement efforts should focus on the masterminds behind illegal immigration, including networks involved in human smuggling and trafficking, providing fake documents, facilitating illegal border crossings and arranging unlawful employment.

He also stressed that employers who knowingly hired undocumented workers must be held accountable, rather than allowing action to focus solely on the migrants.

On border security, Lee called for greater use of modern surveillance technology, intelligence-sharing and coordinated operations involving the Immigration Department, police, Malaysian Maritime Enforcement Agency and other relevant agencies.

He said vulnerable entry points, particularly along coastal areas and land borders, required greater attention.

Lee also called for improvements to immigration detention depot management, stressing that the welfare, safety, health and human dignity of detainees must not be overlooked.

"Overcrowding, inadequate sanitation, insufficient medical attention and prolonged detention are matters requiring urgent attention.

"Every detainee should receive proper medical screening, timely healthcare, adequate food and clean living conditions," he said.

He proposed a more efficient digital case management system to monitor detainees' identities, legal status, documentation and repatriation arrangements.

Independent monitoring and greater transparency should also be encouraged to ensure accountability and prevent misconduct, he added.

Lee said the Government should also review the foreign worker recruitment and employment system by addressing weaknesses in existing channels, improving accountability among recruitment agencies and reducing opportunities for exploitation.

A properly regulated foreign worker system, he said, would help reduce demand for undocumented labour.

He further called for stronger cooperation with neighbouring countries, particularly in intelligence-sharing, border surveillance, identification and repatriation arrangements, noting that illegal immigration and human smuggling were transnational issues.

Lee emphasised that firm immigration enforcement and respect for human rights were not mutually exclusive.

"Malaysia has every right and responsibility to protect its national sovereignty, security and the integrity of its immigration system.

"At the same time, all individuals in detention must be treated humanely and with dignity, regardless of their immigration status," he said.

He said the success of the country's immigration policy should not be measured solely by the number of undocumented migrants arrested or repatriated, but by how effectively illegal entry was prevented, smuggling networks dismantled and opportunities for illegal employment eliminated.

"Malaysia needs a sustainable solution, not merely a temporary reduction in the number of undocumented migrants in the country," he added.

SCOTT DETROW, HOST:

A new term at the Supreme Court is just getting started, but one theme is already clear. Immigration will dominate the justices' time. NPR's Carrie Johnson reports.

CARRIE JOHNSON, BYLINE: University of Virginia law professor Amanda Frost counts a half dozen immigration cases on the high court calendar, with more on the way.

AMANDA FROST: It's looking to be a blockbuster term for immigration law.

JOHNSON: She says the Trump administration has been pushing the envelope to stretch old laws to do drastic new things.

FROST: This administration is trying to rewrite immigration law without actually getting Congress to do so.

JOHNSON: Congress has failed to act on immigration for decades. So presidents from both parties have used executive action to advance their agenda. Chad Maisel, a former official in the Trump Justice Department, says immigration has been top of mind for the president since his first political campaign.

CHAD MAISEL: Part of the reason why we're seeing so much of this is that that was Trump's promise to the American people that he was going to take border enforcement seriously.

JOHNSON: A Justice Department spokesman says the administration's approach is, quote, "grounded in common sense measures that uphold both the law and the integrity of our borders." Chad Maisel says if history is a guide, the president and his policies are in line for some significant victories.

MAISEL: The president has an unprecedented track record of success at the Supreme Court and nowhere is that more true than when we're talking about the immigration docket and the immigration cases.

JOHNSON: But civil liberties and immigrant rights groups say the human cost of Trump's tough enforcement could be devastating. Trina Realmuto is executive director at the National Immigration Litigation Alliance. She's been fighting for migrants at risk of being deported to third countries where they have no prior ties.

TRINA REALMUTO: They have families, they have jobs, and under this policy, they are being abruptly and suddenly ripped from their communities and their loved ones and being sent to third countries.

JOHNSON: A lower court judge has ruled the migrants need a chance to argue they could face torture or persecution before they're deported. But the Supreme Court has repeatedly bigfooted that judge in Massachusetts and allowed those deportations to proceed for now. The administration says it won assurances from third countries that the migrants will not be abused. But Trina Realmuto says her class members have routinely described being detained abroad by armed guards in what she calls horrendous living conditions.

REALMUTO: What we know is that those so-called assurances aren't worth the piece of paper that they're written on.

JOHNSON: The justices are set to hear the case about third country removals in December. Legal experts say a separate immigration case will be among the most important of the term. That case revolves around the president's effort to use mandatory detention for migrants without giving them access to a bond hearing. Michael Tan of the American Civil Liberties Union explains.

MICHAEL TAN: The policy at issue in these cases is truly a radical break with the law. For decades, it's been universally understood, including by the first Trump administration, that immigrants who are living in the country and detained for a deportation proceeding generally have the right to seek release at a bond hearing before an immigration judge.

JOHNSON: Last July, Tan says, the Trump administration declared those immigrants would be locked up even if they were in the process of seeking legal status.

TAN: If allowed, this rule would literally subject millions of immigrants to mandatory detention, amounting to the largest mandatory detention regime in U.S. history.

JOHNSON: Meanwhile the solicitor general has asked the justices to accept another set of immigration cases about an effort to revoke visas for scholars at Georgetown and Columbia University. The administration says their presence in the U.S. compromises the nation's foreign policy. They say they were being targeted for their speech, which should be protected by the First Amendment. Former Columbia student Mahmoud Khalil put it this way recently.

(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)

MAHMOUD KHALIL: Our question is simple. Can the government weaponize immigration laws to punish someone's speech, then tell federal court that they have no power to step in?

JOHNSON: The high court could weigh whether to hear the case sometime next year. Carrie Johnson, NPR News.

(SOUNDBITE OF EMOTIONAL ORANGES SONG, "TALK ABOUT US") Transcript provided by NPR, Copyright NPR.

text:
A deported immigrant who was profiled in a CalMatters story earlier this week failed to disclose his criminal record and deportation history to the news organization.

CalMatters learned of his background through a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement social media post attacking the news organization Thursday.

ICE’s X (Twitter) account said Luis Arreguin had been deported five times and had “a criminal history including aggravated assault with a weapon, firearms offenses, and DUI,” and said that CalMatters failed to include that context in its story published Wednesday.

CalMatters editor in chief Kristen Go said the nonprofit news outlet’s reporter tried, twice, to reach ICE’s media team over a period of six days, with no response. The reporter also looked into Arreguin’s background in a court database and a public records database, neither of which turned up the records ICE described.

“We always want to believe what our sources tell us, but as journalists, we also take steps to verify that information,” Go said. “In this case, we did a background check and reached out to ICE two times. It wasn’t until after our story ran that ICE decided to provide the information we had requested.

“We believe in transparency from the people we cover and extend that standard to our reporting as well.”

Arreguin was arrested on an assault charge in Fresno County one year ago. The District Attorney’s Office declined to prosecute him and did not press charges, a spokesperson said.

The reporter, Wendy Fry, sent ICE’s media team seven questions about Arreguin’s immigration history on the evening of Oct. 21 seeking the legal basis for Arreguin’s deportation and the basic facts of his detention.

“We did not find any recent criminal history for Mr. Arreguin, did ICE or the federal government consider him a threat to public safety. If so, why?” Fry asked in the email.

The rest of the questions sought to confirm elements of Arreguin’s account of his detention and deportation flight.

Fry sent a follow-up email to ICE the following Tuesday “Circling this back on top. Our story is publishing tomorrow.”

Go said Fry received no response to those questions.

In her story, Fry quoted Arreguin family members, who repeated his account. CalMatters has reached out to them, and to Arreguin, for comment but has received no response.

Reached Thursday, Arreguin’s daughter said her father was focused on describing his ordeal in his interview with the reporter and did not intend to conceal his deportation and criminal history.

On Thursday, a day after Fry’s story published, a Fox News reporter wrote on social media that he was told by sources in the federal government that Arreguin has been deported five times.

Exactly 30 minutes later, ICE quoted the Fox News reporter’s message in its own social media post.

“We’d like to believe that government agencies operate in good faith — but there is a valid question as to why ICE waited until after publication and even so, (did) not contact the reporter directly,” Go said.

ICE did not immediately respond to questions about its response from CalMatters, or whether the social media team has access to records that are unavailable to the media team responding to reporter requests.

The agency has still not responded to Fry’s initial questions.

Edward Wasserman, a journalism professor and former dean of UC Berkeley Graduate School of Journalism, said it’s impossible to know whether an agency as large as ICE “deliberately stonewalled.”

“It’s dangerous to speculate whether they had a motive,” Wasserman said.

From a “hard-nosed PR perspective,” Wasserman said, the strategy of releasing information after a story published doesn’t help an agency’s cause.

“It doesn’t really serve their own purposes,” he said.

text:
By Dan Israel/Hudson County View

On July 24th, Jersey City resident Raul Raagas, 62, was pulled over for a traffic violation in Palisades Park before being arrested and transferred to the Hudson County Correctional Facility (HCCF) in Kearny on an outstanding warrant for failing to pay child support.

While Raagas was later released the same day after a virtual court hearing, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detained him shortly afterwards. He was taken to an ICE processing center before being transferred to the CoreCivic Elizabeth Detention Center in Elizabeth.

On August 21st, Raagas was transferred to the Adams County Correctional Center in Mississippi.

After 10 weeks in ICE custody, Raagas was eventually granted bond on September 30th, and is now back home in Jersey City.

Hudson County Executive Craig Guy told HCV he was first notified back in September that an inmate at the Hudson County Correctional Facility was improperly transferred by Correctional Center staff to the custody of ICE agents.

Guy said he subsequently requested a thorough investigation of the incident, to be conducted by both the Hudson County Law Department and the Department of Corrections.

According to Guy, the investigation confirmed Corrections Department personnel notified ICE and facilitated the transfer of the inmate to ICE.

Guy underscored not only that this was in violation of the State of New Jersey’s Immigrant Trust Directive, but also his executive order banning federal immigration authorities from county-owned property, as HCV first reported.

As for the corrections officers involved? Their discipline is still pending but they have been reassigned, Guy said.

“We are currently exploring disciplinary actions for the personnel involved in this investigation and have taken immediate corrective action in assigning the personnel in question to a new post. I take the results of this investigation very seriously,” Guy said in a statement.

“Hudson County has been at the forefront of protecting the most vulnerable members of our community, from developing Executive Orders to keep our communities safe from unlawful federal immigration tactics to bolstering the county budget with funding for constituent legal services, rental assistance, and food security programs.”

Guy touted actions his administration has taken against ICE, including forming two committees on the topic- the Safe Communities Committee and the Immigrant Community Safety Committee, as well as adopting a $1.3 million budget amendment which was approved by the board and pushed by Guy after advocates rallied for $2 million to provide rental assistance, legal services, and food security programs.

According to Guy, as a result of this investigation the Corrections Department has strengthened its procedures and begun additional training.

He said the department also established new policy guidelines such as supervisory review, senior leadership approval, documentation requirements, and controls over ICE access to the facility.

Additionally, Guy said he has ordered an investigation into all of ICE’s interactions with the Corrections Department since the implementation of his executive order banning federal immigration authorities from county-owned property.

“We are committed to full transparency and reinforcing our policies to ensure federal immigration authorities follow the law when conducting operations,” he added.
